items.title: Researchers dispute whether AI has passed the Turing test
items.summary: The Turing test was proposed by British mathematician Alan Turing in 1950 as a way of assessing whether a machine could demonstrate humanlike intelligence. In its best-known form, a person communicates with both a human and a machine without knowing which is which and tries to identify the machine.

items.title: NightOwl for Firefox: True Dark Mode for Every Website (Even Sites Without CSS Dark Mode)
items.summary: Night mode for the web is inconsistent — some sites respect your OS dark mode preference, others have their own dark mode settings, and some don't support dark mode at all. NightOwl is a Firefox extension that applies dark mode universally across all websites, using intelligent color inversion that preserves images and media. The Problem with Dark Mode on the Web OS-level dark mode ( prefers-color-scheme: dark ) only works if the website implements CSS dark mode: /* Site developer wrote this */ @media ( prefers-color-scheme : dark ) { body { background : #111 ; color : #eee ; } } Most modern sites do implement this. But many older sites, documentation pages, and blogs don't — they're always white backgrounds. Browser dark mode (about:config → layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override ) forces all sites to pretend you prefer dark. This works with sites that implemented dark mode CSS. Still doesn't affect sites with no dark mode support. Extension-based dark mode — tools like NightOwl — apply dark mode even to sites that have zero dark mode CSS. They do this by inverting colors, inverting again for images (so images look natural), and applying heuristic rules to avoid turning things like checkboxes inside-out. Installing NightOwl Install from Firefox Add-ons (AMO): Search "NightOwl" at https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/extensions/ One-click install, no account required After installation, a moon icon appears in the Firefox toolbar. How NightOwl Works NightOwl injects CSS into every page that: Inverts all colors — white backgrounds become dark, dark text becomes light Inverts images/videos again — double-inversion returns them to original appearance Adjusts hue — pure color inversion makes blues look orange; NightOwl adjusts the hue to maintain natural color appearance Preserves media — images, videos, and SVGs are double-inverted to preserve their original appearance The result: a consistently dark experience on any website, with photos and media looking natural. NightOwl vs. Dark Reader Dark Reader is the most popular dark mode extension. Comparison: Feature NightOwl Dark Reader Performance Low overhead Higher overhead (CSS regeneration) Approach CSS filter inversion Dynamic style generation Customization On/off + site exceptions Brightness, contrast, sepia, fonts AMO Recommended Not yet ✅ Recommended badge Size ~50KB ~2MB Algorithm Fast CSS filter Smart inversion + custom styles NightOwl is a lightweight option for users who want simple, performant dark mode. Dark Reader is better for users who want more control and a wider algorithm. Site Exceptions Some sites look better with their native dark mode: Click the NightOwl toolbar icon Toggle "Disable on this site" Sites like GitHub, Twitter, and most Google products have native dark modes that look better than NightOwl's inversion Or schedule NightOwl to activate at specific hours — useful if you only want dark mode at night. Pairing with OS Dark Mode The ideal setup: Enable OS dark mode (macOS: System Preferences → Appearance; Linux: GNOME/KDE settings) Install NightOwl for sites without dark mode CSS Disable NightOwl on sites with good native dark modes This way: sites with native dark mode ( prefers-color-scheme: dark ) use their optimized dark theme, and sites without it get NightOwl's inversion. Power Users: Keyboard Shortcut You can assign a keyboard shortcut to toggle NightOwl: Go to about:addons → click the gear icon → "Manage Extension Shortcuts" Find NightOwl → set your preferred shortcut Toggle quickly without clicking the toolbar icon Why Not Just Use Firefox's Built-In Dark Mode? Firefox 96+ added a forced dark mode via layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override = 0 . This works on sites that have implemented prefers-color-scheme: dark . It doesn't work on sites that have no dark mode CSS at all. NightOwl fills the gap — it inverts those "no dark mode" sites, while sites with native dark modes respond to the OS preference and look correct natively. Performance Consideration CSS filter-based dark mode (NightOwl's approach) runs on the GPU — it applies a pixel-level filter to the rendered output rather than regenerating all CSS. This is very lightweight. Most users report no noticeable performance impact. Sites with heavy animations may have slight performance differences because the filter is applied after rendering. For sites where this matters (browser games, WebGL demos), disable NightOwl on that site. Accessibility: High Contrast Mode NightOwl's inversion can actually help users with certain visual impairments — high contrast between light text and dark background reduces eye strain in low-light environments. This is a common accessibility need (not just a comfort preference). For users who need Windows High Contrast mode or macOS Increase Contrast, NightOwl complements but doesn't replace those OS-level settings.
items.summary_html:
Night mode for the web is inconsistent — some sites respect your OS dark mode preference, others have their own dark mode settings, and some don't support dark mode at all. NightOwl is a Firefox extension that applies dark mode universally across all websites, using intelligent color inversion that preserves images and media.

The Problem with Dark Mode on the Web

OS-level dark mode (prefers-color-scheme: dark) only works if the website implements CSS dark mode:

/* Site developer wrote this */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  body { background: #111; color: #eee; }
}

Most modern sites do implement this. But many older sites, documentation pages, and blogs don't — they're always white backgrounds.

Browser dark mode (about:config → layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override) forces all sites to pretend you prefer dark. This works with sites that implemented dark mode CSS. Still doesn't affect sites with no dark mode support.

Extension-based dark mode — tools like NightOwl — apply dark mode even to sites that have zero dark mode CSS. They do this by inverting colors, inverting again for images (so images look natural), and applying heuristic rules to avoid turning things like checkboxes inside-out.

Installing NightOwl

Install from Firefox Add-ons (AMO):

  • Search "NightOwl" at https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/extensions/
  • One-click install, no account required

After installation, a moon icon appears in the Firefox toolbar.

How NightOwl Works

NightOwl injects CSS into every page that:

  1. Inverts all colors — white backgrounds become dark, dark text becomes light
  2. Inverts images/videos again — double-inversion returns them to original appearance
  3. Adjusts hue — pure color inversion makes blues look orange; NightOwl adjusts the hue to maintain natural color appearance
  4. Preserves media — images, videos, and SVGs are double-inverted to preserve their original appearance

The result: a consistently dark experience on any website, with photos and media looking natural.

NightOwl vs. Dark Reader

Dark Reader is the most popular dark mode extension. Comparison:

Feature NightOwl Dark Reader Performance Low overhead Higher overhead (CSS regeneration) Approach CSS filter inversion Dynamic style generation Customization On/off + site exceptions Brightness, contrast, sepia, fonts AMO Recommended Not yet ✅ Recommended badge Size ~50KB ~2MB Algorithm Fast CSS filter Smart inversion + custom styles

NightOwl is a lightweight option for users who want simple, performant dark mode. Dark Reader is better for users who want more control and a wider algorithm.

Site Exceptions

Some sites look better with their native dark mode:

  1. Click the NightOwl toolbar icon
  2. Toggle "Disable on this site"
  3. Sites like GitHub, Twitter, and most Google products have native dark modes that look better than NightOwl's inversion

Or schedule NightOwl to activate at specific hours — useful if you only want dark mode at night.

Pairing with OS Dark Mode

The ideal setup:

  1. Enable OS dark mode (macOS: System Preferences → Appearance; Linux: GNOME/KDE settings)
  2. Install NightOwl for sites without dark mode CSS
  3. Disable NightOwl on sites with good native dark modes

This way: sites with native dark mode (prefers-color-scheme: dark) use their optimized dark theme, and sites without it get NightOwl's inversion.

Power Users: Keyboard Shortcut

You can assign a keyboard shortcut to toggle NightOwl:

  1. Go to about:addons → click the gear icon → "Manage Extension Shortcuts"
  2. Find NightOwl → set your preferred shortcut
  3. Toggle quickly without clicking the toolbar icon
Why Not Just Use Firefox's Built-In Dark Mode?

Firefox 96+ added a forced dark mode via layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override = 0. This works on sites that have implemented prefers-color-scheme: dark. It doesn't work on sites that have no dark mode CSS at all.

NightOwl fills the gap — it inverts those "no dark mode" sites, while sites with native dark modes respond to the OS preference and look correct natively.

Performance Consideration

CSS filter-based dark mode (NightOwl's approach) runs on the GPU — it applies a pixel-level filter to the rendered output rather than regenerating all CSS. This is very lightweight. Most users report no noticeable performance impact.

Sites with heavy animations may have slight performance differences because the filter is applied after rendering. For sites where this matters (browser games, WebGL demos), disable NightOwl on that site.

Accessibility: High Contrast Mode

NightOwl's inversion can actually help users with certain visual impairments — high contrast between light text and dark background reduces eye strain in low-light environments. This is a common accessibility need (not just a comfort preference).

For users who need Windows High Contrast mode or macOS Increase Contrast, NightOwl complements but doesn't replace those OS-level settings.

items.title: SellCraft AI: Local-First Product Listings for Independent Sellers
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle . What I Built SellCraft AI is a local-first product listing studio for independent sellers. It turns confirmed product details into editable: Titles Descriptions Features Keywords and tags Social captions FAQs Markdown, text, and CSV exports It is designed for sellers who want help writing listings without sending product information to a paid cloud AI API. SellCraft can help someone selling handmade goods, clothing, electronics, collectibles, or other products create a stronger first draft faster. The seller remains responsible for reviewing every claim before publishing. Demo SellCraft runs locally: npm ci npm run dev Open: http://127.0.0.1:5173 The model can be downloaded from the Settings page or installed with: npm run setup:model After setup, generation works without an internet connection as long as the local SellCraft service remains running. Code Public repository: View SellCraft AI on GitHub The project is organized around a small local Node service and a React frontend. Important areas include: App.tsx for the listing workflow and editor listings for prompts and output normalization model-manager for model setup and verification model-store.ts for project-local model storage engine.ts for local inference storage for IndexedDB persistence listing.ts for warnings and exports The model files are stored inside the project’s models directory and are not committed to Git. How I Built It SellCraft uses the open-weight SmolLM2 360M Instruct model in quantized ONNX format. The model runs locally through: Transformers.js ONNX Runtime A Node.js worker thread A loopback HTTP service A React and Vite frontend The application does not use Ollama, a cloud generation fallback, a global model cache, or a paid AI API. The model is downloaded only when explicitly requested. Every model artifact has a pinned size and SHA-256 checksum. Invalid or incomplete files are rejected. The application asks the model to generate one listing section at a time. This keeps the response format simple and allows individual sections to be regenerated without replacing the rest of the listing. Generated output is normalized before it reaches the editor. For example, feature responses wrapped in JSON are converted into plain editable feature lines. Measured Results The project was tested on Windows with Node.js 24.14.0 and Google Chrome. Model setup passed using the existing verified local files. Unit tests: 15/15 passed. End-to-end tests: 9/9 passed. Production build passed. Model load time: approximately 2.12 seconds . Sample generation time: approximately 13.0–22.9 seconds per listing section set. Section-only regeneration preserved unrelated listing sections. Saved listings remained available with external network requests blocked. Markdown, plain text, and CSV exports were tested. The compact model is useful for creating first drafts, but it is not perfect. Real model evaluation showed that it can sometimes repeat text, produce prompt-like filler, omit FAQs, or invent unsupported compatibility and benefit claims. SellCraft treats AI output as a draft rather than a source of truth. Sellers must verify every generated claim. Offline Behavior Initial installation and model setup require internet access. After that: Start the local service with npm run dev or npm start . Keep the local service running. Disconnect from the internet if desired. Continue generating listings and opening saved products locally. Saved listings are stored in browser IndexedDB. They are not synchronized or encrypted, so important work should also be exported. Photos remain local references. The text model does not analyze or upload them. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation made it possible to build a private, local workflow without depending on a paid AI provider. Using an open-weight model means: Product details stay on the seller’s device. There is no per-request API fee. The model can be inspected, replaced, or customized. The application can continue working without internet after setup. The project does not depend on a single commercial AI platform. The trade-off is that local inference requires CPU, memory, disk space, and human review. A small open model can be practical, but it cannot replace seller knowledge or factual verification. Final Thoughts SellCraft AI is built around a simple idea: AI should help sellers get past the blank page without taking control of their product data. The model writes the first draft. The seller decides what is true.
items.summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

What I Built

SellCraft AI is a local-first product listing studio for independent sellers.

It turns confirmed product details into editable:

  • Titles
  • Descriptions
  • Features
  • Keywords and tags
  • Social captions
  • FAQs
  • Markdown, text, and CSV exports

It is designed for sellers who want help writing listings without sending product information to a paid cloud AI API.

SellCraft can help someone selling handmade goods, clothing, electronics, collectibles, or other products create a stronger first draft faster. The seller remains responsible for reviewing every claim before publishing.

Demo

SellCraft runs locally:

npm ci
npm run dev

Open:

http://127.0.0.1:5173

The model can be downloaded from the Settings page or installed with:

npm run setup:model

After setup, generation works without an internet connection as long as the local SellCraft service remains running.

Code

Public repository: View SellCraft AI on GitHub

The project is organized around a small local Node service and a React frontend.

Important areas include:

  • App.tsx for the listing workflow and editor
  • listings for prompts and output normalization
  • model-manager for model setup and verification
  • model-store.ts for project-local model storage
  • engine.ts for local inference
  • storage for IndexedDB persistence
  • listing.ts for warnings and exports

The model files are stored inside the project’s models directory and are not committed to Git.

How I Built It

SellCraft uses the open-weight SmolLM2 360M Instruct model in quantized ONNX format.

The model runs locally through:

  • Transformers.js
  • ONNX Runtime
  • A Node.js worker thread
  • A loopback HTTP service
  • A React and Vite frontend

The application does not use Ollama, a cloud generation fallback, a global model cache, or a paid AI API.

The model is downloaded only when explicitly requested. Every model artifact has a pinned size and SHA-256 checksum. Invalid or incomplete files are rejected.

The application asks the model to generate one listing section at a time. This keeps the response format simple and allows individual sections to be regenerated without replacing the rest of the listing.

Generated output is normalized before it reaches the editor. For example, feature responses wrapped in JSON are converted into plain editable feature lines.

Measured Results

The project was tested on Windows with Node.js 24.14.0 and Google Chrome.

  • Model setup passed using the existing verified local files.
  • Unit tests: 15/15 passed.
  • End-to-end tests: 9/9 passed.
  • Production build passed.
  • Model load time: approximately 2.12 seconds.
  • Sample generation time: approximately 13.0–22.9 seconds per listing section set.
  • Section-only regeneration preserved unrelated listing sections.
  • Saved listings remained available with external network requests blocked.
  • Markdown, plain text, and CSV exports were tested.

The compact model is useful for creating first drafts, but it is not perfect. Real model evaluation showed that it can sometimes repeat text, produce prompt-like filler, omit FAQs, or invent unsupported compatibility and benefit claims.

SellCraft treats AI output as a draft rather than a source of truth. Sellers must verify every generated claim.

Offline Behavior

Initial installation and model setup require internet access.

After that:

  1. Start the local service with npm run dev or npm start.
  2. Keep the local service running.
  3. Disconnect from the internet if desired.
  4. Continue generating listings and opening saved products locally.

Saved listings are stored in browser IndexedDB. They are not synchronized or encrypted, so important work should also be exported.

Photos remain local references. The text model does not analyze or upload them.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation made it possible to build a private, local workflow without depending on a paid AI provider.

Using an open-weight model means:

  • Product details stay on the seller’s device.
  • There is no per-request API fee.
  • The model can be inspected, replaced, or customized.
  • The application can continue working without internet after setup.
  • The project does not depend on a single commercial AI platform.

The trade-off is that local inference requires CPU, memory, disk space, and human review. A small open model can be practical, but it cannot replace seller knowledge or factual verification.

Final Thoughts

SellCraft AI is built around a simple idea: AI should help sellers get past the blank page without taking control of their product data.

The model writes the first draft. The seller decides what is true.

items.title: Plausible vs Umami vs Fathom: Privacy-First Analytics in 2026
items.summary: Best Privacy-First Analytics Tools for Indie Developers in 2026: Plausible, Umami, and the Alternatives If you are an indie developer bootstrapping a product, you probably do not want Google Analytics. It is heavyweight, it raises privacy concerns, and for a small site it is overkill. The good news: there is now a mature crop of privacy-first, lightweight analytics tools designed exactly for you. Plausible, Umami, and Fathom lead the pack, with several open-source alternatives close behind. This guide compares the top options for indie developers who want real data without the cookie banners and the privacy baggage. Quick Verdict Choose Plausible if you want a polished, hosted, privacy-first solution with a strong brand and simple setup. Choose Umami if you want to self-host on your own server with zero recurring cost. Choose Fathom if you want a hosted option with a slightly different interface and similar privacy guarantees. For most indie developers, Plausible is the best balance of ease and trust, and Umami is the best free option. Feature Comparison Category Plausible Umami Fathom Hosting Hosted (SaaS) Self-hosted or cloud Hosted (SaaS) Price From $9/mo Free (self-host) From $14/mo Cookieless Yes Yes Yes GDPR compliant Yes Yes Yes Open source Yes Yes No Self-hosting Possible First-class No E-commerce Basic Basic Basic Goals / events Yes Yes Yes Quick Picks Breakdown Plausible — best overall for most indie developers Plausible is the most polished hosted option. It is cookieless by default (no GDPR cookie banner needed), GDPR-compliant, and open source. Setup is a single script tag. The dashboard is clean and fast, showing pageviews, top pages, referrers, and countries at a glance. At $9/month for a small site it is affordable, and the brand has strong trust within the privacy-focused web community. The main downside: it is a recurring cost, and while you can self-host the open-source version, you lose the managed convenience. Umami — best free self-hosted option Umami is fully open source and designed to be self-hosted. You can deploy it on a small VPS or a free-tier platform and track unlimited sites with zero cost. It is lightweight (uses a small footprint), GDPR-compliant, and cookieless. The dashboard is modern and supports custom events and goals. The trade-off: you are responsible for hosting, maintenance, uptime, and database backups. For a developer comfortable with a VPS, it is an excellent free solution. Fathom — polished hosted alternative Fathom is a hosted, privacy-first analytics tool very similar to Plausible in philosophy. It is cookieless and GDPR-compliant, with a clean dashboard. It is slightly more expensive ($14/month) than Plausible and is not open source. It is a fine choice if you prefer its interface or brand, but for most indie developers, Plausible offers equivalent value at a lower price point. Open-Source Alternatives Worth Knowing Beyond the big three, there are credible open-source options: GoatCounter (minimal, free, self-hostable), Matomo (the full-featured open-source GA alternative, heavier than the privacy-first tools), and PostHog (product analytics with a generous free tier, but more complex than a simple analytics dashboard). For simple pageview analytics, the privacy-first tools above are usually the right fit; Matomo and PostHog are for teams that need deeper product analytics. Limitations Plausible: Recurring subscription cost. Basic e-commerce tracking compared to Google Analytics. Umami: Self-hosting responsibility (maintenance, uptime, backups). No managed support unless you use the cloud version. Fathom: More expensive than Plausible. Not open source, so less community transparency. All privacy-first tools: None match Google Analytics' depth of insight, funnel analysis, or integration ecosystem. If you need advanced behavioral analytics, these are not a drop-in replacement. The Bottom Line For indie developers who want real, privacy-respecting analytics without the complexity of Google Analytics, the choice is clear: Plausible if you want a managed solution, Umami if you want to self-host for free, and Fathom if you prefer its specific flavor. All three give you the essential data — pageviews, sources, and engagement — without cookie banners or privacy compromises. Start with Plausible's free trial, and if cost is a concern, self-host Umami. Deeper Analysis: Plausible vs Umami costs The cost difference between hosted and self-hosted analytics is a meaningful decision point for indie developers. Plausible at $9/month is not expensive, but it is a recurring cost that adds up over time. Self-hosting Umami on a $5/month VPS handles unlimited sites and unlimited pageviews, making it dramatically cheaper at scale. The trade-off is your time: setting up Umami requires configuring a PostgreSQL database, deploying the app, handling backups, and monitoring uptime. For a developer who already manages a server, the marginal cost of adding Umami is near zero. For a developer who wants zero infrastructure management, Plausible's $9/month is a bargain. The hidden cost of self-hosting is not the server — it is the incidental maintenance. Database updates, security patches, and the occasional bug fix all consume time that you could spend on your product. If your time is valuable, paying for a managed service is often the economical choice, even if the server cost is higher. Additional Considerations The data accuracy of privacy-first analytics tools is a topic that deserves more attention than it gets. Because these tools are cookieless, they cannot track individual users across sessions in the same way that Google Analytics does. This affects metrics like bounce rate, session duration, and user counts. Plausible and Umami use different approaches to estimate unique visitors — Plausible uses a daily hash based on IP and user agent, while Umami uses a similar approach but with different deduplication logic. These differences mean that the same site can show different visitor counts in different tools. The consensus among users is that the numbers are close enough for practical decision-making, but they are not identical to Google Analytics. For most indie developers, the trade-off of less precise analytics in exchange for privacy compliance and simplicity is worthwhile. If you need pixel-perfect analytics data, you need a traditional cookie-based approach, with all the privacy implications that entails. Additional Considerations: Privacy analytics The integration ecosystem is where privacy-first analytics tools differ most from Google Analytics. Google Analytics has a plugin for nearly everything — e-commerce platforms, form builders, advertising platforms, and CRMs. Plausible, Umami, and Fathom have smaller integration ecosystems. Plausible has a well-maintained API and a growing set of integrations, including e-commerce tracking for platforms like Shopify and WooCommerce. Umami supports custom events and has some integrations through its API. Fathom has a basic API. If your analytics needs are simple — pageviews, referrers, and basic goal tracking — the privacy-first tools cover them well. If you need deep integration with a complex e-commerce or marketing stack, you may find the integration ecosystem limiting. Evaluate your specific integration needs before choosing, and be prepared to use the API to build custom integrations where gaps exist. Plausible and Umami use different approaches to estimate unique visitors — Plausible uses a daily hash based on IP and user agent, while Umami uses a similar approach but with different deduplication logic. These differences mean that the same site can show different visitor counts in different tools. The consensus among users is that the numbers are close enough for practical decision-making, but they are not identical to Google Analytics. For most indie developers, the trade-off of less precise analytics in exchange for privacy compliance and simplicity is worthwhile. If you need pixel-perfect analytics data, you need a traditional cookie-based approach, with all the privacy implications that entails.

Additional Considerations: Privacy analytics

The integration ecosystem is where privacy-first analytics tools differ most from Google Analytics. Google Analytics has a plugin for nearly everything — e-commerce platforms, form builders, advertising platforms, and CRMs. Plausible, Umami, and Fathom have smaller integration ecosystems. Plausible has a well-maintained API and a growing set of integrations, including e-commerce tracking for platforms like Shopify and WooCommerce. Umami supports custom events and has some integrations through its API. Fathom has a basic API. If your analytics needs are simple — pageviews, referrers, and basic goal tracking — the privacy-first tools cover them well. If you need deep integration with a complex e-commerce or marketing stack, you may find the integration ecosystem limiting. Evaluate your specific integration needs before choosing, and be prepared to use the API to build custom integrations where gaps exist.

items.summary_html:
Search traffic used to mean one thing: Google results. Now a growing share of questions go to AI assistants like ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini. If you ship a product or docs site, it's worth knowing whether those assistants mention you.

This post walks through a simple, repeatable way to check. It needs a spreadsheet, a bit of discipline and, optionally, a small script.

1. Write prompts the way users ask

Don't test with your brand name. Test with the problems your users have.

Good sources for prompts:

  • Questions from support tickets and onboarding calls.
  • Queries in Google Search Console's Performance report.
  • "People also ask" boxes on Google for your main topics.
  • Threads on Reddit, Stack Overflow or GitHub Discussions in your niche.

Aim for 10 to 20 prompts. Mix broad ones ("best tool to monitor cron jobs") with specific ones ("how do I alert on a missed cron run in Node").

2. Set up a tracking sheet

Use one row per prompt per assistant per check. These columns are enough:

date | assistant | prompt | brand_mentioned (y/n) | our_url_cited (y/n) | cited_urls | competitors_named | notes

Record the cited URLs, not only whether you appeared. The list of cited domains is the most useful part. It shows which pages assistants trust for your topic.

3. Run the checks consistently

AI answers vary between runs, accounts and locations. You can't remove that noise, but you can keep it steady.

  • Use a fresh or logged-out session where possible.
  • Use the same wording every time.
  • Run each prompt twice and note if the answers differ.
  • Repeat the full set every two weeks, not every day.

Assistants that browse the web, like Perplexity, show sources directly. For others, ask a follow-up such as "which sources did you use?" and note what you get.

4. Optional: script part of it

If an assistant offers an API, you can loop over your prompts and save the raw answers. API answers can differ from the consumer chat apps, so treat them as a signal, not ground truth.

import csv, datetime, re

def extract_urls(text):
    return re.findall(r"https?://[^\s)\]]+", text)

def log_answer(writer, assistant, prompt, answer, brand, domain):
    urls = extract_urls(answer)
    writer.writerow([
        datetime.date.today().isoformat(),
        assistant,
        prompt,
        "y" if brand.lower() in answer.lower() else "n",
        "y" if any(domain in u for u in urls) else "n",
        " ".join(urls),
    ])

# answers = {prompt: call_your_assistant_api(prompt) for prompt in prompts}
# with open("ai-checks.csv", "a", newline="") as f:
#     w = csv.writer(f)
#     for p, a in answers.items():
#         log_answer(w, "assistant-name", p, a, "YourBrand", "yourdomain.com")
5. Read the results like a developer

Look for patterns, not single answers.

  • Cited, not named: your page is used but your brand isn't stated. Put your product name near the answer on the page.
  • Named, not cited: assistants know you from elsewhere, like directories or reviews. Make sure those third-party pages are accurate.
  • Competitors cited instead: open their cited pages. Note how they structure the answer, and where it sits on the page.
  • Nobody cited: the topic may be open. A clear, focused page could fill it.
6. Fix what you can control

Most fixes are ordinary web hygiene:

  • Put a direct one or two sentence answer under each question-style heading.
  • Make sure pages render meaningful HTML without needing client-side JavaScript.
  • Don't block search and AI crawlers in robots.txt by accident.
  • Add structured data that matches visible content, such as Organization, SoftwareApplication or FAQPage.
  • Keep pricing and feature facts consistent across your site and listings.
Wrapping up

A small, steady checking habit beats guessing. Twenty prompts, a sheet and a fortnightly rerun will show you more than any single screenshot.

I work on Serpair, which runs this kind of Google and AI-answer tracking for you. But the manual method above works fine on its own, and it's a good place to start.

items.title: Muse Spark Open: what Meta's "open-weight" license actually lets you do
items.summary: On October 15, 2026, Meta released the weights of Muse Spark Open, a natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 816B total parameters (42B active per token) and a 1M-token context window, built for coding and agentic work. Meta calls it "the most capable US open-weight model to date". That line is Meta's own claim, based on Meta's own benchmark table. What happened Weights are on Hugging Face (BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints), plus Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden and Microsoft Foundry Models. Hosted APIs launched the same day at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. It runs on SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Transformers, MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Meta shows it running on two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 512 GB each. Architecture (Hugging Face model card): 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token; text, image, audio and video in, text out. Why people care Chinese labs (Qwen, Kimi, GLM) have led open weights for most of 2026. This is a US lab answering with a large, agent-focused model that you can actually download and self-host. What the coverage skips 1. Active vs total parameters. 42B active sets the compute per token. All 816B weights still have to sit in memory. The model card asks for roughly 700 GB of VRAM for NVFP4 and about 2 TB for BF16. Cheap per token is not cheap to host. 2. The license is not OSI open source. The Muse Model License opens like MIT ("free of charge... without restriction"), then adds conditions: Section 2: any product that uses the model or a "Derivative" must prominently display "Built with Muse Spark Open" (UI, docs, website or settings). "Derivatives" includes any model "trained, modified (including fine-tuned), distilled, or otherwise improved using the Software or any outputs or results thereof". A small model you fine-tune on Muse outputs counts. Section 3: if you sell model access via an API ("Model as a Service") and your group's gross revenue passes $20 million in any 12 months, you must sign a separate agreement with Meta first. Internal use, research, and powering features of your own product are exempt. The attached Usage Policy rules out, among other things, operating critical infrastructure, transportation technologies or heavy machinery, and says the model is not intended for anyone under 18. 3. The benchmarks are self-reported. Meta says a fuller evaluation report is coming. Independent indexes so far place it behind the strongest Chinese open models on general intelligence scores. Facts vs prediction Everything above comes from Meta's announcement, the Hugging Face model card and the license text. My read, a prediction rather than a fact: most teams will use it through hosted APIs, not local hardware, and the derivative clause will matter more than the $20M clause for small teams running distillation pipelines. Practical takeaway Read LICENSE.md before you build anything on it, especially if you plan to distill or fine-tune on its outputs. Add the "Built with Muse Spark Open" line wherever you ship it. Run 20 to 50 of your own real tasks through a hosted endpoint before trusting any leaderboard. Sources: Meta AI Research, Introducing Muse Spark Open (Oct 15, 2026): https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-spark-open Muse Model License: https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B/blob/main/LICENSE.md Hugging Face launch post: https://huggingface.co/blog/meta-muse-spark-open This post was written with AI assistance and edited for accuracy.

  • "Derivatives" includes any model "trained, modified (including fine-tuned), distilled, or otherwise improved using the Software or any outputs or results thereof". A small model you fine-tune on Muse outputs counts.

items.title: Can AI screen for heart disease using photos of your tongue and face?
items.summary: Lee Charlie/Shutterstock.com An AI system trained on photographs of the face and tongue correctly identified every patient with coronary heart disease (CHD) in a small test, according to a new study from China. The researchers recruited 518 people : 200 with diagnosed CHD and 318 healthy volunteers. Each had their face and tongue photographed with a purpose-built scanning system. The pictures were analysed using deep learning, a type of AI that learns to spot patterns in images. The system examined the tongue and face photographs separately, then combined what each had picked up to predict who had CHD. Using both together performed better than either alone. The best-performing version was 98% accurate in a test of 104 people, correctly identifying all 40 patients with CHD, although two healthy participants were wrongly classified as having the condition – so-called “false positives”. The AI focused on the centre of the tongue, its surface coating, the skin around the mouth and the cheeks. Some patients with CHD had darker tongues, thicker coatings or changes in facial pigmentation. The researchers say the areas highlighted by the AI are consistent with traditional Chinese medicine teachings about links between the tongue, face and heart. Reading disease from appearance is not unique to traditional Chinese medicine. Doctors have long recognised that some visible features can point to underlying medical problems. Blue lips can signal low oxygen levels in the blood, and fatty yellow deposits around the eyelids, known as xanthelasma , can point to very high cholesterol, often caused by an inherited condition. Coronary heart disease explained. Whether a tongue or a cheek can reveal blocked arteries is a different matter. Skin tone, lighting, age, medication and smoking all change how a face and tongue look, and the study does not establish that these features are caused by blocked coronary arteries. AI may pick up associations that humans struggle to recognise, but that does not explain what causes them. CHD develops when the arteries supplying the heart muscle narrow because of fatty deposits called plaques, a process known as atherosclerosis. This restricts blood flow and can eventually cause a heart attack. For many people, the first sign of a problem is chest pain, a heart attack or another life-threatening event, so spotting the disease earlier is an important goal of preventive medicine. Doctors currently estimate risk using factors including age, smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes. If CHD is suspected, tests can include an electrocardiogram (ECG), blood tests or specialised scans. A quick, painless, low-cost photographic test could help decide who needs those investigations, particularly in communities where access to specialist healthcare is limited. A promising result, with questions remaining The study, published in Scientific Reports, compared people already diagnosed with CHD against healthy volunteers, which is very different from screening the general public, where people have a mix of other illnesses and levels of cardiovascular risk. The photographs were also taken under controlled lighting with specialised equipment. The model has not been tested on people from other hospitals or settings. AI systems sometimes perform very well on the data used to build them but less well in different hospitals, ethnic groups or healthcare settings. Not all the healthy volunteers were assessed with coronary imaging, so undetected disease cannot be ruled out. The AI may also have been picking up differences linked to age, other illnesses or other characteristics of the participants rather than heart disease. Screening adds a further problem. Even a highly accurate test can produce large numbers of false-positive diagnoses when it is used on a population in which the disease is relatively uncommon. Larger studies following people over time would need to show whether this approach can pick up disease that has gone unnoticed, tell it apart from other conditions and lead to better health. Researchers would also need to compare it directly with existing ways of assessing risk. If it proves useful, it could eventually be used alongside standard heart disease risk checks, cholesterol tests and blood pressure measurements. David C. items.title: AI Experts Already Doomsday Prepping for When AI Takes Out the Entire Financial System
items.summary: Powerful AI models are going on hacking sprees — or helping humans with them — left and right. If the AI industry doesn’t get its collective act together and stop its products from being used to such dangerous ends, it could be only a matter of time before one of these AI-powered hacks targets our essential infrastructure. This is a scenario that some AI researchers are apparently already preparing for. Andreas Stuhlmüller, CEO and cofounder of the AI research company Elicit, recently rattled off a prepper-esque checklist of how to prepare for when AI-powered cyberattacks could take out financial systems, power grids, the internet, and all the other infrastructure that underpins modern life. “Cash: Get a few weeks of spending in cash,” he recommended in a tweet . Then he suggests, in greater detail than we’ll get into here, getting a Starlink terminal in case your local internet network goes down; a battery, generator and solar panels for power; weeks worth of water and food; and a hand-crank emergency radio. Stuhlmüller’s paranoid recommendations come after a shocking cyberattack that targeted the refrigerator systems used in hundreds of grocery stores across France. The as-yet unknown perpetrators cranked up the fridge temperatures up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, spoiling food and even causing fires. The CEO of one chain targeted by the attack, Intermarche, said it caused losses amounting to “tens ​of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.” AI’s role in the attack hasn’t been confirmed. But given AI’s ubiquity among coders, it’s likely that it was used to some degree. On top of churning out code, the tech is alarmingly good at identifying vulnerabilities . A recent CrowdStrike report found that there was a nearly 90 percent year over year increase in AI-enabled cyberattacks. There’s also, of course, the recent disclosures from frontier AI labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, over how their agentic AI systems broke out of their testing environments and launched cyberattacks against other companies’ websites and computer systems. Powerful AI models are going on hacking sprees — or helping humans with them — left and right. If the AI industry doesn’t get its collective act together and stop its products from being used to such dangerous ends, it could be only a matter of time before one of these AI-powered hacks targets our essential infrastructure.

This is a scenario that some AI researchers are apparently already preparing for. Andreas Stuhlmüller, CEO and cofounder of the AI research company Elicit, recently rattled off a prepper-esque checklist of how to prepare for when AI-powered cyberattacks could take out financial systems, power grids, the internet, and all the other infrastructure that underpins modern life.

“Cash: Get a few weeks of spending in cash,” he recommended in a tweet. Then he suggests, in greater detail than we’ll get into here, getting a Starlink terminal in case your local internet network goes down; a battery, generator and solar panels for power; weeks worth of water and food; and a hand-crank emergency radio.

Stuhlmüller’s paranoid recommendations come after a shocking cyberattack that targeted the refrigerator systems used in hundreds of grocery stores across France. The as-yet unknown perpetrators cranked up the fridge temperatures up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, spoiling food and even causing fires. The CEO of one chain targeted by the attack, Intermarche, said it caused losses amounting to “tens ​of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.”

AI’s role in the attack hasn’t been confirmed. But given AI’s ubiquity among coders, it’s likely that it was used to some degree. On top of churning out code, the tech is alarmingly good at identifying vulnerabilities. A recent CrowdStrike report found that there was a nearly 90 percent year over year increase in AI-enabled cyberattacks.

There’s also, of course, the recent disclosures from frontier AI labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, over how their agentic AI systems broke out of their testing environments and launched cyberattacks against other companies’ websites and computer systems.

All that being said, it’s a major leap to say that AI models — or humans using them — will go from hacking websites and supermarket fridges to your local power grid and banking system. But we can hardly blame anyone for being worried about this possible eventuality. Better safe than sorry, right?

This is being driven by increasing interest in systems that can autonomously complete genuinely valuable tasks across the enterprise. To some the phrase “AI coworker” sounds dystopian or even threatening, implying AI’s advance into work that humans currently do, or conjuring images of a workplace where we increasingly spend our time communicating with machines at the expense of human interaction. To others, AI coworkers promise a new era of productivity and increased time for human workers to focus on what’s really important while delegating more routine tasks to automated systems. And to a third group, the term may simply sound like corporate marketing without concrete technical background. Debate over the appropriate use and implications of this technology is likely to continue over the coming years and is well beyond the scope of this article. Nevertheless, it is clear that this is becoming an increasingly important subject in the world of enterprise software. So let’s use this article to examine what constitutes an AI coworker, what it takes to build and operate one, and the state of existing tools. AI coworkers differ significantly from consumer AI personal assistants, like Meta’s Muse, because they are strict work tools that sit securely inside corporate software and governed data systems. These systems are being actively developed by major players in the enterprise data space, namely Snowflake (Cortex), Databricks (Genie), and Microsoft (Fabric Agents). For full disclosure I am an employee at Databricks, so my daily experience is naturally skewed towards their platform. Many readers will already be aware of the Databricks Genie suite and I will use it as a case study for this article. However, my goal here is to provide insights rather than promote a specific vendor and I will refrain from corporate terminology where possible. Indeed, there are many interesting vendor-neutral architectural principles — such as integrating LLM intelligence, persistent state, and domain governance — that are required to build any functional AI coworker and make them a fascinating subject for the community at large. 1. Defining the AI Coworker What is the difference between a chatbot, an agent and an AI coworker? We can see these tools as points on a spectrum of autonomy. Conversational chatbots operate as Q/A systems — they take in a prompt along with the user’s question, run it through a single LLM (which at its core is a static set of learned weights) and return its response. Sometimes the input is enriched by context retrieved at runtime via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which enables the LLM to reason over information that may not have been in its training. The response may be helpful but the system is very passive and follows a strict workflow: It receives your question, undertakes a set of pre-defined steps (one of which is an LLM call) and then it’s done. Agentic assistants take this a step along the autonomy spectrum by having access to multiple tools and using LLMs to decide which to call, in what sequence and how to reason over the result. To do this they use the “reasoning and acting” loop, which sees the LLM first reason about input tasks, choose one or more tools to call, analyze the results and decide whether to keep calling tools or stop and compose a response. This loop allows the system to break away from a predefined workflow and act semi-autonomously to solve a problem. Agentic assistants like Claude Code and other coding harnesses are becoming increasingly sophisticated at this, making multiple LLM calls to different models per user request and potentially accessing hundreds of other services via model context protocol (MCP) tools to complete a request. But at their core they remain passive and task-based. They are only as “plugged in” to the enterprise as its security team allows — and, given that they are usually operated by external model providers, there are often good reasons not to grant access. The big difference between agentic assistants and AI coworkers is that the latter operate with autonomy within the business environment and have the capability, understanding and correct permissions to interact with systems across the enterprise. They also have the capability to monitor and take action without being directly asked to do so, therefore becoming active members of the organization. In this way, they mirror the work that human analysts might do. For example, let’s say an executive at a retailer wants to know about how customer lifetime value (LTV) has changed over the past fiscal year and why, they might delegate this task to an analyst who would need to do the following: Locate the organization’s certified, governing definitions of LTV and fiscal year (and confirm whether Finance and Marketing calculate it the same way). Query production databases and inspect active reporting dashboards. Write and validate custom code to segment the data. Synthesize their analytical findings into an executive briefing. Retain their analytical logic so the experiment can be audited, reproduced, and proactively rerun next quarter. It’s critical to point out that intelligence alone is not sufficient for this task. A super intelligent AI can’t be a useful coworker if it doesn’t understand business context. Such context is usually private to the organization so the model would need to be either trained on or able to operate within the secure data environment to know it. Beyond that, it would then need access to all the relevant tools and channels needed to compile and complete the report. Furthermore, it would need long term memory to store the results of past tasks and the ability to learn from that too. This connectivity is what makes AI coworkers challenging to build, and why the LLMs work best when they are brought directly to where enterprise data and governance natively live. Examining how a unified data platform handles this challenge provides an instructive blueprint for how autonomous coworkers will be built moving forward. 2. The Core Components How exactly do these systems embed reasoning directly into the organization’s existing data and security perimeter? Let’s examine the generic coworker stack diagram in figure 1 below. Figure 1: High level architecture of an AI cowork tool. An interaction gateway is needed to coordinate the work of specialist agents, which share an intelligent context layer whose job it is to pass those agents the data they need to complete their tasks. Image generated by the author. We can see that this architecture connects users to governed data through a sequence of intelligent layers with different tasks. We can use the Databricks Genie suite as a practical blueprint to understand these core components, recognizing that the same pattern will occur in other platforms too. An AI coworker requires a primary interface where users can collaborate with it. This gateway handles natural language conversations, maintains interaction history, manages recurring questions, and facilitates shared outputs. In the Databricks ecosystem, the name of this part is Genie One. A robust coworker gateway should also be accessible via standard communication channels, such as Slack, email, or MS Teams, making it as contactable as a human colleague. The gateway routes the task alongside the user’s identity to an execution layer composed of specialized domain agents. Rather than a model attempting to solve every problem, the system uses multiple, purpose-built agents such as the following Analytical Agents: These agents specialize in text-to-SQL generation and/or reasoning over unstructured documents. Their main job is to turn natural language questions into trustworthy insights using the reasoning-action (ReACT) loop we discussed earlier. In Databricks land, this is where Genie Agents operate Developer Agents: These are coding tools, geared specifically toward engineering workflows and able to write code via notebooks and IDEs. Genie Code exemplifies this functionality. Other Domain Agents: Additional specialized agents handle tasks like system monitoring, reporting, research and graphics generation. To extend their reach, these agents increasingly utilize the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect to external data sources (SharePoint, Google Drive, email etc) or tools for specialized work (e.g. Lucidchart for diagramming) What elevates this collection of agents into a “coworker” is connectivity, with a shared context layer. This is the layer that provides the agents with the context they need to actually do their work and it consists of two parts The Semantic Engine: Just like our LTV example, real-world business analytics problems are almost always ambiguous. This engine uses knowledge graphs and asset ranking algorithms to establish the authoritative “definitions of record” so the agents know what terms like “revenue”, “LTV” etc mean to this organization. Catalog & Governance: This is the part that interfaces directly with the data and it manages identity, enforces access permissions, tracks data lineage, and maintains an audit trail. Unity Catalog is an example of such a system. At the foundation sits the organization’s governed data, which is only accessible through the scoped access granted by the shared context layer. This encompasses both structured databases (tables and metrics) and unstructured storage (files and documents). Returning to the top of the stack, we should also not forget the importance of an accessible, appealing and intuitive user interface. Ideally, an AI coworker product should be accessible from multiple devices, including desktop and mobile. It should be easy to schedule and monitor tasks, including long-running tasks that generate multiple outputs. It should be capable of generating and sharing reports with graphics that are both editable and exportable. And it should be comfortable with showing its work in a way that is easy to understand! All of these features, and most notably the critical point about sharing the same underlying data context layer explain why AI coworkers should be elevated along the spectrum beyond the standard agent — not because they are necessarily smarter or better as standalone tools, but because they are connected differently. Let’s examine this connectivity in detail next. 3. The Semantic Engine Let’s return to our executive’s question about LTV: “How has customer LTV changed over the last fiscal year and why?” This is exactly the type of question that a good AI coworker should be able to answer reliably, and is one that a typical chatbot or agent is likely to hallucinate over. There are three problems: The question is ambiguous but only a small number of interpretations matter to the user, the answer relies on a very specific calculation that produces numerically correct answers in order to be useful and the question provides no hints about where the required data lives. How are customer LTV and fiscal year defined at this organization? What types of changes does this executive care about? What other metrics or events might influence LTV to answer the “why”? What should we do if the data is sparse or unreliable? And where is all this data stored anyway? These are the types of questions that a human analyst would need to ask to get a good answer, and they provide many opportunities for LLMs to trip up — just a few generated tokens down the wrong path could mean a completely wrong and therefore useless answer. Figure 2: Diagram showing how an analytical agent interacts with a semantic engine to gather the context it needs to answer a user’s question. Image generated by the author. How do we supply an LLM with the right context to tackle this? The instinctive fix is to embed every table description and retrieve the nearest neighbors. But embedding similarity measures how alike two pieces of text sound, not which one is the source of truth. A table called prod_cust_ltv_v2_deprecated with a well-written description can easily outscore agg_finance_metrics_monthly, the table Finance actually reads for their reporting. What’s missing is a stage that understands how assets relate to one another and how much the organization trusts each one. In practice that means two cooperating components: a knowledge graph that captures relationships, and a ranking layer that scores authority. 3.1 A living knowledge graph A practical and adaptable approach to build a knowledge graph is to infer it from metadata and activity the platform already produces. This includes structural metadata like schemas, column types and table lineage, semantic metadata such as table and column descriptions, and operational data such as query history, including which tables and dashboards people actually use. This data may be messy and imprecise, but is rich and provides context that no single source holds and which naturally evolves over time. The agent no longer just knows that Table A and Table B share a customer_id column; it knows they are joined on that key every day by a production pipeline feeding a certified executive dashboard owned by the central analytics team. 3.2 Asset ranking: PageRank for data Continuing with our example, let’s say that the knowledge graph has surfaced some plausible candidates for “LTV”. Now we have to choose which one to select. This is similar to a problem that search engines originally faced over 30 years ago and solved with the PageRank algorithm. The core insight here is that authority can be inferred from structure, and a page linked to many authoritative pages is probably also authoritative. The same concept can be applied to enterprise data, and Databricks has a blog post about its approach here. If the data platform offers some mode of explicit human endorsement like “certification”, that is an excellent signal. Measures of centrality in the knowledge graph are another, which measures how many downstream pipelines, dashboards, and recurring queries depend on this asset. Then we have ownership signals — is it maintained by a team or a production service vs living in one user’s personal folder. Finally there are usage and freshness signals, which are an indication of how valuable the asset is within the organization. Figure 3 highlights these ideas in a diagram. Figure 3: Diagram showing how authority signals can be used to establish the correct meaning of business terminology. Image generated by the author. How these signals are weighted and combined is where most of the effort lies, and the companies building these systems are understandably tight-lipped about this part. Certain themes are likely present in all implementations though — for example, a way of dealing with cold starts, such as a newly certified metric with no usage history. Acknowledgement and suppression of positive feedback loops is also needed — these occur when the agent keeps recommending the most-used assets, making them even more well used. Furthermore, even authority as inferred from all the aforementioned platform signals needs to be weighed against the intent of the user asking the question — after all, in our example the “right” LTV for a Finance user may legitimately differ from the right one for Product, so authority can’t always be a single score across all users. For our executive, the effect is decisive: several deprecated tables and a marketing sandbox experiment are suppressed, and the agent is grounded in the certified LTV definition maintained by Finance — the definition of record. 3.3 Permissions: Action on Behalf of the User An AI coworker that has even a tiny chance of surfacing data a user isn’t authorized to see presents a security risk and is therefore a non-starter. It is essential that all aspects of the system we just discussed inherit the permissions of the user asking the question. In practice, this means that knowledge graph traversal is limited by gathering the user’s entitlements and identity before any search happens, and metadata access is also restricted accordingly. This is why unified governance in the data platform layer is so important. Indeed, when agents are attached to a data platform from the outside there is a risk that they might run under a broadly privileged service account and fill the context window with assets the end user could never query directly. Keeping retrieval inside the same governance layer as the data closes that gap securely. 3.4 Resolving the LTV question With this foundation in place, we can see how an AI coworker might tackle our question about LTV 1. Resolve the entities: Establish that “LTV” maps to the Finance-certified metric. “Customer” and “fiscal year” inherit that metric’s definitions rather than being guessed. 2. Plan, generate and execute the queries: Using observed lineage and join patterns in the knowledge graph to determine how to connect the metric to customer and transaction tables. All queries run on the warehouse under the user’s credentials and the results are checked and retried if needed. 3. Explain the “why.” Even if correct, the numbers only say what changed and the question asks for more than that. The system therefore decomposes the change across meaningful dimensions such as segment, region and acquisition cohort to locate where the shift occurred, and, where it has access to unstructured sources such as earnings-call notes or customer interviews, adds that valuable context. 4. Show its work! The answer comes back with the executed SQL and links to the specific assets used, so a human can verify rather than simply trust. 5. Generate a report with visuals. Humans are visual learners and we much more quickly understand graphs and charts than tabular results. The AI coworker should respect this and generate an easily digestible, visually appealing report that is preferably editable, exportable and sharable within the team. Now, let’s take a quick look at the current competitive landscape of AI coworkers and some of the challenges they face. 4. The Landscape and the Future The warehouse-native AI coworker is a relatively new product offering but it is being aggressively worked on by major players like Databricks, Snowflake and Microsoft. There are also warehouse-agnostic companies like Atlan and Cube, who argue that the semantic layer can be decoupled entirely and span multi-cloud environments rather than living inside any single execution engine. Understandably, deep technical details of how all these systems work are not readily available but it is likely that they all share similar principles as discussed in this article. These coworkers do face some interesting challenges though, which are worth keeping in mind for anyone trying them out for the first time. The first is a cold start problem, which exists whenever an organization onboards fresh to whatever platform is supplying the co-worker. Data, business logic and other assets must typically first be migrated from legacy systems before the semantic engine can work well. Workspace organization is also important — if there are many incomplete or outdated datasets, duplicated assets or sparse platform usage, the quality of the authority signal diminishes and the agents inside the cowork system may find themselves flipping back and forth between substandard assets when trying to answer questions. This can create consistency problems where the AI coworker might give different answers to the same question multiple times because it accesses different versions of the data. This emphasizes the requirement for it to show its work in a way that can be easily traced and steered mid-flow. As data and assets get added, there is also a potential for drift that leads to different results over time. What happens when the semantic layer decides that dashboard A is the most authoritative source for some metric in one week, but by the following week dashboard B has been marked certified and it becomes the source? Dashboard B may be more accurate, but anyone asking about the metric in both weeks might see a step change and be confused. Consistency issues can also occur due to differing access. Let’s say for example a company’s finance and marketing teams have different established definitions of customer churn. Executive A only has access to the finance team’s tables and metrics, while executive B has access to both finance and marketing’s tables. Both could ask the same question about churn and get different answers, and A’s coworker wouldn’t be able to explain why because it wouldn’t even know that an alternative definition exists. Ideally AI coworkers with adequate access should be able to flag discrepancies like this and pause their work to ask, but it is unclear if they are capable of this yet. There is also the challenge of long running tasks. Preparing a report about LTV is one thing, but something like designing, testing and monitoring a modification to a customer-facing app to examine how it affects LTV is another. Certainly all of the individual tasks are doable by agents, but it’s not clear to me how an AI co-worker could orchestrate such a task in one continuous process in a way that is followable and steerable by humans. No doubt this type of autonomy is coming though! Note that the bottlenecks described above are not about the models. Models are already incredibly capable. It’s the semantic foundation underneath the model and connectivity surrounding it. Organizations that invest in rigorous semantic modeling, asset certification, organization and governance will likely capture real benefits from AI coworkers. And those that don’t will simply automate organizational confusion! This is why, for the time being at least, human beings with deep experience and understanding of the connections that exist within their organization remain indispensable to the successful adoption and use of AI at enterprise scale. Disclosure: I work at Databricks. Opinions here are my own. The Anatomy of an AI Coworker: Why Context beats Intelligence was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

But embedding similarity measures how alike two pieces of text sound, not which one is the source of truth. A table called prod_cust_ltv_v2_deprecated with a well-written description can easily outscore agg_finance_metrics_monthly, the table Finance actually reads for their reporting.

What’s missing is a stage that understands how assets relate to one another and how much the organization trusts each one. In practice that means two cooperating components: a knowledge graph that captures relationships, and a ranking layer that scores authority.

3.1 A living knowledge graph

A practical and adaptable approach to build a knowledge graph is to infer it from metadata and activity the platform already produces. This includes structural metadata like schemas, column types and table lineage, semantic metadata such as table and column descriptions, and operational data such as query history, including which tables and dashboards people actually use.

This data may be messy and imprecise, but is rich and provides context that no single source holds and which naturally evolves over time. The agent no longer just knows that Table A and Table B share a customer_id column; it knows they are joined on that key every day by a production pipeline feeding a certified executive dashboard owned by the central analytics team.

3.2 Asset ranking: PageRank for data

Continuing with our example, let’s say that the knowledge graph has surfaced some plausible candidates for “LTV”. Now we have to choose which one to select. This is similar to a problem that search engines originally faced over 30 years ago and solved with the PageRank algorithm. The core insight here is that authority can be inferred from structure, and a page linked to many authoritative pages is probably also authoritative.

The same concept can be applied to enterprise data, and Databricks has a blog post about its approach here. If the data platform offers some mode of explicit human endorsement like “certification”, that is an excellent signal. Measures of centrality in the knowledge graph are another, which measures how many downstream pipelines, dashboards, and recurring queries depend on this asset. Then we have ownership signals — is it maintained by a team or a production service vs living in one user’s personal folder. Finally there are usage and freshness signals, which are an indication of how valuable the asset is within the organization. Figure 3 highlights these ideas in a diagram.

Figure 3: Diagram showing how authority signals can be used to establish the correct meaning of business terminology. Image generated by the author.

How these signals are weighted and combined is where most of the effort lies, and the companies building these systems are understandably tight-lipped about this part. Certain themes are likely present in all implementations though — for example, a way of dealing with cold starts, such as a newly certified metric with no usage history. Acknowledgement and suppression of positive feedback loops is also needed — these occur when the agent keeps recommending the most-used assets, making them even more well used. Furthermore, even authority as inferred from all the aforementioned platform signals needs to be weighed against the intent of the user asking the question — after all, in our example the “right” LTV for a Finance user may legitimately differ from the right one for Product, so authority can’t always be a single score across all users.

For our executive, the effect is decisive: several deprecated tables and a marketing sandbox experiment are suppressed, and the agent is grounded in the certified LTV definition maintained by Finance — the definition of record.

3.3 Permissions: Action on Behalf of the User

An AI coworker that has even a tiny chance of surfacing data a user isn’t authorized to see presents a security risk and is therefore a non-starter. It is essential that all aspects of the system we just discussed inherit the permissions of the user asking the question. In practice, this means that knowledge graph traversal is limited by gathering the user’s entitlements and identity before any search happens, and metadata access is also restricted accordingly.

This is why unified governance in the data platform layer is so important. Indeed, when agents are attached to a data platform from the outside there is a risk that they might run under a broadly privileged service account and fill the context window with assets the end user could never query directly. Keeping retrieval inside the same governance layer as the data closes that gap securely.

3.4 Resolving the LTV question

With this foundation in place, we can see how an AI coworker might tackle our question about LTV

1. Resolve the entities: Establish that “LTV” maps to the Finance-certified metric. “Customer” and “fiscal year” inherit that metric’s definitions rather than being guessed.

2. Plan, generate and execute the queries: Using observed lineage and join patterns in the knowledge graph to determine how to connect the metric to customer and transaction tables. All queries run on the warehouse under the user’s credentials and the results are checked and retried if needed.

3. Explain the “why.” Even if correct, the numbers only say what changed and the question asks for more than that. The system therefore decomposes the change across meaningful dimensions such as segment, region and acquisition cohort to locate where the shift occurred, and, where it has access to unstructured sources such as earnings-call notes or customer interviews, adds that valuable context.

4. Show its work! The answer comes back with the executed SQL and links to the specific assets used, so a human can verify rather than simply trust.

5. Generate a report with visuals. Humans are visual learners and we much more quickly understand graphs and charts than tabular results. The AI coworker should respect this and generate an easily digestible, visually appealing report that is preferably editable, exportable and sharable within the team.

Now, let’s take a quick look at the current competitive landscape of AI coworkers and some of the challenges they face.

4. The Landscape and the Future

The warehouse-native AI coworker is a relatively new product offering but it is being aggressively worked on by major players like Databricks, Snowflake and Microsoft. There are also warehouse-agnostic companies like Atlan and Cube, who argue that the semantic layer can be decoupled entirely and span multi-cloud environments rather than living inside any single execution engine. Understandably, deep technical details of how all these systems work are not readily available but it is likely that they all share similar principles as discussed in this article.

These coworkers do face some interesting challenges though, which are worth keeping in mind for anyone trying them out for the first time. The first is a cold start problem, which exists whenever an organization onboards fresh to whatever platform is supplying the co-worker. Data, business logic and other assets must typically first be migrated from legacy systems before the semantic engine can work well.

Workspace organization is also important — if there are many incomplete or outdated datasets, duplicated assets or sparse platform usage, the quality of the authority signal diminishes and the agents inside the cowork system may find themselves flipping back and forth between substandard assets when trying to answer questions. This can create consistency problems where the AI coworker might give different answers to the same question multiple times because it accesses different versions of the data. This emphasizes the requirement for it to show its work in a way that can be easily traced and steered mid-flow.

As data and assets get added, there is also a potential for drift that leads to different results over time. What happens when the semantic layer decides that dashboard A is the most authoritative source for some metric in one week, but by the following week dashboard B has been marked certified and it becomes the source? Dashboard B may be more accurate, but anyone asking about the metric in both weeks might see a step change and be confused.

Consistency issues can also occur due to differing access. Let’s say for example a company’s finance and marketing teams have different established definitions of customer churn. Executive A only has access to the finance team’s tables and metrics, while executive B has access to both finance and marketing’s tables. Both could ask the same question about churn and get different answers, and A’s coworker wouldn’t be able to explain why because it wouldn’t even know that an alternative definition exists. Ideally AI coworkers with adequate access should be able to flag discrepancies like this and pause their work to ask, but it is unclear if they are capable of this yet.

There is also the challenge of long running tasks. Preparing a report about LTV is one thing, but something like designing, testing and monitoring a modification to a customer-facing app to examine how it affects LTV is another. Certainly all of the individual tasks are doable by agents, but it’s not clear to me how an AI co-worker could orchestrate such a task in one continuous process in a way that is followable and steerable by humans. No doubt this type of autonomy is coming though!

Note that the bottlenecks described above are not about the models. Models are already incredibly capable. It’s the semantic foundation underneath the model and connectivity surrounding it. Organizations that invest in rigorous semantic modeling, asset certification, organization and governance will likely capture real benefits from AI coworkers. And those that don’t will simply automate organizational confusion! This is why, for the time being at least, human beings with deep experience and understanding of the connections that exist within their organization remain indispensable to the successful adoption and use of AI at enterprise scale.

Disclosure: I work at Databricks. Opinions here are my own.

items.title: HMRC signs £2.4bn CRM contract with Salesforce
items.summary: The UK’s tax agency has signed a £2.4 billion ($3.2 billion) contract with Salesforce for a new CRM platform, in one of its largest single contracts ever. HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) published details of the 15-year contract on 15 October, including the procurement of services such as Agentforce, Data Cloud, Informatica, and Experience Cloud. "[Salesforce will] unify legacy systems onto a single secure platform, delivering a 360-degree view of taxpayer interactions to enable faster, first-contact query resolution. The platform will equip HMRC teams with real-time taxpayer insights, automated workflows, and AI-assisted tools that significantly reduce manual workloads." Salesforce At a media roundtable attended by The Stack at this week’s Salesforce World Tour London event, UK&I CEO Zahra Bahrololoumi said HMRC wants to be “the most modern department on the planet,” but has struggled with handling multiple IT platforms. He said: “They want a higher yield and a more efficient way to attract and deliver a higher yield. They are the government's revenue engine, and there are individuals and businesses that should legitimately be paying tax, but… it’s not necessarily being collected at the rate that it should be.” The contract began on 30 September 2026 and will last until at least September 2036, with options to extend by a further three years and then a further two years after that up to September 2041. HMRC’s digital transformation
