items.title: Employees are vibe-coding their own apps. Cloudflare open-sources Void to give IT a handle on them
items.summary: Many companies are keen to let employees build their own applications using AI, even those with little or no programming experience. Just yesterday, Gergely Orosz of The Pragmatic Engineer highlighted the likes of Ramp and Stripe , which have developed internal tools that allow non-engineers to create software for their colleagues to use. But this newfound freedom also creates a headache for IT departments. Who tracks these applications, what company data can they access, and who’s responsible for ensuring they’re secure? In many regards, vibe-coded apps are the new shadow IT , with employees deploying software beyond the oversight of their IT teams. And that’s why Cloudflare wants to bring some order to proceedings. On Thursday, the company announced the release of Void , a collection of three open-source tools that includes a self-hosted platform where companies can deploy and manage their employees’ AI-built applications. The idea is to give staff somewhere to publish their wares, all the while letting admins control who can deploy and access them. Cloudflare’s growing JavaScript empire Cloudflare has compiled quite the collection of JavaScript expertise over the past year. Just last week, the company announced its acquisition of Deno , the company behind the JavaScript runtime founded by Node.js creator Ryan Dahl . And way back in January, it snapped up the team behind Astro , the open-source web framework. Then in June, it acquired VoidZero , the open-source tooling company founded by Vue.js and Vite creator Evan You . All three operate within the JavaScript ecosystem, albeit with different specialties spanning web frameworks, development tooling, and server-side runtimes. You formally unveiled VoidZero in October 2024, with a founding mission to bring together the disparate tools developers rely on when writing JavaScript. It already had considerable open-source pedigree, with its team contributing to established projects such as Vite and the Vitest testing framework , alongside developing the Rust-based Rolldown bundler and Oxc , a collection of tools for processing and analyzing JavaScript code. In October 2025, VoidZero announced Vite+ , an effort to bring its various development tools together under a single command-line interface (CLI). Originally conceived as a commercial offering, Vite+ was eventually released as open source under the MIT license in March, while that same month, the company also introduced Void , an early-access deployment service for Vite applications, which it hoped would provide a way to generate revenue from its open-source ecosystem. “We started working on Void before the acquisition, originally intended to make it a commercial product. But now we no longer need to, so we’ve made it open source!” Since the Cloudflare acquisition , Vite+ has continued to develop, reaching beta over the summer before its stable 1.0 release at the tail-end of September . But the biggest change, arguably, has been to Void, with Cloudflare’s ownership prompting a rethink of how the deployment platform would be offered. Indeed, the acquisition has eased the pressure on VoidZero to find its own sources of revenue, something You acknowledged on X following Thursday’s announcement. “We started working on Void before the acquisition, originally intended to make it a commercial product,” You writes . “But now we no longer need to, so we’ve made it open source!” Let's go!!! We started working on Void before the acquisition, originally intended to make it a commercial product. But now we no longer need to, so we've made it open source! You can deploy the Void platform to your own Cloudflare account and get your own instance of it :) https://t.co/iFf4AZZaIH — Evan You (@evanyou) October 15, 2026 Into the void: Full-stack apps via Vite Void comprises three main components, each serving a different purpose. The Void SDK provides the building blocks for creating full-stack applications with Vite, including server-side functionality and integrations with databases and other services. The Void CLI , meanwhile, handles deployment, automatically provisioning the necessary Cloudflare resources, while Void Platform provides a shared environment where companies can host applications and manage them through an administrative dashboard. The SDK and CLI were already distributed through npm under the MIT license, but Thursday’s release makes the full source code, including the platform, publicly available alongside Void 1.0. Running void deploy initiates the application build, provisions the required infrastructure, and publishes the finished application to Cloudflare, including applying any necessary database migrations. Deploying a Vite application to Cloudflare via the Void CLI. (credit: Cloudflare) The self-hosted platform represents a significant departure from VoidZero’s original plans. Michael Dong , who joined Cloudflare from VoidZero and is now a strategy lead at the company, says the acquisition prompted a substantial overhaul of the technology. “After the Cloudflare acquisition of VoidZero, we rebuilt the platform from the ground up to work as a self-hosted platform that anyone can install and self-host on Cloudflare.” “After the Cloudflare acquisition of VoidZero, we rebuilt the platform from the ground up to work as a self-hosted platform that anyone can install and self-host on Cloudflare,” Dong tells The New Stack . Companies can install their own instance using the void platform install command, which guides administrators through setting up authentication, database connections and storage. Installing a self-hosted Void Platform. (credit: Cloudflare) The original Void Cloud service, meanwhile, remains in operation privately. Christoph Nakazawa , formerly a product lead at VoidZero and now director of engineering at Cloudflare, says access has been limited to the company’s own team and a small group of invited testers. “It was never made publicly available,” Nakazawa tells The New Stack . Dong also says more than 100 beta users have deployed applications through the Void SDK, although he didn’t specify whether they used Void Cloud or deployed directly to Cloudflare. Keeping employees’ apps in check Void Platform gives administrators the ability to determine who can deploy applications and who can access them. They can also inspect deployments, review logs, monitor resource consumption and impose usage limits. Integration with identity providers and Cloudflare Access allows companies to restrict applications to authorised employees. Void also provides tools for troubleshooting applications after deployment. Developers can inspect error logs through the CLI and roll back problematic deployments to earlier versions. Inspecting application error logs and rolling back to a previous deployment. (credit: Cloudflare) Dong says Cloudflare is already using Void Platform internally, with corporate authentication providing a measure of protection against employees inadvertently exposing company information. “We have a Void Platform at Cloudflare that is only accessible to employees, preventing data leaks through vibe coded apps by default,” Dong says. There are limits to this protection, however. Restricting access to an application doesn’t necessarily prevent that application from retrieving sensitive information or sending it elsewhere. Moreover, Void’s documentation confirms that administrators can configure new applications to be public by default, while individual project owners can subsequently make their own applications publicly accessible. Void’s documented deployment process also contains no mandatory IT security review before an application goes live. Asked specifically whether administrators can review or approve applications before deployment, Nakazawa points to the platform’s existing access controls and the freedom companies have to extend them. “Since Void is open source, other companies can adjust the platform to their needs.” “Since Void is open source, other companies can adjust the platform to their needs,” Nakazawa says. That could mean developing additional approval mechanisms or more restrictive access policies, though organizations would have to implement those measures themselves. There is also the matter of cost. Companies self-hosting Void Platform require a paid Cloudflare Workers for Platforms plan, which starts at $25 per month, with additional charges depending on usage. The installation also requires R2 storage and a separately hosted PostgreSQL database, bringing further potential expenses. Dong confirms that developers using the Void SDK to deploy applications directly to Cloudflare don’t need a paid Cloudflare plan. However, companies hoping Cloudflare will operate their Void Platform for them are out of luck for now, with no fully managed version currently available. For Cloudflare, then, there’s a potential commercial upside to making Void open source. While the software itself is freely available, companies running their own Void Platform will consume Cloudflare infrastructure, with all the associated costs. In effect, Cloudflare stands to benefit from wider adoption of the software through the underlying services that power it. And those infrastructure requirements raise another question: how closely tied to Cloudflare will Void remain? Cloudflare has pledged to keep Vite and VoidZero’s other established development tools vendor-neutral, while Void’s automatic infrastructure provisioning currently depends on Cloudflare. Nakazawa says this reflects the platform’s origins, with Void having been designed around Cloudflare’s infrastructure from the outset. That may change as the open-source project develops, although Nakazawa stopped short of committing to support for competing cloud providers. “Now that it’s open source, we look forward to working with the community to provide support for additional providers that offer the same baseline capabilities,” Nakazawa says.

Many companies are keen to let employees build their own applications using AI, even those with little or no programming experience. Into the void: Full-stack apps via Vite

Void comprises three main components, each serving a different purpose. The Void SDK provides the building blocks for creating full-stack applications with Vite, including server-side functionality and integrations with databases and other services. The Void CLI, meanwhile, handles deployment, automatically provisioning the necessary Cloudflare resources, while Void Platform provides a shared environment where companies can host applications and manage them through an administrative dashboard.

The SDK and CLI were already distributed through npm under the MIT license, but Thursday’s release makes the full source code, including the platform, publicly available alongside Void 1.0.

Running void deploy initiates the application build, provisions the required infrastructure, and publishes the finished application to Cloudflare, including applying any necessary database migrations.

Deploying a Vite application to Cloudflare via the Void CLI. (credit: Cloudflare)

The self-hosted platform represents a significant departure from VoidZero’s original plans. Michael Dong, who joined Cloudflare from VoidZero and is now a strategy lead at the company, says the acquisition prompted a substantial overhaul of the technology.

“After the Cloudflare acquisition of VoidZero, we rebuilt the platform from the ground up to work as a self-hosted platform that anyone can install and self-host on Cloudflare.”

“After the Cloudflare acquisition of VoidZero, we rebuilt the platform from the ground up to work as a self-hosted platform that anyone can install and self-host on Cloudflare,” Dong tells The New Stack.

Companies can install their own instance using the void platform install command, which guides administrators through setting up authentication, database connections and storage.

Installing a self-hosted Void Platform. (credit: Cloudflare)

The original Void Cloud service, meanwhile, remains in operation privately. Christoph Nakazawa, formerly a product lead at VoidZero and now director of engineering at Cloudflare, says access has been limited to the company’s own team and a small group of invited testers.

“It was never made publicly available,” Nakazawa tells The New Stack.

Dong also says more than 100 beta users have deployed applications through the Void SDK, although he didn’t specify whether they used Void Cloud or deployed directly to Cloudflare.

Keeping employees’ apps in check

Void Platform gives administrators the ability to determine who can deploy applications and who can access them. They can also inspect deployments, review logs, monitor resource consumption and impose usage limits. Integration with identity providers and Cloudflare Access allows companies to restrict applications to authorised employees.

Void also provides tools for troubleshooting applications after deployment. Developers can inspect error logs through the CLI and roll back problematic deployments to earlier versions.

Inspecting application error logs and rolling back to a previous deployment. (credit: Cloudflare)

Dong says Cloudflare is already using Void Platform internally, with corporate authentication providing a measure of protection against employees inadvertently exposing company information.

“We have a Void Platform at Cloudflare that is only accessible to employees, preventing data leaks through vibe coded apps by default,” Dong says.

There are limits to this protection, however. Restricting access to an application doesn’t necessarily prevent that application from retrieving sensitive information or sending it elsewhere. Moreover, Void’s documentation confirms that administrators can configure new applications to be public by default, while individual project owners can subsequently make their own applications publicly accessible.

Void’s documented deployment process also contains no mandatory IT security review before an application goes live. Asked specifically whether administrators can review or approve applications before deployment, Nakazawa points to the platform’s existing access controls and the freedom companies have to extend them.

“Since Void is open source, other companies can adjust the platform to their needs.”

“Since Void is open source, other companies can adjust the platform to their needs,” Nakazawa says.

That could mean developing additional approval mechanisms or more restrictive access policies, though organizations would have to implement those measures themselves.

There is also the matter of cost. Companies self-hosting Void Platform require a paid Cloudflare Workers for Platforms plan, which starts at $25 per month, with additional charges depending on usage. While the software itself is freely available, companies running their own Void Platform will consume Cloudflare infrastructure, with all the associated costs. Cloudflare has pledged to keep Vite and VoidZero’s other established development tools vendor-neutral, while Void’s automatic infrastructure provisioning currently depends on Cloudflare. items.title: Jambavan: My Own Local AI Coding Assistant
items.summary: How I’m using VS Code, Ollama, repository summaries, and reviewable edits to build a local-first coding companion. AI-generated illustration created by the author using OpenAI image-generation tools. Disclosure: The project implementation and engineering decisions described here are my own. I used AI assistance to edit and restructure portions of this article. We’ve all seen it: an AI assistant gives a confident answer about a codebase, but the suggestion doesn’t fit the project. It may miss a dependency, overlook a convention, or propose a change that makes sense in isolation but not in the system where it needs to live. The problem isn’t always the model. Sometimes it simply doesn’t have the right context. I think about it like a volleyball team. A player can have an excellent serve and a powerful spike, but individual skill isn’t enough. They need to understand the formation, read their teammates, and adjust to the play already in motion. A coding assistant needs a similar awareness of the project it has joined. That idea led me to build Jambavan , an experimental, local-first AI coding assistant inside VS Code. It connects to an Ollama model, gathers selected repository context, creates project notes, remembers developer feedback, and proposes code changes for review. It is not an autonomous coding system, and I want to be clear about that distinction. The name Jambavan comes from the Ramayana. Jambavan is the wise King of the Bears who guides Rama in his search for Sita. I liked the idea of an assistant that helps a developer understand a problem and make a better decision without taking control away from them. The Architecture: Keep the Model Behind a Controlled Workflow Simplified architecture of Jambavan, showing how the VS Code extension connects to a local AI model and uses repository context, project notes, and saved preferences to assist with coding. Diagram by the author. I built the extension with TypeScript and the VS Code Extension API. The chat interface lives in an Activity Bar webview, but the webview does not read workspace files directly. It sends messages to the extension host, which gathers context, calls the configured Ollama endpoint, and returns the answer to the UI. The basic flow is: VS Code chat → extension host → bounded workspace context → Ollama /api/chat → answer and context list That separation matters. The extension host is responsible for deciding what information to include; the model doesn’t get unrestricted access to the repository just because I asked it a question. The model name and Ollama URL are configurable. The defaults are qwen3.5:9b and http://localhost:11434. The key engineering question turned out not to be how to connect a chat window to a model. It was how to choose the information the model should see—and how to handle what it returns. 1. Give the Model a Bounded View of the Repository Sending an entire repository with every prompt is wasteful and can bury the useful details in unrelated material. Jambavan assembles a limited context based on the request. In the chat flow, that can include up to 15 repository paths, up to 800 characters of project guidance, up to 1,800 characters from the active file, up to two selected files with 900 characters each, repository notes, and a limited amount of recent conversation. Those numbers are implementation limits, not a claim that this is the ideal context size for every project. I chose them to keep the request focused and predictable while I learn what information helps most. I also show a collapsible list of the context items supplied with each answer. That small UI detail has been useful for debugging. If the answer is wrong, I can ask: Did Jambavan include the relevant file? Was project guidance missing? Did it only send an excerpt that left out an important function? Jambavan shows the files included in the context sent to the model. Screenshot by the author. The list shows what went into the request; it cannot prove which parts the model relied on internally. Still, the visibility makes the system easier to investigate than a chat box that hides its inputs. 2. Give the Repository a Memory That Can Be Updated Incrementally I wanted Jambavan to retain a map of the codebase so I wouldn’t need to explain the project from scratch in every conversation. Its scanner examines supported source, text, configuration, and documentation files. It skips common generated and dependency directories, ignores files above its size limit, and caps the repository inventory at 1,000 files. For each eligible file, it calculates a SHA-256 hash. If the hash matches the version already in the index, the scanner skips the summarization request. If the file changed, Jambavan sends a bounded excerpt to Ollama and asks for a short summary. The summarization prompt tells the model to treat repository text as untrusted data, summarize only what the source supports, identify the file path, and avoid inventing behavior. That is a useful boundary, though it is not a substitute for verifying the source. The core decision is small. This excerpt is from the current implementation in repoKnowledge.ts : const sha256 = createHash("sha256").update(bytes).digest("hex"); if (index[candidate.path]?.sha256 === sha256) { unchanged += 1; continue; } The hash doesn’t tell Jambavan what the code means. It simply tells the scanner whether the file has changed, so unchanged files don’t need to be summarized again. The scanner also has explicit processing limits. It considers up to 1,000 eligible repository files, skips files larger than 100 KB, and sends a maximum of 6,000 characters from each changed file to Ollama. Each generated summary is capped at 900 characters, and changed files are processed in batches of up to 20. After each summary is completed, Jambavan saves its hash and summary and regenerates the readable notes. A successful scan can continue through additional batches while changed files remain. If a scan is cancelled, summaries already saved are retained. Jambavan writes the results to two locations: JAMBAVAN_NOTES.md is a readable map of the repository for a developer. .jambavan/scan-index.json stores the file hashes and summaries used by later scans. Generated repository notes and the scan index from a separate test repository analyzed by Jambavan. Screenshot by the author. The notes are a navigation aid, not a source of truth. A summary can be incomplete or wrong, so I still need to check the original file before acting on a recommendation. 3. Remember Useful Feedback Without Pretending to Train the Model Repository notes capture information about the codebase, but they don’t capture every preference that emerges while working with an assistant. I added local conversation history and three feedback actions: Helpful , Not helpful , and Remember . Jambavan includes three feedback actions: Helpful , Not helpful , and Remember . Screenshot by the author. Chat history and saved choices live in VS Code extension storage, separately from the repository notes. When I ask a new question, Jambavan uses keyword overlap to select a small number of relevant saved choices and can include them in the prompt. The current memory store can retain up to 100 chat messages and 100 saved feedback choices for a workspace. When I ask a new question, Jambavan ranks saved choices using keyword overlap and selects up to five matches, with the combined text capped at 2,500 characters. This is intentionally simple. It isn’t semantic search, a vector database, or model training. It doesn’t change Qwen’s weights. If I describe the same idea using different words, keyword matching may fail to retrieve a relevant preference. Making memory inspectable, editable, and easier to clear is still on my roadmap. For now, the point is to preserve selected context between interactions without claiming the model has learned in the machine-learning sense. 4. Treat Code Edits as Proposals, Not Commands Explanations are relatively easy to discard. A source-code change can quietly break something. I didn’t want Jambavan to overwrite a file as soon as the model returned text, so I built an edit workflow around review. When I enter /edit followed by a request, Jambavan reads the active file along with bounded project guidance and repository notes. For supported, smaller files, it asks the model for a complete replacement, validates the response, and opens a VS Code diff. The original file remains unchanged until I choose to apply the proposal. If I apply it, the editor buffer changes; I still review and save it myself. The extension also checks whether the active file changed while the model was generating the proposal. It rejects empty or suspiciously shortened outputs rather than treating every response as valid code. The current full-file workflow is limited to files of 7,000 characters or fewer, and Jambavan does not run tests or terminal commands after an edit. If a full-file proposal fails its validation checks, Jambavan tries a focused fallback. For other supported requests, it asks the model for an anchored edit: an operation such as inserting before or after one exact, existing line. The extension only applies that proposal to a temporary copy if the anchor is unique, then opens the result in a diff. When Jambavan couldn’t safely generate a complete file edit, it offered a focused code suggestion instead. The proposed comment is anchored before the INSERT IGNORE INTO TRANSACTIONS statement, leaving the original file unchanged until I review and apply the suggestion. Screenshot by the author. One failure made me add a more specific recovery path. When I asked Jambavan to add an index to a SQL table, Qwen sometimes failed to return the structured edit the extension expected. A stronger prompt alone wasn’t a sufficient fallback. I added a narrow SQL index handler. It checks that the active SQL file contains the requested table definition, verifies that the requested columns are declared, and rejects the request if an equivalent index is already present. If those checks pass, Jambavan prepares the index change and opens it in a diff for review. This handler supports a specific table-definition pattern; it is not a general SQL migration engine. A request to index MEMBER_ID and LAST_4 produces a proposed SQL change in VS Code's diff view. The new index is presented for review rather than applied automatically. Screenshot by the author. That distinction is important: the fallback is deliberately constrained. It doesn’t give the model unrestricted permission to modify a file. It handles one predictable kind of request when the model’s formatting fails, while keeping the developer in the approval loop. 5. A Timeout Forced Me to Make Scans Recoverable The first scanning approach assumed the work would finish in one uninterrupted run. During testing, Ollama returned a response-header timeout after several files had already been summarized. The problem wasn’t only that a request failed. It was that a long-running batch needed a better strategy for receiving output and retaining completed work. I changed the scanner to consume streamed responses from Ollama. More importantly, it now saves each completed file’s summary and hash to the index and updates JAMBAVAN_NOTES.md before moving on. If a later request fails, summaries that were already saved remain available. A subsequent scan can use the hashes to skip unchanged files. Jambavan displays scan progress while updating repository notes in batches. Making progress visible helps distinguish a long-running scan from an operation that has stopped responding. Screenshot by the author. The scan therefore isn’t treated as a single all-or-nothing operation. It can preserve completed work and make a later scan more efficient by skipping files that have already been summarized and haven’t changed. That is a familiar idea from data engineering: make each unit of work observable and recoverable instead of assuming the happy path will always succeed. Local-First Is a Trade-Off, Not a Guarantee I chose Ollama because I wanted to experiment with an assistant that could run on my machine. Local inference can avoid sending prompts to a hosted model service when the endpoint is genuinely local, and it can avoid some network round trips. It may also reduce per-request API costs for workloads that would otherwise use a paid remote model. Those benefits aren’t automatic. Local models can be slower or less capable than hosted alternatives, and hardware, electricity, maintenance, and model upgrades still have costs. I haven’t benchmarked Jambavan against a hosted coding assistant, so I won’t claim it is faster or cheaper overall. My goal is to explore which everyday tasks a local model can handle usefully and where a remote model might still be the better option. Privacy also depends on the full data flow. Jambavan’s default Ollama URL is local, but the URL is configurable; prompts go wherever that configured endpoint points. Chat history and saved choices live in VS Code extension storage, while generated repository notes are written into the workspace. During scanning, Jambavan skips files whose names look sensitive and redacts several common secret formats from excerpts. That is a basic precaution, not a comprehensive secret detector. Developers should inspect the context list and avoid putting credentials in prompts or source files. For me, local-first doesn’t mean that every task must stay on-device. It means I can make that choice deliberately instead of making remote inference an unavoidable default. Try the Development Version Jambavan is an early prototype. You can explore the source on GitHub . To run the current development version, you’ll need VS Code, Node.js with npm, Ollama, and the configured model available locally. Clone the Jambavan repository and open the folder in VS Code. In the integrated terminal, run npm install. Start Ollama and make sure the configured model is available. The default model tag is qwen3.5:9b; ollama list can show which models are installed. Press F5 . VS Code opens an Extension Development Host window for testing the extension. In that second window, open Jambavan from the Activity Bar. Ask a question, run /scan to refresh repository notes, or use /edit followed by a request to propose a change to the active file. F5 runs the development version in a temporary test window. The project is not yet packaged as a regular VS Code extension. It also does not have an automated test script, does not execute shell commands, and does not monitor GitHub directly. Local workspace changes become visible after they are present in the checkout. What I Want to Build Next There are still a few things I want to improve in Jambavan. I want it to do a better job of finding the right files for a question, give me more control over what it remembers, and eventually help me run tests and understand failures — with my permission before it executes anything. I’m not trying to build all of this at once. I’d rather add one feature, test it, see where it breaks, and then move on to the next. Just calling something an AI agent doesn’t make it a good one. It needs to behave predictably, and I need to be able to trust what it’s doing. Building Jambavan has reminded me of a lesson from data engineering: model output is only one part of a dependable system. Context selection, persistence, validation, failure handling, visibility, and user control determine whether that output becomes useful in practice. The code is available on GitHub . I’m still building, testing, and discovering where the design needs to improve. That’s part of the project, not something I want to hide. For me, the bigger question is this: Can I build an AI coding assistant that understands my project well enough to be a useful teammate, while still leaving the important decisions in my hands? That’s what I want to find out with Jambavan. Jambavan: My Own Local AI Coding Assistant was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

We’ve all seen it: an AI assistant gives a confident answer about a codebase, but the suggestion doesn’t fit the project. It may miss a dependency, overlook a convention, or propose a change that makes sense in isolation but not in the system where it needs to live.

The problem isn’t always the model. Sometimes it simply doesn’t have the right context.

I think about it like a volleyball team. A player can have an excellent serve and a powerful spike, but individual skill isn’t enough. They need to understand the formation, read their teammates, and adjust to the play already in motion. A coding assistant needs a similar awareness of the project it has joined.

That idea led me to build Jambavan, an experimental, local-first AI coding assistant inside VS Code. It connects to an Ollama model, gathers selected repository context, creates project notes, remembers developer feedback, and proposes code changes for review. It is not an autonomous coding system, and I want to be clear about that distinction.

The name Jambavan comes from the Ramayana. Jambavan is the wise King of the Bears who guides Rama in his search for Sita. I liked the idea of an assistant that helps a developer understand a problem and make a better decision without taking control away from them.

The Architecture: Keep the Model Behind a Controlled WorkflowSimplified architecture of Jambavan, showing how the VS Code extension connects to a local AI model and uses repository context, project notes, and saved preferences to assist with coding. Diagram by the author.

I built the extension with TypeScript and the VS Code Extension API. The chat interface lives in an Activity Bar webview, but the webview does not read workspace files directly. It sends messages to the extension host, which gathers context, calls the configured Ollama endpoint, and returns the answer to the UI.

The basic flow is:

VS Code chat → extension host → bounded workspace context → Ollama /api/chat → answer and context list

That separation matters. The extension host is responsible for deciding what information to include; the model doesn’t get unrestricted access to the repository just because I asked it a question.

The model name and Ollama URL are configurable. The defaults are qwen3.5:9b and http://localhost:11434. The key engineering question turned out not to be how to connect a chat window to a model. It was how to choose the information the model should see—and how to handle what it returns.

If the answer is wrong, I can ask: Did Jambavan include the relevant file? Was project guidance missing? Did it only send an excerpt that left out an important function?

The list shows what went into the request; it cannot prove which parts the model relied on internally. Still, the visibility makes the system easier to investigate than a chat box that hides its inputs.

Its scanner examines supported source, text, configuration, and documentation files. It skips common generated and dependency directories, ignores files above its size limit, and caps the repository inventory at 1,000 files.

For each eligible file, it calculates a SHA-256 hash. If the hash matches the version already in the index, the scanner skips the summarization request. If the file changed, Jambavan sends a bounded excerpt to Ollama and asks for a short summary. The summarization prompt tells the model to treat repository text as untrusted data, summarize only what the source supports, identify the file path, and avoid inventing behavior. That is a useful boundary, though it is not a substitute for verifying the source.

The core decision is small. This excerpt is from the current implementation in repoKnowledge.ts:

const sha256 = createHash("sha256").update(bytes).digest("hex");

if (index[candidate.path]?.sha256 === sha256) {
  unchanged += 1;
  continue;
}

The hash doesn’t tell Jambavan what the code means. It simply tells the scanner whether the file has changed, so unchanged files don’t need to be summarized again.

The scanner also has explicit processing limits. It considers up to 1,000 eligible repository files, skips files larger than 100 KB, and sends a maximum of 6,000 characters from each changed file to Ollama. Each generated summary is capped at 900 characters, and changed files are processed in batches of up to 20.

After each summary is completed, Jambavan saves its hash and summary and regenerates the readable notes. A successful scan can continue through additional batches while changed files remain. If a scan is cancelled, summaries already saved are retained.

Jambavan writes the results to two locations:

  • JAMBAVAN_NOTES.md is a readable map of the repository for a developer.
  • .jambavan/scan-index.json stores the file hashes and summaries used by later scans.
Generated repository notes and the scan index from a separate test repository analyzed by Jambavan. Screenshot by the author.

The notes are a navigation aid, not a source of truth. A summary can be incomplete or wrong, so I still need to check the original file before acting on a recommendation.

3. Remember Useful Feedback Without Pretending to Train the Model

Repository notes capture information about the codebase, but they don’t capture every preference that emerges while working with an assistant. I added local conversation history and three feedback actions: Helpful, Not helpful, and Remember.

Jambavan includes three feedback actions: Helpful, Not helpful, and Remember. Screenshot by the author.

Chat history and saved choices live in VS Code extension storage, separately from the repository notes. When I ask a new question, Jambavan uses keyword overlap to select a small number of relevant saved choices and can include them in the prompt.

The current memory store can retain up to 100 chat messages and 100 saved feedback choices for a workspace. When I ask a new question, Jambavan ranks saved choices using keyword overlap and selects up to five matches, with the combined text capped at 2,500 characters.

This is intentionally simple. It isn’t semantic search, a vector database, or model training. It doesn’t change Qwen’s weights. If I describe the same idea using different words, keyword matching may fail to retrieve a relevant preference. Making memory inspectable, editable, and easier to clear is still on my roadmap.

For now, the point is to preserve selected context between interactions without claiming the model has learned in the machine-learning sense.

4. Treat Code Edits as Proposals, Not Commands

Explanations are relatively easy to discard. A source-code change can quietly break something. I didn’t want Jambavan to overwrite a file as soon as the model returned text, so I built an edit workflow around review.

When I enter /edit followed by a request, Jambavan reads the active file along with bounded project guidance and repository notes. If I apply it, the editor buffer changes; I still review and save it myself.

The extension also checks whether the active file changed while the model was generating the proposal. It rejects empty or suspiciously shortened outputs rather than treating every response as valid code. The current full-file workflow is limited to files of 7,000 characters or fewer, and Jambavan does not run tests or terminal commands after an edit.

If a full-file proposal fails its validation checks, Jambavan tries a focused fallback. For other supported requests, it asks the model for an anchored edit: an operation such as inserting before or after one exact, existing line. The extension only applies that proposal to a temporary copy if the anchor is unique, then opens the result in a diff.

When Jambavan couldn’t safely generate a complete file edit, it offered a focused code suggestion instead. The proposed comment is anchored before the INSERT IGNORE INTO TRANSACTIONS statement, leaving the original file unchanged until I review and apply the suggestion. Screenshot by the author.

One failure made me add a more specific recovery path. When I asked Jambavan to add an index to a SQL table, Qwen sometimes failed to return the structured edit the extension expected. A stronger prompt alone wasn’t a sufficient fallback.

I added a narrow SQL index handler. It checks that the active SQL file contains the requested table definition, verifies that the requested columns are declared, and rejects the request if an equivalent index is already present. If those checks pass, Jambavan prepares the index change and opens it in a diff for review. This handler supports a specific table-definition pattern; it is not a general SQL migration engine.

A request to index MEMBER_ID and LAST_4 produces a proposed SQL change in VS Code's diff view. The new index is presented for review rather than applied automatically. Screenshot by the author.

That distinction is important: the fallback is deliberately constrained. It doesn’t give the model unrestricted permission to modify a file. It handles one predictable kind of request when the model’s formatting fails, while keeping the developer in the approval loop.

5. A Timeout Forced Me to Make Scans Recoverable

The first scanning approach assumed the work would finish in one uninterrupted run. During testing, Ollama returned a response-header timeout after several files had already been summarized.

The problem wasn’t only that a request failed. It was that a long-running batch needed a better strategy for receiving output and retaining completed work.

I changed the scanner to consume streamed responses from Ollama. More importantly, it now saves each completed file’s summary and hash to the index and updates JAMBAVAN_NOTES.md before moving on. If a later request fails, summaries that were already saved remain available. A subsequent scan can use the hashes to skip unchanged files.

Jambavan displays scan progress while updating repository notes in batches. Making progress visible helps distinguish a long-running scan from an operation that has stopped responding. Screenshot by the author.

The scan therefore isn’t treated as a single all-or-nothing operation. It can preserve completed work and make a later scan more efficient by skipping files that have already been summarized and haven’t changed. That is a familiar idea from data engineering: make each unit of work observable and recoverable instead of assuming the happy path will always succeed.

Local-First Is a Trade-Off, Not a Guarantee

I chose Ollama because I wanted to experiment with an assistant that could run on my machine. Local inference can avoid sending prompts to a hosted model service when the endpoint is genuinely local, and it can avoid some network round trips. It may also reduce per-request API costs for workloads that would otherwise use a paid remote model.

Those benefits aren’t automatic. Local models can be slower or less capable than hosted alternatives, and hardware, electricity, maintenance, and model upgrades still have costs. I haven’t benchmarked Jambavan against a hosted coding assistant, so I won’t claim it is faster or cheaper overall. My goal is to explore which everyday tasks a local model can handle usefully and where a remote model might still be the better option.

Privacy also depends on the full data flow. Jambavan’s default Ollama URL is local, but the URL is configurable; prompts go wherever that configured endpoint points. Chat history and saved choices live in VS Code extension storage, while generated repository notes are written into the workspace. During scanning, Jambavan skips files whose names look sensitive and redacts several common secret formats from excerpts. That is a basic precaution, not a comprehensive secret detector. Developers should inspect the context list and avoid putting credentials in prompts or source files.

For me, local-first doesn’t mean that every task must stay on-device. It means I can make that choice deliberately instead of making remote inference an unavoidable default.

Try the Development Version

Jambavan is an early prototype. You can explore the source on GitHub. To run the current development version, you’ll need VS Code, Node.js with npm, Ollama, and the configured model available locally.

  1. Clone the Jambavan repository and open the folder in VS Code.
  2. In the integrated terminal, run npm install.
  3. Start Ollama and make sure the configured model is available. The default model tag is qwen3.5:9b; ollama list can show which models are installed.
  4. Press F5. VS Code opens an Extension Development Host window for testing the extension.
  5. In that second window, open Jambavan from the Activity Bar. Ask a question, run /scan to refresh repository notes, or use /edit followed by a request to propose a change to the active file.

F5 runs the development version in a temporary test window. The project is not yet packaged as a regular VS Code extension. It also does not have an automated test script, does not execute shell commands, and does not monitor GitHub directly. Local workspace changes become visible after they are present in the checkout.

There are still a few things I want to improve in Jambavan. I want it to do a better job of finding the right files for a question, give me more control over what it remembers, and eventually help me run tests and understand failures — with my permission before it executes anything.

I’m not trying to build all of this at once. I’d rather add one feature, test it, see where it breaks, and then move on to the next. Just calling something an AI agent doesn’t make it a good one. It needs to behave predictably, and I need to be able to trust what it’s doing.

Building Jambavan has reminded me of a lesson from data engineering: model output is only one part of a dependable system. Context selection, persistence, validation, failure handling, visibility, and user control determine whether that output becomes useful in practice.

The code is available on GitHub. I’m still building, testing, and discovering where the design needs to improve. That’s part of the project, not something I want to hide.

For me, the bigger question is this: Can I build an AI coding assistant that understands my project well enough to be a useful teammate, while still leaving the important decisions in my hands?

That’s what I want to find out with Jambavan.

items.title: Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra: NVIDIA RTX Spark means business
items.summary: NVIDIA officially entered the Windows PC race this week, and its arrival brings a formidable new competitor to the premium AI PC market. With its RTX Spark platform, NVIDIA is bringing its Grace Arm CPU architecture, Blackwell GPU technology and extensive software ecosystem together in a new generation of Windows laptops. Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra is among the first systems to showcase this collaboration, leveraging NVIDIA’s tech and putting it squarely in competition with Intel, AMD, Qualcomm and even Apple for high-performance local AI and creation-optimized laptops. For Microsoft, the partnership expands the capabilities of Windows on Arm considerably, particularly for local AI development, content creation and other demanding professional workloads. Starting at $2,599.99, Surface Laptop Ultra is clearly a premium offering, but its combination of processing horsepower, large, unified memory capacity, and premium industrial design gives it an interesting position in the market. My personal testing suggests NVIDIA and Microsoft have delivered a compelling platform with strong AI throughput, graphics performance and competitive CPU compute. Just as importantly, the Surface Laptop Ultra offers a glimpse of how AI development and local AI agent workflows could become more practical on a portable Windows PC. NVIDIA RTX Spark brings Grace Blackwell to Windows on Arm At the heart of Surface Laptop Ultra is NVIDIA’s RTX Spark N1X SoC, combining up to 20 Grace Arm CPU cores with a Blackwell GPU featuring up to 6,144 CUDA cores. Configurations support up to 128GB of unified memory, shared between CPU and GPU. The Surface Laptop Ultra model I tested has this full-fat configuration with an eye-watering $5,899.99 price tag (thanks, memory crunch ), though there are lower-cost base configs as noted previously, offering an 18-core CPU with a 5,120-core GPU and 24GB of unified memory. NVIDIA and Microsoft Regardless, this architecture is particularly powerful for running on-device AI. Rather than being constrained by the dedicated graphics memory found in conventional laptops with discrete GPUs, RTX Spark can make a much larger pool of memory available to GPU-accelerated applications. This allows larger language models, longer context windows and demanding inference workloads to run locally. It’s similar in design to AMD’s Ryzen AI Max series, aka Strix Halo, in that regard, but with a more potent GPU engine on board. NVIDIA’s CUDA ecosystem is another important advantage. Developers can leverage familiar tools including TensorRT, PyTorch and llama.cpp, with a base software foundation that also extends into NVIDIA-powered workstations and data center infrastructure. For organizations building AI applications, this offers a solid development path. Models and workflows can be prototyped locally before moving to larger systems, reducing cloud compute and token expense while allowing sensitive data to remain on-device. (See: Around the corner: Agentic AI PCs that cut token costs .) Microsoft has also optimized Windows 11 for RTX Spark, with improvements to workload scheduling, power management, memory allocation and application compatibility. These platform-level investments were essential to making NVIDIA’s Arm architecture practical for everyday Windows computing, and I was able to put some of them to the test in the few days I’ve had the machine on hand. Surface Laptop Ultra: Premium design meets practical function Microsoft has given RTX Spark an appropriately premium home with this machine. The Surface Laptop Ultra features a 15-inch PixelSense Ultra mini-LED touch display with up to 2,000 nits of claimed peak HDR brightness, a 120Hz refresh rate and excellent potential for creative work requiring high accuracy and wide gamut coverage. Dave Altavilla The machine’s aluminum chassis is less than 18 mm thick, and it weighs in at under 4.5 pounds. It’s not an ultraportable per se, but considering the horsepower on board, Microsoft has struck a reasonable balance between portability and performance. The design is refreshingly understated, with clean lines and rigid aluminum construction. My initial hands-on impressions have been particularly positive, thanks to the keyboard’s tactile response, smooth and responsive haptic touchpad, and bright, high-contrast display. The larger touchpad should be especially welcome for users navigating complex applications, while the touchscreen adds flexibility for reviewing documents, annotating designs, and interacting directly with creative content. Connectivity options are also very good, relative to other premium laptops. Microsoft includes three USB-C ports, HDMI, USB-A, an SD card reader and a headphone jack. One USB-C connection features Microsoft’s new magnetic charging mechanism, combining the convenience and safety of a breakaway power connector with the versatility of a standard USB-C port. Microsoft has also designed the cooling system with large fans and significant thermal capacity, while making the machine’s internal SSD removable and offering good internal serviceability in general. These are practical considerations for professional users and IT departments concerned with reliability, maintenance and long-term ownership. Battery life and sustained performance under prolonged workloads are important aspects Microsoft focused on for the overall experience, particularly for a machine designed to deliver workstation-class capabilities away from a desk. More on this shortly. Local AI agents: Moving from inference to action RTX Spark also supports locally running autonomous AI agents, including one that I tested out called Hermes, which can execute multi-step workflows, access files and interact with applications. Its potential impact spans software development, research, document analysis, business automation and many other disciplines. Hermes provides the agent framework, while supported models leverage RTX Spark’s CUDA-accelerated inference and unified memory. For businesses, local agents can keep sensitive data on-device and reduce cloud inference costs, provided they’re configured appropriately. However, granting agents access to files, code execution and corporate systems introduces security risks. Microsoft’s Execution Containers and NVIDIA’s OpenShell aim to provide isolation and access controls, though their effectiveness depends on proper enterprise policy implementation. Hermes running Qwen3.8-27B locally on Surface Laptop Ultra, generating a benchmark report. Dave Altavilla To test this capability, I ran Hermes with the Qwen3.8-27B language model locally on the Surface Laptop Ultra. I asked it to extract benchmark charts from an Excel spreadsheet and create a formatted Word report with performance commentary. Hermes autonomously generated and executed Python scripts, processed the spreadsheet and assembled the document in approximately five minutes. Color me impressed. That’s a respectable turnaround for a task requiring several manual steps. My results demonstrate how local AI agents can streamline reporting and analysis without cloud-hosted model inference. Human review remains essential, but this was a promising demonstration of practical, real-world agentic AI on a Windows laptop. AI performance: Strong results as expected My team’s preliminary AI benchmarks highlight the advantages of NVIDIA’s RTX Spark architecture. However, we’re still digging deeper into AI-enabled use cases and performance. In UL Procyon’s AI Text Generation benchmark using Phi 3.5, a family of lightweight, open-source small language models (SLMs) released by Microsoft, the Surface Laptop Ultra scored 2,703, compared with 2,027 for Lenovo’s Intel Core Ultra X9 388H-powered IdeaPad Pro 5, an advantage of approximately 33%. Dave Altavilla The difference was even more substantial in MLPerf’s Flux 2 Klein 4B image generation workload, where the Surface Laptop Ultra delivered 26.97 images per minute versus 9.96 for the Lenovo machine, or roughly 2.7 times the throughput. These results demonstrate the platform’s potential for accelerating local inference, image generation, agentic workflows and other AI workloads. Actual application performance will depend on model selection, software optimization and available system memory, though NVIDIA does provide a nice memory partitioning tool in the NVIDIA App for Windows. Content creation, gaming and battery life: Blackwell’s versatility RTX Spark’s Blackwell GPU delivers impressive graphics performance, extending the Surface Laptop Ultra’s capabilities beyond AI development and everyday creation or productivity tasks. Dave Altavilla In 3DMark Steel Nomad Lite, the Surface Laptop Ultra achieved 98.29 FPS, more than double the 46.07 FPS of Lenovo’s Core Ultra X9-powered IdeaPad Pro 5. In the ray-tracing-focused 3DMark Speed Way test, it delivered 30.31 FPS versus 19.72 FPS for the ASUS ROG Flow Z13, powered by AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ 395 and Radeon 8060S graphics. Dave Altavilla Actual gaming performance was similarly strong. In Cyberpunk 2077 , the Surface Laptop Ultra averaged 71.05 FPS, ahead of the ROG Flow Z13’s 63.76 FPS. However, the AMD system narrowly led in The Talos Principle 2 , delivering 89.5 FPS versus the Surface’s 84.5 FPS at 1080p medium settings. CPU performance for tasks like 3D rendering also holds up well. In Cinebench 2026, the Surface scored 6,787 in the multi-threaded test, edging out the AMD-powered ROG Flow Z13’s 6,546. Notably, the Surface retained 99% of its multi-threaded performance on battery power as well. For creative professionals, native Arm applications including Blender, DaVinci Resolve and Adobe Photoshop offer opportunities to leverage RTX Spark’s potent GPU. However, Windows on Arm compatibility remains a consideration. Microsoft’s Prism translation supports many x86 applications, but specialized software, drivers and certain games (like EA anti-cheat-supported titles currently) may still encounter limitations. Dave Altavilla Battery endurance was respectable for the Surface Laptop Ultra, at 14 hours and 35 minutes in my PCMark video playback testing, though competing mainstream thin-and-light laptops lasted considerably longer. The Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark operate within a different power envelope, however, more akin to a beefier gaming laptop, rather than a svelte 2 – 3-lb business machine. Final thoughts: A serious new AI Windows PC competitor The Surface Laptop Ultra marks an important milestone for NVIDIA’s expansion into Windows PCs and Microsoft’s ambitions for high-performance Arm-based computing. My initial testing shows the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra delivers exceptionally strong AI acceleration, competitive multi-threaded CPU performance and impressive graphics horsepower. Combined with Microsoft’s premium industrial design, extensive connectivity and I/O options, and Windows platform integration, RTX Spark makes a convincing first impression. Starting at $2,600, this is a specialized, premium system, and mainstream business users will find more economical alternatives to be sure. However, for developers (even vibe coders), creative professionals and organizations evaluating local AI workflows, the Surface Laptop Ultra offers a compelling combination of performance, beautiful industrial design, portability and local AI capability, especially with its higher-tier memory configurations. NVIDIA has arrived in the Windows PC market with serious technology, and Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra is an impressive first showcase of what this new partnership can deliver.

NVIDIA officially entered the Windows PC race this week, and its arrival brings a formidable new competitor to the premium AI PC market. With its RTX Spark platform, NVIDIA is bringing its Grace Arm CPU architecture, Blackwell GPU technology and extensive software ecosystem together in a new generation of Windows laptops. Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra is among the first systems to showcase this collaboration, leveraging NVIDIA’s tech and putting it squarely in competition with Intel, AMD, Qualcomm and even Apple for high-performance local AI and creation-optimized laptops.

For Microsoft, the partnership expands the capabilities of Windows on Arm considerably, particularly for local AI development, content creation and other demanding professional workloads. Starting at $2,599.99, Surface Laptop Ultra is clearly a premium offering, but its combination of processing horsepower, large, unified memory capacity, and premium industrial design gives it an interesting position in the market.

My personal testing suggests NVIDIA and Microsoft have delivered a compelling platform with strong AI throughput, graphics performance and competitive CPU compute. Just as importantly, the Surface Laptop Ultra offers a glimpse of how AI development and local AI agent workflows could become more practical on a portable Windows PC.

NVIDIA RTX Spark brings Grace Blackwell to Windows on Arm

At the heart of Surface Laptop Ultra is NVIDIA’s RTX Spark N1X SoC, combining up to 20 Grace Arm CPU cores with a Blackwell GPU featuring up to 6,144 CUDA cores. Configurations support up to 128GB of unified memory, shared between CPU and GPU. The Surface Laptop Ultra model I tested has this full-fat configuration with an eye-watering $5,899.99 price tag (thanks, memory crunch), though there are lower-cost base configs as noted previously, offering an 18-core CPU with a 5,120-core GPU and 24GB of unified memory.

NVIDIA and Microsoft

Regardless, this architecture is particularly powerful for running on-device AI. Rather than being constrained by the dedicated graphics memory found in conventional laptops with discrete GPUs, RTX Spark can make a much larger pool of memory available to GPU-accelerated applications. This allows larger language models, longer context windows and demanding inference workloads to run locally. It’s similar in design to AMD’s Ryzen AI Max series, aka Strix Halo, in that regard, but with a more potent GPU engine on board.

NVIDIA’s CUDA ecosystem is another important advantage. Developers can leverage familiar tools including TensorRT, PyTorch and llama.cpp, with a base software foundation that also extends into NVIDIA-powered workstations and data center infrastructure.

For organizations building AI applications, this offers a solid development path. Models and workflows can be prototyped locally before moving to larger systems, reducing cloud compute and token expense while allowing sensitive data to remain on-device. (See: Around the corner: Agentic AI PCs that cut token costs.)

Microsoft has also optimized Windows 11 for RTX Spark, with improvements to workload scheduling, power management, memory allocation and application compatibility. These platform-level investments were essential to making NVIDIA’s Arm architecture practical for everyday Windows computing, and I was able to put some of them to the test in the few days I’ve had the machine on hand.

Surface Laptop Ultra: Premium design meets practical function

Microsoft has given RTX Spark an appropriately premium home with this machine. The Surface Laptop Ultra features a 15-inch PixelSense Ultra mini-LED touch display with up to 2,000 nits of claimed peak HDR brightness, a 120Hz refresh rate and excellent potential for creative work requiring high accuracy and wide gamut coverage.

Dave Altavilla

The machine’s aluminum chassis is less than 18 mm thick, and it weighs in at under 4.5 pounds. It’s not an ultraportable per se, but considering the horsepower on board, Microsoft has struck a reasonable balance between portability and performance.

The design is refreshingly understated, with clean lines and rigid aluminum construction. My initial hands-on impressions have been particularly positive, thanks to the keyboard’s tactile response, smooth and responsive haptic touchpad, and bright, high-contrast display.

The larger touchpad should be especially welcome for users navigating complex applications, while the touchscreen adds flexibility for reviewing documents, annotating designs, and interacting directly with creative content.

Connectivity options are also very good, relative to other premium laptops. Microsoft includes three USB-C ports, HDMI, USB-A, an SD card reader and a headphone jack. One USB-C connection features Microsoft’s new magnetic charging mechanism, combining the convenience and safety of a breakaway power connector with the versatility of a standard USB-C port.

Microsoft has also designed the cooling system with large fans and significant thermal capacity, while making the machine’s internal SSD removable and offering good internal serviceability in general. These are practical considerations for professional users and IT departments concerned with reliability, maintenance and long-term ownership.

Battery life and sustained performance under prolonged workloads are important aspects Microsoft focused on for the overall experience, particularly for a machine designed to deliver workstation-class capabilities away from a desk. More on this shortly.

Local AI agents: Moving from inference to action

RTX Spark also supports locally running autonomous AI agents, including one that I tested out called Hermes, which can execute multi-step workflows, access files and interact with applications. Its potential impact spans software development, research, document analysis, business automation and many other disciplines. Hermes provides the agent framework, while supported models leverage RTX Spark’s CUDA-accelerated inference and unified memory.

For businesses, local agents can keep sensitive data on-device and reduce cloud inference costs, provided they’re configured appropriately. However, granting agents access to files, code execution and corporate systems introduces security risks. Microsoft’s Execution Containers and NVIDIA’s OpenShell aim to provide isolation and access controls, though their effectiveness depends on proper enterprise policy implementation.

Hermes running Qwen3.8-27B locally on Surface Laptop Ultra, generating a benchmark report.

Dave Altavilla

To test this capability, I ran Hermes with the Qwen3.8-27B language model locally on the Surface Laptop Ultra. I asked it to extract benchmark charts from an Excel spreadsheet and create a formatted Word report with performance commentary. Hermes autonomously generated and executed Python scripts, processed the spreadsheet and assembled the document in approximately five minutes. Color me impressed.

That’s a respectable turnaround for a task requiring several manual steps. My results demonstrate how local AI agents can streamline reporting and analysis without cloud-hosted model inference. Human review remains essential, but this was a promising demonstration of practical, real-world agentic AI on a Windows laptop.

AI performance: Strong results as expected

My team’s preliminary AI benchmarks highlight the advantages of NVIDIA’s RTX Spark architecture. However, we’re still digging deeper into AI-enabled use cases and performance.

In UL Procyon’s AI Text Generation benchmark using Phi 3.5, a family of lightweight, open-source small language models (SLMs) released by Microsoft, the Surface Laptop Ultra scored 2,703, compared with 2,027 for Lenovo’s Intel Core Ultra X9 388H-powered IdeaPad Pro 5, an advantage of approximately 33%.

Dave Altavilla

The difference was even more substantial in MLPerf’s Flux 2 Klein 4B image generation workload, where the Surface Laptop Ultra delivered 26.97 images per minute versus 9.96 for the Lenovo machine, or roughly 2.7 times the throughput.

These results demonstrate the platform’s potential for accelerating local inference, image generation, agentic workflows and other AI workloads. Actual application performance will depend on model selection, software optimization and available system memory, though NVIDIA does provide a nice memory partitioning tool in the NVIDIA App for Windows.

Content creation, gaming and battery life: Blackwell’s versatility

RTX Spark’s Blackwell GPU delivers impressive graphics performance, extending the Surface Laptop Ultra’s capabilities beyond AI development and everyday creation or productivity tasks.

Dave Altavilla

In 3DMark Steel Nomad Lite, the Surface Laptop Ultra achieved 98.29 FPS, more than double the 46.07 FPS of Lenovo’s Core Ultra X9-powered IdeaPad Pro 5. In the ray-tracing-focused 3DMark Speed Way test, it delivered 30.31 FPS versus 19.72 FPS for the ASUS ROG Flow Z13, powered by AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ 395 and Radeon 8060S graphics.

Dave Altavilla

Actual gaming performance was similarly strong. In Cyberpunk 2077, the Surface Laptop Ultra averaged 71.05 FPS, ahead of the ROG Flow Z13’s 63.76 FPS. However, the AMD system narrowly led in The Talos Principle 2, delivering 89.5 FPS versus the Surface’s 84.5 FPS at 1080p medium settings.

CPU performance for tasks like 3D rendering also holds up well. In Cinebench 2026, the Surface scored 6,787 in the multi-threaded test, edging out the AMD-powered ROG Flow Z13’s 6,546. Notably, the Surface retained 99% of its multi-threaded performance on battery power as well.

For creative professionals, native Arm applications including Blender, DaVinci Resolve and Adobe Photoshop offer opportunities to leverage RTX Spark’s potent GPU. However, Windows on Arm compatibility remains a consideration. Microsoft’s Prism translation supports many x86 applications, but specialized software, drivers and certain games (like EA anti-cheat-supported titles currently) may still encounter limitations.

Dave Altavilla

Battery endurance was respectable for the Surface Laptop Ultra, at 14 hours and 35 minutes in my PCMark video playback testing, though competing mainstream thin-and-light laptops lasted considerably longer. The Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark operate within a different power envelope, however, more akin to a beefier gaming laptop, rather than a svelte 2 – 3-lb business machine.

Final thoughts: A serious new AI Windows PC competitor

The Surface Laptop Ultra marks an important milestone for NVIDIA’s expansion into Windows PCs and Microsoft’s ambitions for high-performance Arm-based computing.

My initial testing shows the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra delivers exceptionally strong AI acceleration, competitive multi-threaded CPU performance and impressive graphics horsepower. Combined with Microsoft’s premium industrial design, extensive connectivity and I/O options, and Windows platform integration, RTX Spark makes a convincing first impression.

Starting at $2,600, this is a specialized, premium system, and mainstream business users will find more economical alternatives to be sure. However, for developers (even vibe coders), creative professionals and organizations evaluating local AI workflows, the Surface Laptop Ultra offers a compelling combination of performance, beautiful industrial design, portability and local AI capability, especially with its higher-tier memory configurations.

NVIDIA has arrived in the Windows PC market with serious technology, and Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra is an impressive first showcase of what this new partnership can deliver.

items.title: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft's promises
items.summary: Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn't feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly. Microsoft is throwing both arms around the new Nvidia RTX Spark platform with the Surface Laptop Ultra—and setting its sights on the would-be MacBook Pro buyer, or as the company called it, "a high performance audience." The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both. The Surface Laptop Ultra arrives at a strange time in personal computing. Recent industry numbers showed a 20 percent drop in total PC shipments year over year in the third quarter of 2026. That's not just consumer purchasing either—that's across the board. Between the RAMpocalypse that has exploded consumer prices and an industry fixated on enterprise money, there hasn't been much new hardware to excite PC enthusiasts. Read full article Comments

items.title: Running local AI models on Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra: What we found
items.summary: Microsoft is positioning the new Surface Laptop Ultra as an alternative to Apple’s MacBook Pros for creatives and developers — and especially AI developers. Built on Nvidia’s N1X-based RTX Spark platform , with a Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores, a CPU with up to 20 cores, up to 128GB of unified memory, and a price that undercuts Apple, it’s a tempting alternative if you want to run local AI models and also want to have a powerful machine for editing videos and gaming on the go. This is The New Stack , so I’m leaving the gaming benchmarks and creator use cases to others. My focus in testing the unit was on running AI workloads. I’ve been using the Surface Laptop Ultra in its high-end $4,300 GPU and CPU configuration with 64GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD for the last week, including while on the road. Typically, I use a Mac Studio with the M4 Max chip at home, which happily runs most local models I throw at it (as long as they fit into the 48 GB of RAM). I installed all the usual tools I use to run local models on the laptop. Think Unsloth Studio, Ollama, Hermes Agent, etc. At no point did I feel like I was making a compromise in running those on the laptop. Indeed, if anything, the Blackwell GPU was generally a bit faster than my Mac Studio. Fast local inference (with the right models) Since the new Nemotron 3.5 Bolt model launched earlier this week, I also took that one for a spin. It answered queries at an impressive 56 to 60 tokens per second — and sometimes more. That makes it a great model for running in Hermes Agent or OpenCode, for example. It’s a heavily quantized model with 9B active parameters, so you would expect it to be fast, of course. Yet, while the laptop has the unified memory to run it, the dense Qwen 3.8 27B at 8-bit quantization never achieved more than 8 or 9 tokens per second in Unsloth Studio. That’s not quite usable, but with these dense models, that’s virtually always due to memory bandwidth. But bringing it down to a 4-bit quantization brought the speed up to a respectable 25 to 28 tokens per second. Using the 8-bit Gemma 4 26B-A4B shows how the mixture-of-experts technique is really what you need to run virtually any model locally at reasonable speeds. For this model, the Surface Laptop Ultra generally hit around 40 tokens per second. I don’t have an M5-based MacBook or Mac Studio at hand, but Tom’s Hardware reports that the Ultra generally outperforms the M5 Max in a MacBook Pro in AI use cases. Unsloth on the Surface Pro Ultra. Credit: The New Stack. Performance drops when you unplug All of those previous numbers were with the laptop on its 140W charger. Microsoft says it tuned the system so that running on battery would still give users most of the full performance. Microsoft claims its benchmarks showed that the laptop retained 99.6% of its performance when running on battery, but at least for the AI workloads I tested, that drop was far more noticeable. The 4-bit Qwen 3.8 model, for example, dropped from its 25-28 tokens per second to around 18 tokens per second on battery. For Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, the performance dropped to around 42 to 45 tokens per second. Overall, it seems fair to expect around a 20% to 25% loss in performance when on battery when running AI workloads (and games show a very similar drop). I did not run any formal battery life tests. Microsoft says users can expect 12 hours of active web usage. If you are consistently running local AI workloads, though, I wouldn’t expect more than a few hours of battery life based on my observations. The RAM questions Having 64GB of RAM puts you in a bit of an odd situation given that most smaller models right now are in the 27B to 30B league. The extra RAM gives you plenty of headroom for the KV cache and other applications, but there aren’t a lot of models in the 32-48GB range, for example, that the machine could also handle. Going for 128GB of RAM brings the price of the Surface Laptop Ultra to $5,900 The trade-off for all that power: heat and noise Unsurprisingly, all of the compute power (Microsoft says you get up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance) creates a bit of heat. Nobody is going to argue that the Surface Laptop Ultra is whisper-quiet when you run AI applications. The noise its dual fans make isn’t extreme, but enough to get a bit on your nerves while you are working. That’s especially noticeable when Hermes or your favorite coding agent is chugging along for a while on a more complex query. There is a reason the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box , which is built on top of the same N1X platform, has a thousand air vents, after all (which will also likely allow it to push its performance beyond the N1X in the laptop). Outside of that, the laptop is very quiet, though, and the fans remain off for most day-to-day use cases. It also quiets down very fast once the GPU load drops again. The new Surface Magnetic Connect and 140W charging brick. Credit: The New Stack. A few more observations I would feel remiss if I didn’t highlight a few other things I found while testing the Ultra. This is, after all, Microsoft’s most ambitious laptop yet. The touchpad is huge and has haptic feedback. There are only a few applications that support it so far, including DaVinci Resolve, for example. Having that feedback makes editing faster, as you can feel when the playhead snaps into place, for example. I want more touchpads with that feature. Whatever Microsoft did with the speakers works wonders. There are side vents near the front of the laptop that create a surprisingly wide stereo field, something you will definitely notice in games. The new magnetic USB-C charging connector is nice. It feels a lot like the magnetic Connect on other Surface devices. I just worry I’ll lose the cable sooner rather than later. Microsoft is not positioning this as a gaming PC, but with that GPU, people will try to play a few games, and so did I. Gaming on a Windows ARM machine is still in its early days, but thanks to Microsoft’s emulation, it generally works without too much overhead. Games that rely more on the GPU than the CPU will fare better, but I was able to play Cyberpunk 2077 in 2K with ray tracing turned on at around 60fps. With frame generation and a few settings tweaks, even 4K gaming is an option. With ray tracing off, the remaster of The Witcher 3 also happily ran at 60fps in 4K. But since the 15-inch, 3:2 touchscreen (3270×2180) is essentially a better 3K screen, you wouldn’t want to run a game in 4K anyway unless you plug in an external monitor. The screen looks great and can get very bright, but it is also highly reflective. That’s often distracting. Overall, Windows on ARM feels a lot more solid now than it did a year ago. Surely there are some applications and games that won’t run (or run well), but I haven’t come across any issues. Increasingly, developers (like OpenCode) offer Windows ARM64 versions of the desktop apps. Having two USB-C, one USB-A, and an HDMI port is such a joy if you have any older accessories. Add the headphone jack and SD card reader, and you don’t even need to carry a USB-C hub. I’ve gotten used to my MacBook Air. The Laptop Ultra is heavy at 4.41lbs (2kg). The SSD is replaceable. There are four screws underneath the laptop, and you don’t void your warrenty of you open the machine up. Apple should pay attention.

Built on Nvidia’s N1X-based RTX Spark platform, with a Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores, a CPU with up to 20 cores, up to 128GB of unified memory, and a price that undercuts Apple, it’s a tempting alternative if you want to run local AI models and also want to have a powerful machine for editing videos and gaming on the go.

At no point did I feel like I was making a compromise in running those on the laptop. Indeed, if anything, the Blackwell GPU was generally a bit faster than my Mac Studio.

Fast local inference (with the right models)

Using the 8-bit Gemma 4 26B-A4B shows how the mixture-of-experts technique is really what you need to run virtually any model locally at reasonable speeds. For this model, the Surface Laptop Ultra generally hit around 40 tokens per second.

I don’t have an M5-based MacBook or Mac Studio at hand, but Tom’s Hardware reports that the Ultra generally outperforms the M5 Max in a MacBook Pro in AI use cases.

I did not run any formal battery life tests. Microsoft says users can expect 12 hours of active web usage. If you are consistently running local AI workloads, though, I wouldn’t expect more than a few hours of battery life based on my observations.

Having 64GB of RAM puts you in a bit of an odd situation given that most smaller models right now are in the 27B to 30B league. The extra RAM gives you plenty of headroom for the KV cache and other applications, but there aren’t a lot of models in the 32-48GB range, for example, that the machine could also handle.

Going for 128GB of RAM brings the price of the Surface Laptop Ultra to $5,900

The trade-off for all that power: heat and noise

The noise its dual fans make isn’t extreme, but enough to get a bit on your nerves while you are working. Outside of that, the laptop is very quiet, though, and the fans remain off for most day-to-day use cases. It also quiets down very fast once the GPU load drops again.
