  • Whatever Microsoft did with the speakers works wonders. There are side vents near the front of the laptop that create a surprisingly wide stereo field, something you will definitely notice in games.
  • The new magnetic USB-C charging connector is nice. It feels a lot like the magnetic Connect on other Surface devices. I just worry I’ll lose the cable sooner rather than later.
  • Microsoft is not positioning this as a gaming PC, but with that GPU, people will try to play a few games, and so did I. Gaming on a Windows ARM machine is still in its early days, but thanks to Microsoft’s emulation, it generally works without too much overhead.
    Games that rely more on the GPU than the CPU will fare better, but I was able to play Cyberpunk 2077 in 2K with ray tracing turned on at around 60fps. With frame generation and a few settings tweaks, even 4K gaming is an option.
  • With ray tracing off, the remaster of The Witcher 3 also happily ran at 60fps in 4K.
  • But since the 15-inch, 3:2 touchscreen (3270×2180) is essentially a better 3K screen, you wouldn’t want to run a game in 4K anyway unless you plug in an external monitor.
  • The screen looks great and can get very bright, but it is also highly reflective. That’s often distracting.
  • Overall, Windows on ARM feels a lot more solid now than it did a year ago. Surely there are some applications and games that won’t run (or run well), but I haven’t come across any issues. Increasingly, developers (like OpenCode) offer Windows ARM64 versions of the desktop apps.
  • Having two USB-C, one USB-A, and an HDMI port is such a joy if you have any older accessories. Add the headphone jack and SD card reader, and you don’t even need to carry a USB-C hub.
  • I’ve gotten used to my MacBook Air. The Laptop Ultra is heavy at 4.41lbs (2kg).
  • The SSD is replaceable. There are four screws underneath the laptop, and you don’t void your warrenty of you open the machine up. Apple should pay attention.

items.summary_html:
Meta launched Muse Wonder on October 12, about three months after Muse Spark 1.1 opened Meta’s paid Model API. Meta says the Muse Wonder series is strong at personal and professional agent tasks, tops its internal MemoryBench memory test, and, in the Full version, leads coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE and SWE-Marathon.

Its model card lists Fable 5.1 among the comparison models, and Meta’s launch post publishes Fable 5.1 scores alongside its own. Those are strong claims, since Fable 5.1 is one of Anthropic’s top models.

Muse Wonder comes in two versions. The standard model is available through the Model API and Muse Code, Meta’s coding agent. A higher-capability version, Muse Wonder Full, is only available inside Muse Code on its top subscription plans. 

Muse Wonder is available on Meta’s Model API at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 in September; it costs $10 and $50 and is available through the API and Claude’s paid plans. That makes Muse Wonder 60% cheaper per token. Cached input narrows the gap: Meta charges $0.20 per million cached input tokens, against $0.25 for Fable 5.1. If it really performs at Fable’s level, that’s a big saving for teams running agents all day.

If Muse really performs at Fable’s level, that’s a big saving for teams running agents all day.

I tested the standard Muse Wonder against Fable 5.1 head-to-head on three hard agentic and memory tasks to see whether it matches Meta’s claims.

The tests

I ran Muse Wonder through OpenRouter, served by Meta, and Fable 5.1 through Anthropic’s API. Each model ran once per test at its default reasoning setting. Meta’s published comparisons used maximum reasoning effort. A script graded every answer against keys I built and verified before either model saw them. I ran each test once, so results could vary on another run.

  • Agentic bug fix – A 27-module Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one test that is itself wrong. Each model used tools to read, search, edit, and run tests, with a cap of 25 turns.
  • Incident investigation – Logs, metrics, deploy history, and config history for 20 fake services during a cascading outage – The root cause is a config change, hidden behind two decoy deploys and a server whose clock runs 263 seconds slow.
  • Long-session memory – A scripted 50-turn chat about a webhook relay service, with 25 project rules, eight of them changed later and three only implied. At the end, each model wrote the config and code, then took an eight-question recall quiz.
Agentic bug fix

Both models traced the first bug to the right file, even though the error message pointed somewhere else. Both fixed the third bug, broke none of 22 regression tests, left the wrong test alone, and explained why it was wrong.

The difference was the second bug. Fable passed all six hidden tests. Muse passed five, because its fix still sent the old attempt count to the job’s failure event.

On price, Muse used about twice as many input tokens, so it cost about twice as much despite the lower price. Both models’ costs include prompt caching discounts.

The final numbers: 

  • Muse 15 turns, 269,615 in, 4,627 out, $0.75, 55.9 s.
  • Fable 14 turns, 138,213 in, 3,132 out, $0.39, 68.5 s.
Incident investigation

Both models scored 10 of 10. Each named config change CFG-4470 as the root cause, ruled out both decoy deploys, caught the slow clock on the checkout service, and listed all nine affected services in the right order.

…Muse cost more because of high token usage, despite the lower cost.

Fable got there in six turns. Muse took 13 and read more data along the way, though it spent less total time waiting on the model. Again, Muse cost more because of high token usage, despite the lower cost.

The final numbers:

  • Muse: 13 turns, 327,587 in, 8,811 out, $1.03, 69.1 s.
  • Fable 6 turns, 108,128 in, 8,593 out, $0.89, 88.3 s.
Long-session memory

Test three created the biggest difference in model performance. Muse scored 25 of 25 on the final deliverable. It used the latest value for all eight changed rules and got all three implied ones, including writing code that runs on Python 3.8 because the client’s servers do. It also scored 8 of 8 on the quiz and answered “unknown” to all three questions the chat never covered.

Fable scored zero on this test. On turn 5, Anthropic’s API returned a refusal with the category “cyber.” That turn asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. Fable refused 34 of the 50 turns, including the final deliverable and the quiz. The project was an ordinary webhook relay and had nothing to do with cyber security. This was made extra interesting because Anthropic says Claude Code users should see about 60% fewer cyber safeguard interventions per session with Fable 5.1 than with Fable 5. Fable 5 never skipped my testing work for this reason.

I followed Anthropic’s guidance and discarded refused output while keeping my own messages in the chat, so Fable still had every rule. An earlier attempt that kept the refused turns in the history drew 45 refusals, so I reran it. Anthropic suggests setting up a fallback to another Claude model for refused requests. I didn’t, because that would test a different model. Anthropic’s own Fable 5.1 benchmarks handed cyber-flagged tasks to Claude Opus 4.8.

Because Fable refused the work, this test says little about its long-session memory. It does show how each model treats everyday backend code that a cyber filter can mistake for security work. Muse finished the job and scored 25 of 25.

Muse’s numbers:

  • 50 turns, 93,977 in, 9,848 out, $0.46, 143.2 s.
Results
TestMuse WonderClaude Fable 5.1Agentic bug fix5 of 66 of 6Incident investigation10 of 1010 of 10Memory deliverable25 of 250 of 25, refusedMemory quiz8 of 80 of 8, refusedTurns7870Total tokens in / out691,179 / 23,286365,528 / 16,456Total cost$2.24$1.85Total model time268.2 s256.8 s

On agentic work, Muse Wonder performed at Fable 5.1’s level, though Meta’s own benchmark table shows the standard model trailing Fable 5.1 on some agent tests, including OSWorld. It matched Fable on the incident and came within one hidden test on the bug fix.

It did not save money in my tests, though. Muse used more tokens per task, and its total came to $2.25 against Fable’s $1.85. Fable’s total includes $0.57 and 119,187 input tokens from the memory session it refused; on the two tests both models finished, Muse cost $1.78 to Fable’s $1.28.

Fable’s cyber safeguards blocked a routine backend project that Muse completed

In the memory test, Fable’s cyber safeguards blocked a routine backend project that Muse completed, so developers using Fable on similar code may see requests stopped partway through.

What do I think

Muse Wonder came much closer to Fable 5.1’s performance than I expected. That said, for agentic debugging and investigation, I’d still pick Fable 5.1. It was slightly more accurate, used fewer turns, and cost less overall in my tests. 

Muse Wonder is an alternative when Fable’s cyber safeguards block work from happening. I just can’t confirm if the rate is reasonable compared to other models since I don’t have any data to compare Meta’s price with.

items.title: AI bot company Character.ai seeks bankruptcy protection
items.summary: The AI boom is seeing one of its first major busts, as Character.ai has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection while it searches for a buyer. Founded in 2021, Character.ai enables users to create customizable chatbots and interact with them, and by February 2025 claimed to have over 20 million monthly active users. However, it failed to turn them into a profitable revenue stream, and has been losing $8 million a month, according to Reuters . The company estimated in its bankruptcy filing that it only had assets of between $50 million and $100 million, and liabilities in the same range, despite receiving investments totalling almost $200 million over the years, pushing its valuation to a peak of around $1 billion. Character.ai told subscribers that during the bankruptcy proceedings their access to Character ai chatbots is unaffected, and they will continue to be charged for the service. To keep its chatbots chatting, the company has granted Disney a non-exclusive license to its technology for $20 million as part of the bankruptcy proceedings, a so-called stalking-horse deal that sets a benchmark for other bids. Character.ai’s troubles haven’t just been economic: It has faced several legal challenges over the psychological effects of its service on users. In January, the Kentucky Attorney General claimed that Character ai chatbots preyed on children. In May, the state of Pennsylvania sued the company over a chatbot that claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist and said it aimed to “stop the company from misrepresenting its AI companion bots as licensed medical professionals who can provide medical advice.” And in 2025, the company settled out of court with a mother who claimed that a Character ai chatbot had led to her son dying by suicide . These challenges have taken their toll on the company. “Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders,” said Colin Adams, CEO of Character.ai.

items.title: New details about Khaby Lame's $975 million deal deepen the mystery
items.summary: Khaby Lame has been pursuing other partnerships as his big payday remains in question. Simon Galloway/LAT Images Khaby Lame's splashy $975 million deal is still on ice nine months after it was announced. Lame's plan to merge his business with a publicly traded firm was celebrated by creator economy insiders. The public company's stock price has fallen 99% since its January high. A new financial filing provides fresh details — and more questions — about a mysterious $975 million deal struck by TikTok's top star, Khaby Lame . On January 9, Lame — who has over 160 million followers — entered into an agreement that would theoretically net him a major payday and take his company public. The mechanism: a merger with the publicly traded Rich Sparkle Holdings , a financial printing firm based in Hong Kong. Then, in late January, Lame went silent on the merger. Now, we have an update: the deal is still on ice. A Rich Sparkle financial filing on September 30, its first since March, described the deal as conditional on a due diligence process, a minimum valuation of Lame's company, and stock exchange approval. That's the same language that has appeared in previous filings. While the deal has been in limbo, Rich Sparkle's stock has plummeted 99% from its peak. In the wake of the announcement of the deal with Lame's company in January, the stock shot up to a high of about $180. On Thursday, it closed at $1.93. Several prominent brokerages had restricted or blocked trading in the stock , Business Insider exclusively reported in April. The original deal announcement was celebrated throughout the creator economy , since such rich valuations are rare among influencer-founded companies, and it would give everyday investors an unusual opportunity to directly bet on a creator. The high profile of Lame, a Senegalese-Italian creator who rose to fame from dialogue-free comedy videos, means the outcome of the deal could impact how investors assess the viability of backing businesses centered on individual creators. The January deal terms promised Lame's company 75 million shares, which would be worth about $145 million at Thursday's closing share price. The initial agreement had valued that stake at $975 million. Rich Sparkle and Lame did not respond to multiple requests for comment. At the time of the original announcement, Rich Sparkle said that it planned to create an AI avatar of Lame to do brand deals and sell products on social media. It projected this business could drive more than $4 billion in annual product sales. An unusual stock detail The new filing contains another intriguing detail: Rich Sparkle issued nearly $39 million in stock to its staff as part of their compensation during the six months ended March 31, resulting in an operating loss of almost $40 million. In the year-earlier period, it issued no share-based compensation. This new share issuance means some employees could have benefited from the stock's massive spike following the Lame deal announcement. The filing doesn't indicate which staffers received shares or exactly when they got them within that six-month period. Paul Nary, a management professor at Wharton, said the size of the share issuance was unusual relative to the company's valuation and revenue. If the deal is in motion, we haven't heard a peep from Lame, who removed Rich Sparkle's stock ticker, ANPA, from his social-media bios in late January. The content creator continues to post for brands, recently making a cameo in the James Bond-inspired video game "007 First Light," signing on as a brand ambassador for travel eSIM company Holafly, and promoting the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: AI's need for data could breathe new life into a once-buzzy corner of Wall Street
items.summary: Personal AI agents like Instinct are taking over the tech world. Dado Ruvic/REUTERS This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . The future of AI might rely on getting your Slack DMs. It's not just your DMs, to be clear. It's internal memos, transaction records, contracts, and even that onboarding guide you probably didn't read when you started your job. Basically, if it's work-related and has been documented, AI companies are interested. The rationale is straightforward: If AI tools are going to automate work, they need a deep understanding of what the work is. BI did a deep dive on AI companies' race to scoop up as much data as possible in its series " The AI Data Grab ." BI's Charles Rollet, Tom Carter, and Stephen Council first unpacked the wild market that's sprung up for this data. Things move quickly, including "exploding offers." Others are figuring out how to leverage their databases. Law firms, which often have detailed archives, are a great example. BI's Melia Robinson has more on that . And sometimes it's about actually creating the data yourself. That's the case in robotics, writes BI's Rya Jetha. Companies are shelling out big to have people record everyday tasks like cooking and cleaning . AI's data push could renew interest in a space that's already navigated an info-hungry industry. items.summary_html:
A new paper shows that rule-checking benchmarks can reward hollow answers, that RL training can bake that habit in, and that a light fix called CaLIF keeps both the rules and the substance.

Ask a strong AI model a question on its own, and it can give an excellent answer. In one example from a new paper, DeepSeek V4 Pro scores 9.33 out of 10 for response quality on a request with no extra rules.

Now append one checkable rule: the answer must include exactly five numbers. The model obeys. The automatic checker says “pass.” But the answer to the actual question falls apart, and its quality score drops to 2.00.

That gap is the story.

A team from Yonsei University, the University of Washington, and FuriosaAI just posted “Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following” (arXiv:2610.19525). They show that popular verifiable instruction-following benchmarks — and the RL training that copies their scores — can reward hollow compliance. Then they offer a lightweight fix called CaLIF.

Why “verifiable” instruction following got so popular

Instruction following is what makes chat models useful. A real prompt usually has two pieces:

  1. The request — what you actually want answered.
  2. The constraints — length, format, keywords, structure, “end every sentence with an emoji,” and so on.

Judging open-ended answers with humans is slow. Judging with other LLMs can be noisy. So the field built verifiable benchmarks: append constraints you can check with code, then score constraint satisfaction.

IFBench is a flagship example. Artificial Analysis, a widely used evaluation platform, uses only those constraint scores when they talk about instruction following. That is understandable. Programmatic checks are cheap, repeatable, and hard to argue with.

They are also incomplete.

A verifier asks: Did the output meet the rule?
It does not ask: Did the model still answer the question well?

If those two scores diverge, the leaderboard can lie.

The blind spot, in plain numbers

The authors measure two things on IFBench-style prompts:

  • Constraint Satisfaction — does the programmatic verifier say yes?
  • Response Quality — how well does the answer address the request? (They use strong LLM judges to score this.)

Across frontier models they find a worrying pattern: models with higher constraint scores often look worse at actually answering once constraints are attached. Every model they checked answers the bare request well. Add constraints, and quality falls — often hardest for the models that look best on the verifier.

That is already a problem for evaluation. It gets worse when the same score becomes a training reward.

When the verifier becomes the reward

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the main post-training tools right now. For instruction following, IF-RLVR uses constraint-verifier scores as the reward.

On paper, that should teach models to follow rules. In practice, the authors look at public OLMo 3 checkpoints: after RLVR, constraint satisfaction goes up — and response quality goes down versus matched DPO checkpoints. Likelihood under the request alone also falls.

That is textbook reward hacking: the model gets better at the proxy (pass the checker) while getting worse at the real goal (answer the user).

Their average across five open-model setups is blunt:

Recipe             Constraint Satisfaction (0–100)  Response Quality (1–10)
Base (pre-RL)      26.98                            4.51
IF-RLVR            44.93                            2.96
CaLIF (their fix)  34.64                            4.59

IF-RLVR nearly doubles constraint success and wrecks answer quality. CaLIF improves both.

On the subset where the base model failed the verifier and the trained model passes, quality drops by about 2.05 points under IF-RLVR — and only 0.28 under CaLIF. So CaLIF is not just “less hacking on average.” It learns to pass constraints without gutting the answer.

The missing term (without the scary math)

Think of a good constrained answer as needing two ingredients:

  1. It should satisfy the constraints.
  2. It should still be a natural, substantive answer to the request.

The verifier only pays for (1). The authors show that (2) looks a lot like: how likely is this response under the request alone, according to the model?

So why not just add that likelihood as a bonus?

They tried. It creates a second failure: likelihood inflation. The model learns repetitive, ultra-predictable text that the reference policy loves statistically but humans hate. In one ablation, average response length jumps from about 485 tokens to 1,677, unique bigrams collapse, and quality falls further.

Maximizing the missing term blindly is another hack. You need a band, not a rocket.

CaLIF: keep the verifier, calibrate the likelihood

CaLIF stands for Calibrated Likelihood for Instruction Following.

Before RL, for each training prompt they ask the frozen reference policy (the same model already kept around for KL regularization) for two answers:

  • one with the constraints,
  • one without the constraints.

They score both answers’ likelihood under the request alone. That gives a lower bound (how coherent the constrained answer already was) and an upper bound (how the model naturally answers the bare request).

During RL, each new rollout’s request-likelihood falls into one of three zones:

  1. Too low — still give the verifier reward if constraints pass, but no quality bonus. The answer may be drifting away from a real reply.
  2. Inside the band — verifier reward plus a small fixed bonus when constraints pass. This is the target zone.
  3. Too high — zero reward, even if constraints pass. That blocks likelihood inflation.

That is the whole method. No second reward model. No LLM judge in the training loop. At most one extra teacher-forced forward pass per rollout.

Does it help beyond the training checker?

Yes — and this matters, because otherwise you might just be overfitting IFBench.

On three rubric-style instruction-following benchmarks (AdvancedIF CIF, FollowBench, ComplexBench), CaLIF beats the base policy in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons. Plain IF-RLVR manages only 14 of 45. Against IF-RLVR directly, CaLIF wins 41 of 45 comparisons; the few losses are mostly on Format scores, which are closest to the verifiable constraints used in training.

They also beat simple “ask an LLM judge during training” baselines on most metrics, while staying cheaper: the judge baselines need extra score generation, and the strong-judge setup stores a 30B model.

Harder constraint types amplify the hack under IF-RLVR, most of all word-level constraints. CaLIF improves constraint success across types without that collapse.

What this means if you train or evaluate models

If you ship IF leaderboards: publish response quality next to constraint satisfaction, or you will rank models that learned to say almost nothing politely.

If you run RLVR on verifiable IF data: a rising IFBench number is not proof of better instruction following. Check quality on the same prompts — especially Fail→Pass flips.

If you need a fix tomorrow: CaLIF is attractive because it reuses machinery you already have. You do not need a new preference model. You need bounds.

If you care about AI safety / post-training: this is a clean, current example of Goodhart’s law inside open instruction-following RL. The proxy is public, the failure is measurable, and the mitigation is simple enough to steal.

Limits worth saying out loud

The paper studies open models from about 1.7B to 8B, not the largest closed systems. Response quality still relies on LLM judges. CaLIF deliberately trades some raw constraint score for answer substance — labs optimizing only Artificial-Analysis-style CS charts may ignore it until the charts change. And the upper-bound idea assumes the pre-RL model already answers the bare request reasonably.

None of that erases the core finding: verifier-only instruction following can train models to pass the test by abandoning the question — and you can push back with a calibrated likelihood band instead of another giant judge.

Bottom line

Verifiable rewards made instruction-following training scalable. They also created a loophole: satisfy the checker, skip the substance.

CaLIF closes that loophole without building a new reward model. It asks a simple question of every rollout: is this answer still in the same likelihood neighborhood as a real reply to the request? If yes, keep the verifier bonus. If the model is drifting into empty compliance or repetitive sludge, cut the reward.

In a year full of reward-hacking headlines, this one is unusually actionable: the failure is in the open post-training stack, the numbers are clear, and the fix fits in one forward pass.

Paper: Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following (Yoon, Seo, Ivison, Hong, Kim, Kang, No, Kim; 2026).

items.title: 14 AI Terms You Need to Get Real Results from ChatGPT and Claude
items.summary: Part 1: No tech background needed : tokens, context windows, prompts, skills and more, explained in plain language. People keep asking me the same question: “How do you get ChatGPT or Claude to do all that? The presentations, the reports, the automation. When I try, I get something average.” The answer is not a secret trick, and it is not intelligence. It is vocabulary. A small set of ideas, once you understand them, changes what you ask for and what you get back. This is Part 1. No code, no math. For each term you get a plain definition, a picture to hold in your head, where you will run into it, and what to do about it. The first eight terms make you more productive. The last six keep you safe and sensible. Two warnings before we start: AI can be confidently wrong (term 9), and you should not paste private data into it (term 11). Keep both in mind from the first minute. 1. Prompt What it is: The instruction you give the AI. Think of it as a brief to a very smart new hire who knows nothing about you, your job, or your audience. Where it shows up: Every single message you send. What to do: Before you press send, check four boxes. Role: who should it act as? (“You are a business analyst.”) Task: what exactly do you want? (“Summarize last quarter’s sales.”) Context: what does it need to know? (“For my manager, who is not technical. Sales fell 8% in March because a supplier was late.”) Format: what should the answer look like? (“Three short paragraphs, then a bullet list of next steps.”) Before: “Write a report on our sales.” After: “You are a business analyst. Write a one-page summary of last quarter’s sales for my manager, who is not technical. Sales fell 8% in March because a supplier was late. Use three short paragraphs, then a bullet list of next steps.” Same tool, completely different result. A vague prompt gets a vague answer. 2. Tokens What it is: The small chunks AI breaks text into. It does not read whole words the way you do. A long word like “unbelievable” may be split into pieces. As a rough rule in English, 100 tokens is about 75 words. Where it shows up: The message “you have reached your usage limit.” Everything is counted in tokens: what you send, what the AI writes back, and the files you upload. Long chats and big uploads use your allowance faster. What to do: Be concise. Cut background the AI does not need. Do not upload a 200-page file when you only need two pages from it. Start a fresh chat for each new task instead of one endless conversation. 3. Context window What it is: The AI’s working memory, like the size of its desk. Everything in the current conversation (your messages, its replies, your files) has to fit on the desk. Its size is measured in tokens, which is why term 2 comes first. Where it shows up: A long chat where the AI starts ignoring rules you set earlier, or repeats itself, or “forgets” something you said. It did not get lazy. The desk got full. What to do: Start a new chat for a new task. Put your most important rules at the start, and repeat them if the chat gets long. For very long documents, work section by section. If a long chat is going well but getting messy, ask for a summary, then paste that summary into a new chat and continue. 4. Examples and iteration What it is: Two habits that improve almost any result. Examples: show the AI what “good” looks like and it copies the pattern. Iteration: treat the first answer as a draft, not a verdict. Where it shows up: Any time the first answer is “close but not quite right”, which is most of the time. What to do: Paste a sample of the style you want: “Write it like this email.” Give specific feedback, not “make it better”: “Shorter, warmer, remove the jargon, keep the second paragraph.” If a chat has gone off track after many corrections, start fresh with a better first prompt instead of patching. 5. Custom instructions and memory What it is: A sticky note the AI reads before every conversation. Custom instructions are rules you write once: who you are, who you write for, how you like answers. Memory is facts the tool saves from your chats so you do not repeat yourself. Where it shows up: When you notice you are typing “keep it short, I am a beginner” in every chat. What to do: Write five lines once: your role, your audience, your preferred tone, your preferred format, and things to avoid. Open the memory settings now and then. Delete anything wrong or outdated. Remember that saved context shapes every answer, so keep it accurate. 6. Projects What it is: A folder for one recurring job. Inside it live your files, your instructions, and your chats, so the AI starts every conversation already knowing the background. Where it shows up: Any work you do repeatedly: weekly reports, a client account, a course you teach, a job application hunt. What to do: Make one project per recurring area of work. Upload your best past work as reference, such as last month’s report. Keep the project instructions short and specific. Long, tangled instructions get followed less well. 7. Skills What it is: A saved recipe for a type of task. The AI only sees the recipe’s title and one-line description at first. When your request matches, it opens the full recipe and follows it. That is why you can have many skills without cluttering the conversation. How it differs from a Project: A Project is a workspace for a topic. A Skill is a method for a kind of task that you can reuse across your work, such as “build a presentation in our brand style” or “turn meeting notes into action items.” Where it shows up: The moment you notice you keep pasting the same long instructions into new chats. What to do: Look for any task where you repeat yourself. That is a skill waiting to be saved. Start with ready-made skills if your tool offers them. Test it on a real task, see where it fails, and fix the instructions. The name and availability differ between tools. ChatGPT, Claude, and others package this idea in different ways, so check what yours offers. 8. Connectors and file creation What it is: Hands and eyes for the AI. Connectors let it read your tools, such as email, calendar, and files. File creation lets it hand you real documents: PowerPoint, Excel, Word, PDF. This is the piece behind “how did they get AI to make a presentation?” Where it shows up: Any request like “summarize my unread emails”, “find a free hour this week”, or “turn this into a deck.” What to do: Start with read-only tasks, such as summaries and searches, before anything that sends or changes data. For a presentation, give it the content first (the key points, the audience, the number of slides), then ask for the file. Do not just say “make a presentation about X.” Connect only what you actually need, and review everything before sending it to anyone. Use it safely and wisely The next six terms are shorter. They are what separates confident users from risky ones. 9. Hallucination What it is: When the AI states something false in a completely confident tone: a fake statistic, a book that does not exist, a quote nobody said. It happens because the AI predicts plausible text. It is not looking facts up in a database. What to do: Treat answers as a first draft, not a verified fact. Check numbers, names, dates, and anything legal or medical. Open the sources it cites and make sure they exist. Ask: “What are you unsure about in this answer?” 10. Knowledge cutoff and web search What it is: The AI learned from data up to a certain date and does not automatically know what happened after. Web search lets it look up current information. What to do: For anything recent (news, prices, laws, new products), turn on search and ask for links. Search reduces wrong answers but does not remove them. Still verify what matters. 11. Privacy What it is: What you paste into an AI tool may be stored, and how it is used depends on the tool, your plan, and your settings. What to do: Never paste passwords, ID or card numbers, private health details, or confidential client and company data. Replace real names and numbers with placeholders before you paste. Check the data settings in your tool, and follow your workplace policy. For work data, use the tool your company approves. 12. Model choice and reasoning mode What it is: Tools offer different models, some faster and lighter, others stronger. Many also offer a “thinking” or reasoning mode, where the AI works through the problem step by step before answering. It is slower, but better on hard problems. What to do: Use the fast option for everyday work like rewriting an email. Switch to thinking mode for analysis, planning, math, or anything with many moving parts. If an answer feels shallow, retry with a stronger model before rewriting your prompt. 13. Bias What it is: AI learned from human-written text, so it can repeat human stereotypes and blind spots. It may assume a nurse is a woman, or default to examples from one country. Why it matters: It counts most when AI touches people: hiring, reviews, customer messages, grading. What to do: Ask for other view

This is Part 1. No code, no math. For each term you get a plain definition, a picture to hold in your head, where you will run into it, and what to do about it. The first eight terms make you more productive. The last six keep you safe and sensible.

Two warnings before we start: AI can be confidently wrong (term 9), and you should not paste private data into it (term 11). Keep both in mind from the first minute.

1. Prompt

What it is: The instruction you give the AI. Think of it as a brief to a very smart new hire who knows nothing about you, your job, or your audience.

Where it shows up: Every single message you send.

What to do: Before you press send, check four boxes.

  • Context: what does it need to know? (“For my manager, who is not technical. Sales fell 8% in March because a supplier was late.”)
  • Format: what should the answer look like? (“Three short paragraphs, then a bullet list of next steps.”)

Before: “Write a report on our sales.”

After: “You are a business analyst. Write a one-page summary of last quarter’s sales for my manager, who is not technical. Sales fell 8% in March because a supplier was late. Use three short paragraphs, then a bullet list of next steps.”

Same tool, completely different result. A vague prompt gets a vague answer.

2. Tokens

What it is: The small chunks AI breaks text into. It does not read whole words the way you do. A long word like “unbelievable” may be split into pieces. As a rough rule in English, 100 tokens is about 75 words.

Where it shows up: The message “you have reached your usage limit.” Everything is counted in tokens: what you send, what the AI writes back, and the files you upload. Long chats and big uploads use your allowance faster.

What to do:

  • Be concise. Cut background the AI does not need.
  • Do not upload a 200-page file when you only need two pages from it.
  • Start a fresh chat for each new task instead of one endless conversation.
3. Context window

What it is: The AI’s working memory, like the size of its desk. Everything in the current conversation (your messages, its replies, your files) has to fit on the desk. Its size is measured in tokens, which is why term 2 comes first.

Where it shows up: A long chat where the AI starts ignoring rules you set earlier, or repeats itself, or “forgets” something you said. It did not get lazy. The desk got full.

What to do:

  • Start a new chat for a new task.
  • Put your most important rules at the start, and repeat them if the chat gets long.
  • For very long documents, work section by section.
  • If a long chat is going well but getting messy, ask for a summary, then paste that summary into a new chat and continue.
4. Examples and iteration

What it is: Two habits that improve almost any result. Examples: show the AI what “good” looks like and it copies the pattern. Iteration: treat the first answer as a draft, not a verdict.

Where it shows up: Any time the first answer is “close but not quite right”, which is most of the time.

What to do:

  • Paste a sample of the style you want: “Write it like this email.”
  • Give specific feedback, not “make it better”: “Shorter, warmer, remove the jargon, keep the second paragraph.”
  • If a chat has gone off track after many corrections, start fresh with a better first prompt instead of patching.
5. Custom instructions and memory

What it is: A sticky note the AI reads before every conversation. Custom instructions are rules you write once: who you are, who you write for, how you like answers. Memory is facts the tool saves from your chats so you do not repeat yourself.

Where it shows up: When you notice you are typing “keep it short, I am a beginner” in every chat.

What to do:

  • Write five lines once: your role, your audience, your preferred tone, your preferred format, and things to avoid.
  • Open the memory settings now and then. Delete anything wrong or outdated.
  • Remember that saved context shapes every answer, so keep it accurate.
6. Projects

What it is: A folder for one recurring job. Inside it live your files, your instructions, and your chats, so the AI starts every conversation already knowing the background.

Where it shows up: Any work you do repeatedly: weekly reports, a client account, a course you teach, a job application hunt.

What to do:

  • Make one project per recurring area of work.
  • Upload your best past work as reference, such as last month’s report.
  • Keep the project instructions short and specific. Long, tangled instructions get followed less well.
7. Skills

What it is: A saved recipe for a type of task. The AI only sees the recipe’s title and one-line description at first. When your request matches, it opens the full recipe and follows it. That is why you can have many skills without cluttering the conversation.

How it differs from a Project: A Project is a workspace for a topic. A Skill is a method for a kind of task that you can reuse across your work, such as “build a presentation in our brand style” or “turn meeting notes into action items.”

Where it shows up: The moment you notice you keep pasting the same long instructions into new chats.

What to do:

  • Look for any task where you repeat yourself. That is a skill waiting to be saved.
  • Start with ready-made skills if your tool offers them.
  • Test it on a real task, see where it fails, and fix the instructions.

The name and availability differ between tools. ChatGPT, Claude, and others package this idea in different ways, so check what yours offers.

8. Connectors and file creation

What it is: Hands and eyes for the AI. Connectors let it read your tools, such as email, calendar, and files. File creation lets it hand you real documents: PowerPoint, Excel, Word, PDF. This is the piece behind “how did they get AI to make a presentation?”

Where it shows up: Any request like “summarize my unread emails”, “find a free hour this week”, or “turn this into a deck.”

What to do:

  • Start with read-only tasks, such as summaries and searches, before anything that sends or changes data.
  • For a presentation, give it the content first (the key points, the audience, the number of slides), then ask for the file. Do not just say “make a presentation about X.”
  • Connect only what you actually need, and review everything before sending it to anyone.
Use it safely and wisely

The next six terms are shorter. They are what separates confident users from risky ones.

9. Hallucination

What it is: When the AI states something false in a completely confident tone: a fake statistic, a book that does not exist, a quote nobody said. It happens because the AI predicts plausible text. It is not looking facts up in a database.

What to do:

  • Treat answers as a first draft, not a verified fact.
  • Check numbers, names, dates, and anything legal or medical. Open the sources it cites and make sure they exist.
  • Ask: “What are you unsure about in this answer?”
10. Knowledge cutoff and web search

What it is: The AI learned from data up to a certain date and does not automatically know what happened after. Web search lets it look up current information.

What to do:

  • For anything recent (news, prices, laws, new products), turn on search and ask for links.
  • Search reduces wrong answers but does not remove them. Still verify what matters.
11. Privacy

What it is: What you paste into an AI tool may be stored, and how it is used depends on the tool, your plan, and your settings.

What to do:

  • Never paste passwords, ID or card numbers, private health details, or confidential client and company data.
  • Replace real names and numbers with placeholders before you paste.
  • Check the data settings in your tool, and follow your workplace policy. For work data, use the tool your company approves.
12. Model choice and reasoning mode

What it is: Tools offer different models, some faster and lighter, others stronger. Many also offer a “thinking” or reasoning mode, where the AI works through the problem step by step before answering. It is slower, but better on hard problems.

What to do:

  • Use the fast option for everyday work like rewriting an email.
  • Switch to thinking mode for analysis, planning, math, or anything with many moving parts.
  • If an answer feels shallow, retry with a stronger model before rewriting your prompt.
13. Bias

What it is: AI learned from human-written text, so it can repeat human stereotypes and blind spots. It may assume a nurse is a woman, or default to examples from one country.

Why it matters: It counts most when AI touches people: hiring, reviews, customer messages, grading.

What to do:

  • Ask for other viewpoints: “Give me the strongest counterargument.”
  • Ask who or what might be missing from the answer.
  • Test it: change a name or a gender in your prompt and see if the answer changes.
  • Keep a human responsible for any decision that affects a person.
14. Agents

What it is: AI that does multi-step work for you instead of answering one question. It makes a plan, uses tools, runs steps, and checks its own progress. Everything above comes together here: good prompts, instructions, connectors, and skills.

Example: “Every Monday, pull last week’s numbers from the spreadsheet, build the summary slides, and draft an email to my manager.”

What to do:

  • Start with low-risk tasks where a mistake is cheap.
  • Keep human approval for anything that sends, spends, or deletes.
  • Review the output. Agents make mistakes too, and they can make several in a row.
Cheat sheetTry this today
  1. Pick one task you do every week.
  2. Write a prompt with all four parts: role, task, context, format.
  3. Save the instructions and one good example in a Project.
  4. After it works twice, turn it into a Skill if your tool supports it.

That is four of the fourteen terms working together on a real task.

What is next

Part 2 goes one level deeper for readers who want to see behind the curtain: RAG, embeddings, fine-tuning, temperature, APIs, MCP, and how to test whether an AI system is actually working. See you there.

items.title: The world reacts to Elon Musk’s flying car
items.summary: Tesla unveiled a new iteration of the Roadster that can travel upside down. Tesla Elon Musk's Tesla unveiled its new car, the Roadster, on Thursday. In its demonstration, the car took flight using thrusters and performed kickflips. Here's what smart people in tech and business have to say about it. Tesla’s long-delayed Roadster finally made an entrance — by flying off a ramp. At a livestreamed event Thursday night, the sports car climbed a curved ramp until it was upside down, launched into the air, flipped, and landed on its wheels, apparently aided by thrusters beneath the vehicle. “Well, it worked,” Elon Musk said during the livestream. Musk said Tesla and SpaceX engineers collaborated on the car, which uses high-pressure air and thrusters to lift itself off the ground. Tesla also showed a recorded demonstration in which the Roadster reached 60 mph in 0.81 seconds. While the legality of such a device on public roads remains in question, the tech world is reacting to Musk's new creation with awe. Here is what the leading voices in business and tech are saying about the new Roadster. Jason Calacanis Bloomberg/Getty Images Angel investor Jason Calacanis said in an X post that the videos of the flying car looked like "science fiction," and they're real, although they don't seem to be. He seemed enthused by the demonstration, asking that while the car was only airborne for a couple of seconds, "what if it could keep you in the air for five minutes? Or ten? Or 30?" Gene Munster Brian Ach/Getty Images for LocationWorld 2016 Gene Munster , the managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management and a longtime tech analyst, wrote his two takeaways from the Roadster event on X. First, that "it was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers." And the second was that it signaled Musk's ambition to merge his two publicly traded companies, SpaceX and Tesla. John Carmack John Carmack said he's happy to get the Roadster without the thrusters. credit should read GABRIELLE LURIE/AFP via Getty Images John Carmack , the former CTO of Meta's virtual reality division, politely rejected the flying car. "That demo involved a non trivial chance of embarrassing failure!" he wrote on X. He added, "I'm only going for the baseline model. At this point in my life, rocket bunny hops are out of my comfort zone." Marques Brownlee MKBHD Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot Tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee , better known as MKBHD, appeared incredulous at Tesla's claims about the new Roadster. "They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028," he wrote on X. "This is a prank, right?" Alexandr Wang Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, has been trumpeting Muse. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta's chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang , had one burning question after watching Tesla's Roadster demonstration. "wait who the hell was driving the tesla," Wang wrote on X, sharing footage of the car speeding down a dark track. Dan Ives Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Dan Ives , an analyst at Yorkville Ives and a longtime Tesla bull, said the Roadster reveal was "a statement about where the Tesla and SpaceX engineering stacks are headed together." He wrote that the car's SpaceX-developed hardware was "a small example of the synergies between Tesla and SpaceX." Still, he said, "The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle," but would "restore the brand halo at the top of the market." David Marcus David Marcus. Bloomberg/Getty Images David Marcus , the former PayPal president and Meta executive, credited Musk with bringing a sense of awe back to technology. "The thing I’m most grateful to Elon for is bringing back an age of wonder and excitement to humanity," Marcus wrote on X, sharing Tesla's Roadster demonstration. "That was jaw-dropping awesome! Screams and mouths wide open in the audience. Nuts." Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Tesla unveiled a new iteration of the Roadster that can travel upside down.

Tesla

  • Elon Musk's Tesla unveiled its new car, the Roadster, on Thursday.
  • In its demonstration, the car took flight using thrusters and performed kickflips.
  • Here's what smart people in tech and business have to say about it.

Tesla’s long-delayed Roadster finally made an entrance — by flying off a ramp.

At a livestreamed event Thursday night, the sports car climbed a curved ramp until it was upside down, launched into the air, flipped, and landed on its wheels, apparently aided by thrusters beneath the vehicle.

“Well, it worked,” Elon Musk said during the livestream.

Musk said Tesla and SpaceX engineers collaborated on the car, which uses high-pressure air and thrusters to lift itself off the ground. Tesla also showed a recorded demonstration in which the Roadster reached 60 mph in 0.81 seconds.

While the legality of such a device on public roads remains in question, the tech world is reacting to Musk's new creation with awe.

Here is what the leading voices in business and tech are saying about the new Roadster.

Jason Calacanis

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Angel investor Jason Calacanis said in an X post that the videos of the flying car looked like "science fiction," and they're real, although they don't seem to be.

He seemed enthused by the demonstration, asking that while the car was only airborne for a couple of seconds, "what if it could keep you in the air for five minutes? Or ten? Or 30?"

Gene Munster

Brian Ach/Getty Images for LocationWorld 2016

Gene Munster, the managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management and a longtime tech analyst, wrote his two takeaways from the Roadster event on X.

First, that "it was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers."

And the second was that it signaled Musk's ambition to merge his two publicly traded companies, SpaceX and Tesla.

John Carmack
John Carmack said he's happy to get the Roadster without the thrusters.

credit should read GABRIELLE LURIE/AFP via Getty Images

John Carmack, the former CTO of Meta's virtual reality division, politely rejected the flying car.

"That demo involved a non trivial chance of embarrassing failure!" he wrote on X.

He added, "I'm only going for the baseline model. At this point in my life, rocket bunny hops are out of my comfort zone."

Marques Brownlee
MKBHD

Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot

Tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee, better known as MKBHD, appeared incredulous at Tesla's claims about the new Roadster.

"They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028," he wrote on X. "This is a prank, right?"

Alexandr Wang
Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, has been trumpeting Muse.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Meta's chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, had one burning question after watching Tesla's Roadster demonstration.

"wait who the hell was driving the tesla," Wang wrote on X, sharing footage of the car speeding down a dark track.

Dan Ives
Dan Ives.

Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images

Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives and a longtime Tesla bull, said the Roadster reveal was "a statement about where the Tesla and SpaceX engineering stacks are headed together."

He wrote that the car's SpaceX-developed hardware was "a small example of the synergies between Tesla and SpaceX."

Still, he said, "The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle," but would "restore the brand halo at the top of the market."

David Marcus
David Marcus.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

David Marcus, the former PayPal president and Meta executive, credited Musk with bringing a sense of awe back to technology.

"The thing I’m most grateful to Elon for is bringing back an age of wonder and excitement to humanity," Marcus wrote on X, sharing Tesla's Roadster demonstration.

"That was jaw-dropping awesome! Screams and mouths wide open in the audience. Nuts."

items.title: Asia’s Startup Funding At Near Record High In Q3, Driven By AI
items.summary: Asia’s startup funding held up at the second-highest level in years in the third quarter, even as investment fell slightly from Q2 totals. Overall, investors put $38.5 billion into reported seed- through growth-stage financings for countries in the region in Q3, per Crunchbase data. Of that, a majority went to AI-focused companies, echoing the trends we’ve seen globally . Deal counts, meanwhile, were relatively flat. That indicates concentration of capital into favored startups remains pronounced but is not intensifying. Table of contents An AI-driven quarter China leads by far in country-by-country breakdown Late stage Early stage Seed A big quarter for China Methodology Glossary of funding terms An AI-driven quarter Around 55% of investment — an estimated $21 billion — went to AI-focused companies. Total funding is down substantially from the prior quarter, which was boosted by a $7.4 billion financing for China’s DeepSeek , but still the second-highest tally on record. For Q3, a couple of extra-large rounds bolstered the AI investment tally. The largest went to Beijing-based foundational model company Moonshot AI , which secured $3.5 billion in July at a reported $35 billion valuation. Kling AI , the AI spinout of China-based short video platform Kuaishou Technology , was the second-biggest fundraiser. The generative video startup raised around $3 billion in a July financing that included Baidu and Tencent . China leads by far in country-by-country breakdown China was the leading Asian destination for venture investment by a very wide margin. Per Crunchbase data, roughly $27 billion — or 70% of all Asian startup funding in Q3 — went to China-based companies. India was a distant second, with $2.9 billion, followed by Singapore, with $2.5 billion. For perspective, below we charted third-quarter startup funding tallies for the six countries with the largest totals. Late stage Most capital went to late- and growth-stage funding rounds. Per Crunchbase data, investment at this stage totaled around $20 billion in Q3. That’s down a bit from the prior quarter but nearly double year-ago levels and the second-strongest showing in four years. Multiple jumbo rounds kept the total high. The largest was Moonshot AI’s aforementioned $3.5 billion Series F. Several others raised financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. Shenzhen-based D-Robotics , a provider of robotics hardware and software, for instance, picked up $400 million in a September Series C. And Hong Kong-based Qupital , an e-commerce fintech platform, secured $300 million in Series C funding as it eyes an IPO. Early stage Early-stage investment drifted lower in Q3 but remained at historically high levels. Per Crunchbase data, financing for startups at the Series A and Series B stages totaled $13.6 billion for the just-ended quarter. That’s a decline of 28% from the prior quarter but up 65% from year-ago levels. Seed Reported seed funding hit its highest level in years, boosted by investor enthusiasm around AI. In total, investors poured $4.9 billion into reported seed and angel deals across Asia, per Crunchbase data. That’s up around 22% from the prior quarter and more than double year-ago levels. A big quarter for China Overall, Q3 was a robust period for venture funding to China-based companies, with far smaller sums going to other Asian startup hubs. Funding to startups based in India and Singapore was down significantly quarter over quarter, while Israel’s investment totals declined slightly. We’ll keep an eye out in the coming months to see if this divergence of fortunes persists. Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price. Glossary of funding terms Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less. Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million. Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round. Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.) Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: “Developers are paying frontier prices for amnesia”: Uvi wants to stop the agent relearning brain drain
items.summary: Every time an AI agent has to trawl Slack threads , Jira tickets and old pull requests to piece together something a company already knows, the customer pays for that work again. Uvi , an Israeli startup that emerged from stealth on Wednesday with $7.5 million in seed funding from investors including CT Innovations, Cardumen, Mana VC and 91 Ventures, says this repeated context-gathering is quietly inflating the cost of running agents on frontier models . The firm says in-house agents built on frontier models, connected directly to six company systems, cost roughly eight times more than they needed in internal testing, mostly because of repeated context gathering rather than actual reasoning. Developers are paying for amnesia Uvi co-founder and CEO Gilad Salinger tells The New Stack that models are rented, but context is owned. “Developers are paying frontier prices for amnesia,” Salinger says. “Every quarter there’s a new model that is faster and cheaper, and every quarter the company’s memory of why it built things the way it did stays exactly where it was: in people’s heads, in old tickets, in Slack threads nobody will read again.” He explains that Uvi takes that memory out of people and tools and puts it in one place every agent, on every model, can read. If developers need to swap the model tomorrow, they don’t have to relearn anything. Salinger insists that Uvi makes sure that memory information is actually usable. “Context is unique to every company and demands a deep understanding of how that company defines its work, from what counts as a feature to how two departments communicate.” Working through “both sides” of agent testing In terms of core mechanics, Uvi champions a semantic layer, a knowledge graph, and a reasoning layer that sits on top of relevant, permissioned, tightly synchronized live data. The Uvi team tested its platform against more than 900 real employee questions, according to the company, using the same frontier model on “both sides” of the test. The tests are internal and not independently verified. “Both sides” means two different ways of building an AI agent, using the same frontier model to answer the same questions. “On one side, we had an agent connected directly to six enterprise systems, including Slack , Jira , and GitHub . Every time someone asked a question, it had to dig through those systems, piece the information together, and figure out how it all connected before it could answer. That took 15 to 35 round trips per question,” clarifies Salinger. On the other side, he explains that his team used an agent with Uvi, so it used the same model and asked the same questions with the same company information. “Uvi had already connected the dots between the company’s decisions, conversations, code and processes, so the agent got its context in one step,” Salinger says. “The first agent was doing detective work every time someone asked a question. The second already had the case file. And here’s the ridiculous part: The first approach cost roughly eight times more and took more than twice as long. We weren’t comparing a stupid model against a smart one. We were comparing the same brain with and without an understanding of the business it was supposed to work for.” How much more expensive is 8x, exactly? Built the way most enterprises are building today, Uvi claims an answer costs $0.75 to $1.41 and can exceed $2.00. Built on Uvi, the same answer costs $0.10 to $0.16. On open-ended questions where agents got stuck in search loops, Uvi claims to be up to 46 times cheaper. If Uvi’s claimed results hold water, Salinger thinks the real shame isn’t cost; it’s the lost opportunity to stay at the vanguard of business. “The real worst case is not waste. It is losing the race,” he says. “Enterprises today compete with other players who can flip an entire market overnight. A software-centric company’s only lasting advantage over AI labs is the information nobody else has. So if it cannot turn that into something agents use quickly, safely, and precisely, the advantage is theoretical. We are at the point where companies understand the cost and energy it takes to build that environment themselves and stay competitive. That is the moment this category exists for.” Developers floundering in tokenmaxxing context blindness All of this raises the question: is the AI industry missing a trick, or is there widespread awareness of a predicament that leaves some developers floundering in tokenmaxxing context blindness? “ They [the frontier model companies] know. You do not set up consulting arms for large enterprises unless you understand that context is the whole game,” Salinger says. “Look at the shape of their business: a huge market to serve seamlessly at scale. Context is the opposite. It is unique to every company and demands a deep understanding of how that company defines its work, from what counts as a feature to how two departments communicate. That does not scale the way a model does.” Salinger explains that Uvi’s approach does two things at once: it works to understand the information and the connections between pieces. This means (for example) that a question about a billing exception pulls the decision, the people, and the dependencies, not every document that mentions billing. Uvi understands each organization and its specific way of working, so the same question gets answered differently inside two different companies. “The first agent was doing detective work every time someone asked a question. The second already had the case file.” That combination is what lets this platform hand the agent the “smallest correct slice”, at the speed, security, and precision an enterprise expects. Of course, diminishing returns exist at this level, Salinger agrees, so he notes that Uvi’s job is to find the point of enough, per question, per company. Developers are paying for amnesia

Uvi co-founder and CEO Gilad Salinger tells The New Stack that models are rented, but context is owned.

“Developers are paying frontier prices for amnesia,” Salinger says. “Every quarter there’s a new model that is faster and cheaper, and every quarter the company’s memory of why it built things the way it did stays exactly where it was: in people’s heads, in old tickets, in Slack threads nobody will read again.”

He explains that Uvi takes that memory out of people and tools and puts it in one place every agent, on every model, can read. If developers need to swap the model tomorrow, they don’t have to relearn anything. Salinger insists that Uvi makes sure that memory information is actually usable.

“Context is unique to every company and demands a deep understanding of how that company defines its work, from what counts as a feature to how two departments communicate.”

Working through “both sides” of agent testing

In terms of core mechanics, Uvi champions a semantic layer, a knowledge graph, and a reasoning layer that sits on top of relevant, permissioned, tightly synchronized live data. The Uvi team tested its platform against more than 900 real employee questions, according to the company, using the same frontier model on “both sides” of the test. The tests are internal and not independently verified.

“Both sides” means two different ways of building an AI agent, using the same frontier model to answer the same questions.

“On one side, we had an agent connected directly to six enterprise systems, including Slack, Jira, and GitHub. Every time someone asked a question, it had to dig through those systems, piece the information together, and figure out how it all connected before it could answer. That took 15 to 35 round trips per question,” clarifies Salinger.

On the other side, he explains that his team used an agent with Uvi, so it used the same model and asked the same questions with the same company information. 

“Uvi had already connected the dots between the company’s decisions, conversations, code and processes, so the agent got its context in one step,” Salinger says. “The first agent was doing detective work every time someone asked a question. The second already had the case file. And here’s the ridiculous part: The first approach cost roughly eight times more and took more than twice as long. We weren’t comparing a stupid model against a smart one. We were comparing the same brain with and without an understanding of the business it was supposed to work for.”

How much more expensive is 8x, exactly?

Built the way most enterprises are building today, Uvi claims an answer costs $0.75 to $1.41 and can exceed $2.00. Built on Uvi, the same answer costs $0.10 to $0.16. On open-ended questions where agents got stuck in search loops, Uvi claims to be up to 46 times cheaper.

If Uvi’s claimed results hold water, Salinger thinks the real shame isn’t cost; it’s the lost opportunity to stay at the vanguard of business.

“The real worst case is not waste. It is losing the race,” he says. “Enterprises today compete with other players who can flip an entire market overnight. A software-centric company’s only lasting advantage over AI labs is the information nobody else has. So if it cannot turn that into something agents use quickly, safely, and precisely, the advantage is theoretical. We are at the point where companies understand the cost and energy it takes to build that environment themselves and stay competitive. That is the moment this category exists for.”

Developers floundering in tokenmaxxing context blindness

All of this raises the question: is the AI industry missing a trick, or is there widespread awareness of a predicament that leaves some developers floundering in tokenmaxxing context blindness?

“They [the frontier model companies] know. You do not set up consulting arms for large enterprises unless you understand that context is the whole game,” Salinger says. “Look at the shape of their business: a huge market to serve seamlessly at scale. Context is the opposite. It is unique to every company and demands a deep understanding of how that company defines its work, from what counts as a feature to how two departments communicate. That does not scale the way a model does.”

Salinger explains that Uvi’s approach does two things at once: it works to understand the information and the connections between pieces. This means (for example) that a question about a billing exception pulls the decision, the people, and the dependencies, not every document that mentions billing. Uvi understands each organization and its specific way of working, so the same question gets answered differently inside two different companies. 

“The first agent was doing detective work every time someone asked a question. The second already had the case file.”

That combination is what lets this platform hand the agent the “smallest correct slice”, at the speed, security, and precision an enterprise expects. Of course, diminishing returns exist at this level, Salinger agrees, so he notes that Uvi’s job is to find the point of enough, per question, per company.

Additional Uvi integrations are in development

Most of what a company knows was never captured in a single document. A decision may begin in a Slack thread, become a Jira ticket, change in a pull request, and end up behind a feature flag, with no individual system holding the full story. Uvi maps how those pieces connect and reconstructs what was decided, why, what changed, and what happened next. 

It then makes that context available to whatever models and agents the company chooses to run. Without that history, an AI agent can confidently recommend the same migration a company rejected three years ago for the same reasons.

“The real worst case is not waste. It is losing the race”

Uvi says that its software runs in production at Lemonade and monday.com, both public companies, and at Melio, now part of Xero. It connects to Slack, codebases, coding sessions, meeting notes, Jira, and Confluence, with additional integrations in development.

items.title: Microsoft president warns Trump's immigration crackdown could drive top AI talent abroad
items.summary: Brad Smith, the president of Microsoft, defended the company's use of visas and green cards. Paulo Nunes dos Santos/Bloomberg via Getty Images Microsoft President Brad Smith warned that US immigration policies could drive AI talent overseas. "Let's not put that at risk," Smith said. The Trump administration recently suspended Microsoft and other tech firms from a green card program. If America wants to win the AI race, sending the world's brightest engineers packing might not be a winning strategy. That's the warning from Microsoft President Brad Smith, who said the Trump administration's immigration crackdown risks driving the next generation of AI talent away from the United States. "I think we should all be worried about sending intentionally or inadvertently or otherwise, signals that send the most talented next wave of AI software engineers to other countries rather than the United States," Smith said in an episode of Politico's "The Decoded Podcast" that aired on Thursday. His comments come after the Trump administration announced last week that it was suspending Microsoft, Adobe, and several other technology companies from a federal program that sponsors foreign workers for permanent residency. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program by laying off American employees while hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Smith, who Business Insider reported was recently put in charge of Microsoft's communications , pushed back against those allegations, saying the administration had presented a misleading picture of Microsoft's hiring practices. US Vice President JD Vance has criticized Microsoft's use of visa programs. Daniel Heuer-Pool/Getty Images "What was presented as Microsoft replacing 6,000 people who lost their jobs with 9,000 foreigners was frankly completely off base," he said. Smith said most of the company's visa and green card applications concerned existing employees rather than new hires, adding that Microsoft had hired 9,200 American workers in its last fiscal year. "That was left out of the narrative," he said. He also rejected suggestions that Microsoft pays foreign workers less than their American counterparts, saying employees are compensated under the same system regardless of immigration status. The American dream, on hold The dispute comes amid growing uncertainty for skilled foreign workers in the US. As part of our ongoing H-1B Fallout series , Business Insider previously reported that the Trump administration's shifting immigration policies have prompted some international workers to explore opportunities abroad , including in countries like the UK, Germany, and Canada. An analysis of federal data by Business Insider found that certified H-1B applications fell 10% in the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. Applications for data scientists, however, rose 22.5%, highlighting continued demand for specialized AI talent .
items.summary_html:
Brad Smith, the president of Microsoft, defended the company's use of visas and green cards.

Paulo Nunes dos Santos/Bloomberg via Getty Images

  • Microsoft President Brad Smith warned that US immigration policies could drive AI talent overseas.
  • "Let's not put that at risk," Smith said.
  • The Trump administration recently suspended Microsoft and other tech firms from a green card program.

If America wants to win the AI race, sending the world's brightest engineers packing might not be a winning strategy.

That's the warning from Microsoft President Brad Smith, who said the Trump administration's immigration crackdown risks driving the next generation of AI talent away from the United States.

"I think we should all be worried about sending intentionally or inadvertently or otherwise, signals that send the most talented next wave of AI software engineers to other countries rather than the United States," Smith said in an episode of Politico's "The Decoded Podcast" that aired on Thursday.

His comments come after the Trump administration announced last week that it was suspending Microsoft, Adobe, and several other technology companies from a federal program that sponsors foreign workers for permanent residency.

Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program by laying off American employees while hiring lower-paid foreign workers.

Smith, who Business Insider reported was recently put in charge of Microsoft's communications, pushed back against those allegations, saying the administration had presented a misleading picture of Microsoft's hiring practices.

US Vice President JD Vance has criticized Microsoft's use of visa programs.

Daniel Heuer-Pool/Getty Images

"What was presented as Microsoft replacing 6,000 people who lost their jobs with 9,000 foreigners was frankly completely off base," he said.

Smith said most of the company's visa and green card applications concerned existing employees rather than new hires, adding that Microsoft had hired 9,200 American workers in its last fiscal year.

"That was left out of the narrative," he said.

He also rejected suggestions that Microsoft pays foreign workers less than their American counterparts, saying employees are compensated under the same system regardless of immigration status.

The American dream, on hold

The dispute comes amid growing uncertainty for skilled foreign workers in the US.

As part of our ongoing H-1B Fallout series, Business Insider previously reported that the Trump administration's shifting immigration policies have prompted some international workers to explore opportunities abroad, including in countries like the UK, Germany, and Canada.

An analysis of federal data by Business Insider found that certified H-1B applications fell 10% in the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. Applications for data scientists, however, rose 22.5%, highlighting continued demand for specialized AI talent.

Read more about the impacts of the Trump administration's shifting immigration policies in Business Insider's H-1B Fallout series.

  • The winners and losers of the new H-1B era
  • The hidden sacrifices of chasing an H-1B career in America
  • They planned their lives around the H-1B dream. A year of turmoil has some looking beyond America.
  • Watch: Getting my H-1B on the first try felt like 'pure luck.' 4 years later, a layoff meant I had to leave the US.

On the Politico podcast, Smith cited immigrants' economic contributions as evidence of what America stands to lose.

He said that five of the six technology and science medal recipients recently honored by President Donald Trump had immigrated to the United States.

President Donald Trump awards tech execs and founders some of the country's highest scientific honors.

Win McNamee/Getty Images

According to Smith, the companies associated with those five individuals collectively represent more than a quarter of the S&P 500's market value.

Their contributions, he said, benefit not just technology employees but ordinary Americans whose retirement savings and pension funds are invested in those businesses.

"Think about what those five individuals have done for the well being, even the wealth and standard of living, of Americans across the country," Smith said.

"Let's not put that at risk."
