items.title: 6 wild ways to make Android widgets more useful
items.summary: Widgets, widgets, widgets. Has there ever been an Android feature so full of promise that went unloved by Google for so very long? Okay, so maybe there has been — erm, lots of times , actually. But even so, Android’s widgets system is a perfect example of an exceptional advantage that Google basically buried, abandoned, and left on the brink of extinction up until its overdue revival in 2021’s Android 12 update . (And that revival, by the way, happened for no apparent reason whatsoever. Just a totally random, unprompted change of heart after a decade of indifference. Riiiiiiiiight .) Google may have given up on widgets for a while, but the good news is that (a) they’re back, baby — still now, more than ever, even in our overly AI-obsessed 2026 timeline — and (b) the Android developer community keeps chuggin’ along and coming up with ever-more creative new ways to embrace widgets beyond what Google itself sees fit to give us. That means no matter what Android version your favorite phone is running, you can step up your own Android widget game and give yourself some fresh and fruitful paths to make the most of your phone’s framework. Here, my dear, are some fantastic beyond-the-basics ways to put your favorite Android widgets to use and change the way you get stuff done on your phone. [Psst: Love learning new things? Get my free Android Intelligence newsletter to get a tasty new tip in your inbox every Friday.] Android widget enhancement #1: The on-demand home screen pop-up Widgets are a wonderful way to interact with all sorts of info without ever having to open up apps, but having too many widgets can quickly lead to a cluttered and overwhelming home screen. Well, here’s a neat way to give yourself the benefit of a widget while still maintaining a neat and minimal space for working: An excellent app called Popup Widget lets you create an on-demand pop-up widget (get it?!) that looks like a regular ol’ icon on your home screen but then loads any widget you want when tapped. See? Any widget, anytime — with Popup Widget on Android. JR Raphael, Foundry You can even get really wild and set up a single icon that opens multiple widgets at the same time — like your inbox and your calendar together: Popup Widget can even let you summon two widgets together with a single tap. JR Raphael, Foundry Not bad, right? Popup Widget costs two bucks and doesn’t require any special permissions or manners of access. And it’s pretty simple and self-explanatory to set up: Once you install and open the app, it’ll walk you through adding in whatever pop-up widgets you want. You can choose the name and even the icon associated with each one along with its precise placement on your screen and how much the screen behind it should dim when it’s loaded. The app will offer to add the shortcut directly onto your home screen for you then, or you can also find all of your Popup Widget creations by pressing and holding the main Popup Widget icon in your app drawer. Alternatively, if you’re already using a custom Android launcher like Smart Launcher or Niagara , you can find similar options for summoning widgets on demand within their settings — no separate apps even required. And that, my widget-loving wallaby, is but our first winning widget possibility. Android widget enhancement #2: The on-demand universal pop-up If you like the idea of having a widget on demand but would rather have it be available to summon from anywhere instead of just from your home screen, this next wacky widget option is just the thing for you. It comes from a spectacular app called Edge Gestures , which works in conjunction with Popup Widget to take that same concept and make it universally accessible. (I told ya it was wacky!) When you first install Edge Gestures, the app will prompt you to enable it as a system accessibility service and to grant it the ability to display over other apps. These permissions sound scary — and they should ! — but in the case of this specific utility, they’re absolutely appropriate and necessary in order for it to operate. The former is the only way an app is able to create a custom system-wide gesture, which we need for this setup to work its magic, and the latter is how your widget is able to be shown on top of whatever else you’re doing. (If you’re at all worried, note that Edge Gestures doesn’t request any other significant system permissions. Beyond that, it’s reputable, it’s been around for quite a long while, and it has a large number of overwhelmingly positive reviews.) Where were we? Oh, right: Once you’re inside the Edge Gestures configuration area, you’ll be able to select exactly what gesture you want to use for pulling up your widget. I’d think carefully about finding something that won’t interfere with anything else, like the system-level Android gestures , and that’ll be convenient to access without being a command you’re likely to trigger by mistake. So, for instance, you might make the gesture a simple swipe downward along the left side of your screen. To do that, you’d find the “Swipe down” option within the app’s “Left” tab, and you’d set it to “Popup Widget” — and then create or select whatever Popup Widget item you want. And remember: You can select one widget or multiple widgets, too. Prepare yourself for some serious oohing and ahhing: Your favorite widgets are never more than a swipe away with Edge Gestures on Android. JR Raphael, Foundry As you can see, this opens up a whole new world of mobile multitasking potential. I mean, really: How could you not love that?! The final thing worth doing is going into all the other gesture options in that same configuration area and tapping “Clear” for each of ’em to get rid of Edge Gestures’ default actions. I’d also go into whichever side of the screen you aren’t using — left or right — and tap the toggle to turn the gestures for that side off entirely. That way, you won’t inadvertently activate any gestures that you don’t actually want or need. Edge Gestures costs $2 to use. Android widget enhancement #3: The camera cutout command center All screen swiping aside, you can create a complete widget-summoning control panel that exists entirely in the camera cutout at the top of your phone’s screen — y’know, that otherwise useless black hole where the front-facing camera is hidden. The secret to this slice of Android widget sorcery is a snazzy little app called Material Capsule . You’ll have to spring for its $3.49 premium version (also available in a 99-cent monthly subscription, if you’d rather go that route) for the app’s widget wonders — but if you like the way it works, it’s well worth it. In short, the app lets you set up to five different gestures for calling up different widgets from anywhere on your device — with a tap, a double tap, a long press, and a swipe to the left or the right across the same camera cutout area. Any of those actions will bring whatever widget you choose into view for easy access, no matter what else you’re doing. Material Capsule’s on-demand camera cutout widgets in action. JR Raphael, Foundry It’s quite the upgrade and one of those things that’ll make you wonder why it wasn’t just built into Android itself from the get-go. I’ve got an entire separate guide to Material Capsule and its many powerful possibilities , if you’re interested in exploring it further. Android widget enhancement #4: The physical key call Next, here’s another interesting twist on that same on-demand Android widget idea: You can make any widget especially easy to access from anywhere without even having to mess around with any on-screen swiping or tapping by setting one of your phone’s physical keys as a trigger for the widget’s appearance. I’ll give you a second to catch your breath and process the sheer splendor of that spell. Back? Cool. So, the key to this feat (har har) is the combination of the aforementioned Popup Widget and a handy Android contraption called Key Mapper — which makes it easy to map your phone’s physical keys to all kinds of crazy custom actions. In this case, we’ll set it up so that pressing and holding one of your volume keys causes whatever widget you want to be summoned, like so: Yes, your volume key can cause a widget to appear (whoa!). JR Raphael, Foundry Pretty nifty, no? I’ve got step-by-step instructions for making this happen in this separate guide . Android widget enhancement #5: The floating bubble If you like the notion of having a widget always available but aren’t so keen on the hidden gesture concept, an app called Overlays will let you create a small floating bubble that you can position anywhere on your screen and then tap to pull any widget up when you want it — just like with Android’s recently revived Bubbles multitasking system , only compatible with any Android device and version and with the simplicity of a widget instead of the complexity of an entire app. Check it out: Overlays puts a floating icon on your screen for easy ongoing widget access. JR Raphael, Foundry By default, Overlays gives you a bunch of its own little widgets to choose from, but the real power comes from adding in widgets from the Android apps you actually rely on. To do that, tap the “Triggers” tab at the bottom of the Overlays configuration area, then tap the red plus button in the lower-right corner of the screen. Select “Manual,” then type in whatever name you want for your widget and tap the icon to pick any icon you like. Tap “Save,” then select “Widget” and find the widget you want from the list. At that point, you’ll see a preview of the widget. Move or resize it if you like, then hit the arrow in the upper-left corner of the screen to exit out of that interface. Last but not least, tap the name of your newly made widget on the screen that comes up next to change its status to “Always on.” As soon as you head out of the app and back to your home screen, your fancy new widget should pop right up. items.summary_html:
Widgets, widgets, widgets. Has there ever been an Android feature so full of promise that went unloved by Google for so very long?

Okay, so maybe there has been — erm, lots of times, actually. But even so, Android’s widgets system is a perfect example of an exceptional advantage that Google basically buried, abandoned, and left on the brink of extinction up until its overdue revival in 2021’s Android 12 update. (And that revival, by the way, happened for no apparent reason whatsoever. Just a totally random, unprompted change of heart after a decade of indifference. Riiiiiiiiight.)

Google may have given up on widgets for a while, but the good news is that (a) they’re back, baby — still now, more than ever, even in our overly AI-obsessed 2026 timeline — and (b) the Android developer community keeps chuggin’ along and coming up with ever-more creative new ways to embrace widgets beyond what Google itself sees fit to give us. That means no matter what Android version your favorite phone is running, you can step up your own Android widget game and give yourself some fresh and fruitful paths to make the most of your phone’s framework.

Here, my dear, are some fantastic beyond-the-basics ways to put your favorite Android widgets to use and change the way you get stuff done on your phone. 

[Psst: Love learning new things? Get my free Android Intelligence newsletter to get a tasty new tip in your inbox every Friday.]

Android widget enhancement #1: The on-demand home screen pop-up

Widgets are a wonderful way to interact with all sorts of info without ever having to open up apps, but having too many widgets can quickly lead to a cluttered and overwhelming home screen.

Well, here’s a neat way to give yourself the benefit of a widget while still maintaining a neat and minimal space for working: An excellent app called Popup Widget lets you create an on-demand pop-up widget (get it?!) that looks like a regular ol’ icon on your home screen but then loads any widget you want when tapped.

See?

Any widget, anytime — with Popup Widget on Android.

JR Raphael, Foundry

You can even get really wild and set up a single icon that opens multiple widgets at the same time — like your inbox and your calendar together:

Popup Widget can even let you summon two widgets together with a single tap.

JR Raphael, Foundry

Not bad, right?

Popup Widget costs two bucks and doesn’t require any special permissions or manners of access. And it’s pretty simple and self-explanatory to set up: Once you install and open the app, it’ll walk you through adding in whatever pop-up widgets you want. You can choose the name and even the icon associated with each one along with its precise placement on your screen and how much the screen behind it should dim when it’s loaded.

The app will offer to add the shortcut directly onto your home screen for you then, or you can also find all of your Popup Widget creations by pressing and holding the main Popup Widget icon in your app drawer.

Alternatively, if you’re already using a custom Android launcher like Smart Launcher or Niagara, you can find similar options for summoning widgets on demand within their settings — no separate apps even required.

And that, my widget-loving wallaby, is but our first winning widget possibility.

Android widget enhancement #2: The on-demand universal pop-up

If you like the idea of having a widget on demand but would rather have it be available to summon from anywhere instead of just from your home screen, this next wacky widget option is just the thing for you.

It comes from a spectacular app called Edge Gestures, which works in conjunction with Popup Widget to take that same concept and make it universally accessible. (I told ya it was wacky!)

When you first install Edge Gestures, the app will prompt you to enable it as a system accessibility service and to grant it the ability to display over other apps. These permissions sound scary — and they should! — but in the case of this specific utility, they’re absolutely appropriate and necessary in order for it to operate. The former is the only way an app is able to create a custom system-wide gesture, which we need for this setup to work its magic, and the latter is how your widget is able to be shown on top of whatever else you’re doing.

(If you’re at all worried, note that Edge Gestures doesn’t request any other significant system permissions. Beyond that, it’s reputable, it’s been around for quite a long while, and it has a large number of overwhelmingly positive reviews.)

Where were we? Oh, right: Once you’re inside the Edge Gestures configuration area, you’ll be able to select exactly what gesture you want to use for pulling up your widget. I’d think carefully about finding something that won’t interfere with anything else, like the system-level Android gestures, and that’ll be convenient to access without being a command you’re likely to trigger by mistake.

So, for instance, you might make the gesture a simple swipe downward along the left side of your screen. To do that, you’d find the “Swipe down” option within the app’s “Left” tab, and you’d set it to “Popup Widget” — and then create or select whatever Popup Widget item you want. And remember: You can select one widget or multiple widgets, too.

Prepare yourself for some serious oohing and ahhing:

Your favorite widgets are never more than a swipe away with Edge Gestures on Android.

JR Raphael, Foundry

As you can see, this opens up a whole new world of mobile multitasking potential. I mean, really: How could you not love that?!

The final thing worth doing is going into all the other gesture options in that same configuration area and tapping “Clear” for each of ’em to get rid of Edge Gestures’ default actions. I’d also go into whichever side of the screen you aren’t using — left or right — and tap the toggle to turn the gestures for that side off entirely. That way, you won’t inadvertently activate any gestures that you don’t actually want or need.

Edge Gestures costs $2 to use.

Android widget enhancement #3: The camera cutout command center

All screen swiping aside, you can create a complete widget-summoning control panel that exists entirely in the camera cutout at the top of your phone’s screen — y’know, that otherwise useless black hole where the front-facing camera is hidden.

The secret to this slice of Android widget sorcery is a snazzy little app called Material Capsule. You’ll have to spring for its $3.49 premium version (also available in a 99-cent monthly subscription, if you’d rather go that route) for the app’s widget wonders — but if you like the way it works, it’s well worth it.

In short, the app lets you set up to five different gestures for calling up different widgets from anywhere on your device — with a tap, a double tap, a long press, and a swipe to the left or the right across the same camera cutout area.

Any of those actions will bring whatever widget you choose into view for easy access, no matter what else you’re doing.

Material Capsule’s on-demand camera cutout widgets in action.

JR Raphael, Foundry

It’s quite the upgrade and one of those things that’ll make you wonder why it wasn’t just built into Android itself from the get-go.

I’ve got an entire separate guide to Material Capsule and its many powerful possibilities, if you’re interested in exploring it further.

Android widget enhancement #4: The physical key call

Next, here’s another interesting twist on that same on-demand Android widget idea: You can make any widget especially easy to access from anywhere without even having to mess around with any on-screen swiping or tapping by setting one of your phone’s physical keys as a trigger for the widget’s appearance.

I’ll give you a second to catch your breath and process the sheer splendor of that spell.

Back? Cool. So, the key to this feat (har har) is the combination of the aforementioned Popup Widget and a handy Android contraption called Key Mapper — which makes it easy to map your phone’s physical keys to all kinds of crazy custom actions.

In this case, we’ll set it up so that pressing and holding one of your volume keys causes whatever widget you want to be summoned, like so:

Yes, your volume key can cause a widget to appear (whoa!).

JR Raphael, Foundry

Pretty nifty, no?

I’ve got step-by-step instructions for making this happen in this separate guide.

Android widget enhancement #5: The floating bubble

If you like the notion of having a widget always available but aren’t so keen on the hidden gesture concept, an app called Overlays will let you create a small floating bubble that you can position anywhere on your screen and then tap to pull any widget up when you want it — just like with Android’s recently revived Bubbles multitasking system, only compatible with any Android device and version and with the simplicity of a widget instead of the complexity of an entire app.

Check it out:

Overlays puts a floating icon on your screen for easy ongoing widget access.

JR Raphael, Foundry

By default, Overlays gives you a bunch of its own little widgets to choose from, but the real power comes from adding in widgets from the Android apps you actually rely on. To do that, tap the “Triggers” tab at the bottom of the Overlays configuration area, then tap the red plus button in the lower-right corner of the screen. Select “Manual,” then type in whatever name you want for your widget and tap the icon to pick any icon you like.

Tap “Save,” then select “Widget” and find the widget you want from the list. At that point, you’ll see a preview of the widget. Move or resize it if you like, then hit the arrow in the upper-left corner of the screen to exit out of that interface. Last but not least, tap the name of your newly made widget on the screen that comes up next to change its status to “Always on.”

As soon as you head out of the app and back to your home screen, your fancy new widget should pop right up. All you’ve gotta do is tap the little downward-facing arrow in its corner to minimize it down to a bubble, which you can then press and hold to move anywhere your widget-worshipping heart desires.

Overlays can also create widgets that automatically appear based on context — so you could have something show up every time you connect to a certain Bluetooth device or Wi-Fi network, for instance. To explore those options, just follow the same steps from above but pick “Event” instead of “Manual” when you reach the “Triggers” tab configuration.

Overlays is free with an optional $4 in-app upgrade that removes some ads from the configuration tool and unlocks a handful of advanced features.

Android widget enhancement #6: The widget stack

Last but not least in our collection of wacky Android widget possibilities is one of my favorite widget wonders — and that’s the ability to stack multiple widgets and then swipe between ’em on your home screen without having ’em take up any extra space.

Check it out:

The space-saving simplicity of stacked widgets, as seen in Smart Launcher.

JR Raphael, Foundry

This enhancement presents a bit of a choose-your-own-adventure-style path:

First, if you’re using a reasonably recent Samsung Galaxy gizmo, the option is should already be present and available in your standard Samsung home screen setup. Just press and hold any open space on your home screen and then select the option to add a widget — then, once the widget is added, press and hold it and look for the “Create stack” command.

With any other Android gadget — or even with a Samsung device, if you want extra options and flexibility — you can use a custom Android launcher like the aforementioned Smart Launcher or Niagara as well as the retro-geeky T9-themed Key Launcher I introduced to you this past summer.

Those launchers replace your phone’s entire home screen environment and give you all sorts of interesting new possibilities for optimizing your interface and making it especially well-suited for you. And the stacked widget feature is just one small sliver of what they offer and how they’ll transform your Android experience.

The setup interface for a widget stack within Smart Launcher.

JR Raphael, Foundry

So there ya have it: six wacky, wild, wonderful ways to make widgets even more wow-inducing. Some days, you’ve just gotta love Android and the endless customization, control, and power it provides.

items.title: TSMC tamps down expectations despite another record quarter
items.summary: Chip manufacturer TSMC has again posted record profit as AI demands continue to outstrip supply, but executives are operating with some discretion amid rising component prices and global instabilities. The company ended the third quarter of 2026 with $46.7 billion in net revenue and a net profit margin of 51.1%, marking its sixth record quarter in a row, and projected further growth for the end of the year. But, CEO C.C. Wei said the company was “being prudent in our business planning” into 2027: “Looking ahead, we continue to observe consumer and price-sensitive end market segments are being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties.” Despite Wei’s comments, TSMC projected Q4 revenue to grow to between $52.3 and $54.3 billion and overall 2026 revenue to rise by around 44%. Chip profits grow, but shares drop

items.title: IBM talent exec says it's better to be a specialist, not a generalist, in the AI era
items.summary: Aparna Nair said that "the world of generalists is long gone." : Lindsey Nicholson/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images "The world of generalists is long gone," said IBM's chief talent, leadership, and culture officer. Aparna Nair said IBM's clients aren't expecting general advice; they're looking for deep expertise. She said even if workers wear many hats, they still need extensive knowledge about their specialty. It's a hotly debated question: Is it better to be an expert or a generalist in the AI era? For Aparna Nair, IBM's chief talent, leadership, and culture officer, there's no debate. She said she doesn't think generalists alone "will cut it" in the workforce in the AI era. "The world of generalists is long gone," Nair said. Aparna Nair is IBM's chief talent, leadership, and culture officer. IBM Nair said that generalists may be able to rely on AI to learn a lot, but at IBM, for example, the company's clients aren't expecting general advice from its workforce. IBM is hired for its deep technological expertise, she said. Nair said the same is true for entry-level hires. IBM, which has committed to doubling down on junior talent , expects new workers to arrive with the skills — and domain expertise — to take on more complex work earlier in their careers, Nair said. She said workers should identify an area that aligns with their employer's needs, become an expert in it, and "go deep." That expectation remains even as engineering roles are starting to blur with AI. In the past, a software engineer might have spent 20% of their time coding and another 20% testing, Nair said. Now, AI can handle much of the coding work , and engineers need the critical-thinking and judgment skills to evaluate what the technology produces, Nair said. They also have more opportunities to work across the business , such as speaking with clients and marketing teams and bringing what they learn back into the products they're building. While today's engineers may wear many hats and work closely with different teams, they still need deep expertise in their field — and an understanding of how their work shapes the experience of clients and colleagues. Without that added knowledge, Nair said, it would be difficult for them "to do anything meaningful." While domain expertise may be valuable, workers should also remain flexible. Nair said that there's "nothing more powerful" than when workers combine deep expertise with the right behaviors, and also use AI to their advantage. "That's a lethal combination," Nair said. items.title: Meta turns Mac into an AI supercomputer
items.summary: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,678 new readers. Earlier this week, Meta caught up with OpenAI and Anthropic with its frontier model Muse Wonder. Turns out, the comeback story had one more chapter: a large open-weight release with an unlikely partner. The company just dropped Muse Spark Open, calling it the “most capable” open-weight AI model from the U.S., and tuned it with Apple so that two Macs can work like an AI supercomputer. In today’s AI rundown: Meta gives the West its best open-weight model Rowan’s Corner: My AI walks my company’s factory floor Turn a ChatGPT answer into a tool you can use Report: Harvard maps AI’s gender divide LATEST DEVELOPMENTS META 🧠 Meta gives the West its best open-weight model Image source: Mark Zuckerberg on X The Rundown: Meta just released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight, 816B-parameter multimodal model built for coding and agentic work, and worked with Apple so that it could run locally on Mac Studios — a first for a model in this size class, Meta says. The details: Two M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 1TB combined memory can run Spark Open via Apple’s updated MLX toolkit, with Meta saying the model shipped iOS app fixes and edited video in DaVinci Resolve without the cloud. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, it sits at 39, ahead of the West’s open-weight models but behind China’s GLM 5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44), and Qwen3.8 (40). Spark Open either matches or tops open rivals on multimodal and knowledge tasks, but Chinese models still code better, with Kimi, GLM, and Qwen all ahead. It’s the third major Western open launch this month, after Reflection AI’s Beam and Mistral’s 1T-parameter Le Chonk, whose weights arrive Oct. 27. Why it matters: Meta built its AI rep on open Llama models before going closed. Now it’s playing both sides with Wonder at the frontier and Spark Open giving devs serious AI they can run on their hardware. China still leads the open-model race, but Meta’s return puts an American heavyweight back in contention . TOGETHER WITH HUBSPOT 💰 Turn AI into your income engine The Rundown: HubSpot’s new free “200+ AI-Powered Income Ideas” guide offers actionable strategies to turn artificial intelligence into your own personal revenue generator — unlocking a gateway to financial innovation in the digital age. With this guide, you can: Explore hundreds of revenue-generating ideas across industries with real-world applications Follow step-by-step instructions that make AI accessible to everyone Adopt cutting-edge strategies to stay ahead in today’s fast-paced market Access your free guide here . ROWAN’S CORNER 🔎 My AI walks my company’s factory floor Rowan: At an in-person company, the CEO can walk the factory floor. You watch how the company actually runs, catch errors in real time, spot slow handoffs, and identify processes worth automating. The best operators do it religiously. The problem is that The Rundown is fully remote and has just over 20 people. There is no floor to walk. So every Friday, I do what I call a digital factory inspection: I pick random important things across the company (support queries, newsletter posts, specific finance items, etc.) and review each one with the same lens. What’s slow? Which handoffs could disappear? What should be automated? This week, I handed the entire prep to AI. A scheduled Claude task now runs every Friday before I wake up, and it: Picks the random areas to inspect (randomness matters so nothing gets gamed) Pre-gathers the samples, links, and data for each area into a report in my Notion Checks last week’s findings against Slack to verify they actually got fixed before I move on If you run a remote company (or any team, or honestly just your own workload), steal this. I put the exact scheduled task prompt in our Workflow Hub , ready to adapt to your tools in about 15 minutes. It’s unglamorous plumbing, but it’s some of the highest-leverage 30 minutes of my week. AI TRAINING 🧮 Turn a ChatGPT answer into a tool you can use The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try ChatGPT’s new Intelligent UI by creating a workshop cost calculator. You’ll change the headcount, check the figures, and ask it to add a budget buffer. Step-by-step: Open ChatGPT in a web browser and start a Chat with GPT-6. Choose Medium where available and leave Pro reasoning off for this exercise Paste the guide’s prompt to create a calculator with editable costs, budget, and attendance. Check that the starting total is $700 for 20 people Change attendance to 30 using its controls. The total should rise to $950 and show that you are $50 over budget Try zero attendees and check that the fixed room fee stays. Test the budget boundary too, so a useful-looking calculator does not hide a wrong result Return to 20 people and ask for a 10% buffer. Check for a $770 final cost and $130 left, then change the headcount again to test the update Pro tip: Tell ChatGPT which inputs should change and which rules stay fixed. After each revision, check one result you know and one new case before using the tool. PRESENTED BY GARTNER 💸 Turn AI investments into scalable business value The Rundown: How are top organizations realizing value as AI spending accelerates? This webinar explores the leadership, operating model, and organizational shifts required to deliver measurable business and financial value with AI. In this webinar, you’ll learn: How to cut through the AI hype Why there is a gap between AI access and business impact What leading CEOs do differently to scale AI Register now . AI RESEARCH 👨🏻‍⚖️ Report: Harvard maps AI’s gender divide Image source: Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center The Rundown: Harvard researchers just found consistent gender gaps in how Americans use AI, get support for it, understand it, and appear in coverage of it, drawing on a survey of 5,400+ adults, browsing data, and 78K news articles. The details: 29% of women said they’d never used AI vs. 22% of men, though browsing data showed no real gap in trying it, only in how much time users spent on it. At work, 64% of employed women reported no AI training vs. 49% of men, with the study linking training and encouragement to higher use and confidence for both. Men answered more AI questions correctly while women chose “not sure” more often, though more men also claimed to recognize made-up AI figures. AI headlines named men 14.6x as often as women, a gap the researchers partly tie to male-led companies, though the gap also held among quoted experts. Why it matters: This is one of the broadest looks yet at how AI’s gender gaps are taking shape. Access looks nearly equal today, but the real divide shows up in training, confidence, and who gets heard. As AI labs pitch superintelligence for everyone, these gaps show how far that promise still has to go. QUICK HITS COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY ▸ Tony used AI agents to build and refine a word puzzle Today’s workflow comes from reader Tony Surfwell : “I’m not a professional developer, but I built Sujido, a live word puzzle, with multiple AI agents. For months, they gave me bloat, lost context, and slop, and neither the models nor I could untangle what had been decided or why. I eventually settled on two agents: one Claude instance that plans and reviews, and another that builds. I imposed rules on both, one failure at a time. None of these rules would surprise a pro engineering team, but nobody handed them to me. That’s the lesson I learned: agents won’t bring the discipline. You have to impose it. When I showed the first game revision to strangers, they said that the first half was ‘boring’ and the second half was novel. It was hard news to hear about my baby, but I took the feedback and cut the game in half. That required surgery on code tangled across both halves, followed by a rebuild under the rules below. Before the rebuild, a separate AI audit graded the codebase B−. Afterward, it graded it A−. The site shrank by 97.5%, and every serious finding was fixed and locked in by an automated test. The models didn’t change drastically, but my operating rules did.” See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub → What have you fixed or built with AI lately? Anthropic said it is giving six METR researchers employee-level access to assess its AI safety practices and publish findings without its approval. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC that the bank hired 1K contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic’s Mythos and other models. OpenAI is training employees to guard against espionage, including “honeypot” schemes, as attempts to steal AI trade secrets intensify, the Wall Street Journal reported. Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,678 new readers. Earlier this week, Meta caught up with OpenAI and Anthropic with its frontier model Muse Wonder. Turns out, the comeback story had one more chapter: a large open-weight release with an unlikely partner.

The company just dropped Muse Spark Open, calling it the “most capable” open-weight AI model from the U.S., and tuned it with Apple so that two Macs can work like an AI supercomputer.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Meta gives the West its best open-weight model

  • Rowan’s Corner: My AI walks my company’s factory floor

  • Turn a ChatGPT answer into a tool you can use

  • Report: Harvard maps AI’s gender divide

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

META🧠 Meta gives the West its best open-weight model

Image source: Mark Zuckerberg on X

The Rundown: Meta just released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight, 816B-parameter multimodal model built for coding and agentic work, and worked with Apple so that it could run locally on Mac Studios — a first for a model in this size class, Meta says.

The details:

  • Two M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 1TB combined memory can run Spark Open via Apple’s updated MLX toolkit, with Meta saying the model shipped iOS app fixes and edited video in DaVinci Resolve without the cloud.

  • On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, it sits at 39, ahead of the West’s open-weight models but behind China’s GLM 5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44), and Qwen3.8 (40).

  • Spark Open either matches or tops open rivals on multimodal and knowledge tasks, but Chinese models still code better, with Kimi, GLM, and Qwen all ahead.

  • It’s the third major Western open launch this month, after Reflection AI’s Beam and Mistral’s 1T-parameter Le Chonk, whose weights arrive Oct. 27.

Why it matters: Meta built its AI rep on open Llama models before going closed. Now it’s playing both sides with Wonder at the frontier and Spark Open giving devs serious AI they can run on their hardware. China still leads the open-model race, but Meta’s return puts an American heavyweight back in contention.

TOGETHER WITH HUBSPOT💰 Turn AI into your income engine

The Rundown: HubSpot’s new free “200+ AI-Powered Income Ideas” guide offers actionable strategies to turn artificial intelligence into your own personal revenue generator — unlocking a gateway to financial innovation in the digital age.

With this guide, you can:

  • Explore hundreds of revenue-generating ideas across industries with real-world applications

  • Follow step-by-step instructions that make AI accessible to everyone

  • Adopt cutting-edge strategies to stay ahead in today’s fast-paced market

Access your free guide here.

ROWAN’S CORNER🔎 My AI walks my company’s factory floor

Rowan: At an in-person company, the CEO can walk the factory floor. You watch how the company actually runs, catch errors in real time, spot slow handoffs, and identify processes worth automating. The best operators do it religiously.

The problem is that The Rundown is fully remote and has just over 20 people.

There is no floor to walk. So every Friday, I do what I call a digital factory inspection: I pick random important things across the company (support queries, newsletter posts, specific finance items, etc.) and review each one with the same lens. What’s slow? Which handoffs could disappear? What should be automated?

This week, I handed the entire prep to AI. A scheduled Claude task now runs every Friday before I wake up, and it:

  1. Picks the random areas to inspect (randomness matters so nothing gets gamed)

  2. Pre-gathers the samples, links, and data for each area into a report in my Notion

  3. Checks last week’s findings against Slack to verify they actually got fixed before I move on

If you run a remote company (or any team, or honestly just your own workload), steal this. I put the exact scheduled task prompt in our Workflow Hub, ready to adapt to your tools in about 15 minutes.

It’s unglamorous plumbing, but it’s some of the highest-leverage 30 minutes of my week.

AI TRAINING🧮 Turn a ChatGPT answer into a tool you can use

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try ChatGPT’s new Intelligent UI by creating a workshop cost calculator. You’ll change the headcount, check the figures, and ask it to add a budget buffer.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open ChatGPT in a web browser and start a Chat with GPT-6. Choose Medium where available and leave Pro reasoning off for this exercise

  2. Paste the guide’s prompt to create a calculator with editable costs, budget, and attendance. Check that the starting total is $700 for 20 people

  3. Change attendance to 30 using its controls. The total should rise to $950 and show that you are $50 over budget

  4. Try zero attendees and check that the fixed room fee stays. Test the budget boundary too, so a useful-looking calculator does not hide a wrong result

  5. Return to 20 people and ask for a 10% buffer. Check for a $770 final cost and $130 left, then change the headcount again to test the update

Pro tip: Tell ChatGPT which inputs should change and which rules stay fixed. After each revision, check one result you know and one new case before using the tool.

PRESENTED BY GARTNER💸 Turn AI investments into scalable business value

The Rundown: How are top organizations realizing value as AI spending accelerates? This webinar explores the leadership, operating model, and organizational shifts required to deliver measurable business and financial value with AI.

In this webinar, you’ll learn:

  • How to cut through the AI hype

  • Why there is a gap between AI access and business impact

  • What leading CEOs do differently to scale AI

Register now.

AI RESEARCH👨🏻‍⚖️ Report: Harvard maps AI’s gender divide

Image source: Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center

The Rundown: Harvard researchers just found consistent gender gaps in how Americans use AI, get support for it, understand it, and appear in coverage of it, drawing on a survey of 5,400+ adults, browsing data, and 78K news articles.

The details:

  • 29% of women said they’d never used AI vs. 22% of men, though browsing data showed no real gap in trying it, only in how much time users spent on it.

  • At work, 64% of employed women reported no AI training vs. 49% of men, with the study linking training and encouragement to higher use and confidence for both.

  • Men answered more AI questions correctly while women chose “not sure” more often, though more men also claimed to recognize made-up AI figures.

  • AI headlines named men 14.6x as often as women, a gap the researchers partly tie to male-led companies, though the gap also held among quoted experts.

Why it matters: This is one of the broadest looks yet at how AI’s gender gaps are taking shape. Access looks nearly equal today, but the real divide shows up in training, confidence, and who gets heard. As AI labs pitch superintelligence for everyone, these gaps show how far that promise still has to go.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Tony used AI agents to build and refine a word puzzle

Today’s workflow comes from reader Tony Surfwell:

“I’m not a professional developer, but I built Sujido, a live word puzzle, with multiple AI agents. For months, they gave me bloat, lost context, and slop, and neither the models nor I could untangle what had been decided or why. I eventually settled on two agents: one Claude instance that plans and reviews, and another that builds. I imposed rules on both, one failure at a time.

None of these rules would surprise a pro engineering team, but nobody handed them to me. That’s the lesson I learned: agents won’t bring the discipline. You have to impose it.

When I showed the first game revision to strangers, they said that the first half was ‘boring’ and the second half was novel. It was hard news to hear about my baby, but I took the feedback and cut the game in half. That required surgery on code tangled across both halves, followed by a rebuild under the rules below.

Before the rebuild, a separate AI audit graded the codebase B−. Afterward, it graded it A−. The site shrank by 97.5%, and every serious finding was fixed and locked in by an automated test. The models didn’t change drastically, but my operating rules did.”

See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

What have you fixed or built with AI lately? Share your workflow, and you could be featured right here in The Rundown.

🛠️ Trending AI Tools

  • 🧠 Muse Spark Open - Meta’s open-weight AI for coding and long-horizon agents

  • 🗣️ GPT-Live-1.1 - OpenAI’s new voice AI with more natural multilingual accents

  • 🤖 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL - Nvidia’s open multimodal AI for specialized AI agents

  • 🖼️ FLUX 3 Image Klein - BFL’s small open model for 4K image generation, editing

📰 Everything else in AI today

Amazon’s Bee launched two AI wearables starting at $74.99 that record conversations, generate summaries and to-dos, and integrate with Alexa and productivity apps.

Anthropic said it is giving six METR researchers employee-level access to assess its AI safety practices and publish findings without its approval.

Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC that the bank hired 1K contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic’s Mythos and other models.

OpenAI is training employees to guard against espionage, including “honeypot” schemes, as attempts to steal AI trade secrets intensify, the Wall Street Journal reported.

OpenAI also launched GPT-Live-1.1 with improved multilingual accents and upgraded ChatGPT’s Chrome extension to let users analyze open tabs, automate browser tasks, and access chat history in the sidebar.

🎓 Highlights: News, Guides & Events

  • Read our last AI newsletter: Rogue AI agents sit for their first interview

  • Read our last Tech newsletter: Apple goes all-in on the home

  • Read our last Robotics newsletter: Inside Amazon’s million-robot experiment

  • Today’s AI tool guide: Turn a ChatGPT answer into a tool you can use

  • RSVP to next workshop on Oct. 21: Get real work out of Microsoft Copilot

See you soon,

Rowan, Zach, Shubham, Jennifer, and Nate — the humans behind The Rundown
