By Anthony King

In cities, air pollution can vary sharply from one street to the next. Fumes may linger between tall buildings, collect at busy junctions or drift towards a school gate. However, cities often lack the detailed forecasts needed to act before levels become dangerous.

For Professor Soledad Le Clainche, an applied mathematician at the Technical University of Madrid and leader of the ModelFLOWs research group, better understanding how air moves through cities could help tackle one of Europe’s biggest environmental health challenges.

As part of an EU-funded research project called MODELAIR, Le Clainche is working with researchers in Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden and the UK to make the invisible, highly local patterns of urban pollution easier for cities to understand.

“Many people develop tools for air pollution, but we are the first to calculate, in real time, the 3D pollution environment of the urban areas we are studying,” she said.

AI-powered virtual cities

The MODELAIR researchers are developing AI-powered, 3D “digital twins” of cities. Combining computer simulations, sensor data and 3D models, they provide a real-time, street-level picture of urban air quality.

The goal is to help city authorities make better-informed decisions on traffic planning, local monitoring and where to apply pollution control measures. The research complements the EU Mission for Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities, which is helping European cities reduce emissions and improve urban life.

The tools are being tested in Brussels, Madrid and Bristol. Each city is exploring a different use, from understanding the effects of urban design to improving local monitoring and testing practical responses.

The vast majority of people in European cities are exposed to air pollution levels above what the World Health Organization (WHO) considers safe. Air pollution increases our risk of heart disease, stroke and various cancers, and worsens asthma and respiratory infections. Though often invisible, it is no small matter.

The European Environment Agency estimated that, in 2023, cutting air pollution to WHO guideline levels could have prevented 182 000 deaths from fine particles, 63 000 from exposure to ozone pollution and 34 000 from nitrogen dioxide gas in the 27 EU Member States.

New evidence also points to air pollution as a possible cause of dementia, WHO said, and eastern and south-eastern countries in Europe suffered the most health impacts from pollution.

Although air pollution has generally improved in Europe, surprising new findings about its harm keep emerging. A 2025 study found that exposure to common tiny particles and nitrogen oxides in the air over the first 18 years of life is linked to poorer cardiovascular health, especially higher blood pressure in young adults.

Getting down to street level

Le Clainche and her colleagues aim to go beyond the usual big-picture view of a city’s overall pollution levels.

The team uses AI “agents”, software assistants that continuously bring together information from sensors, weather forecasts and computer models to produce local forecasts.

Some of the project’s methods are already available through the open-source ModelFLOWs-App.

The models available today can give us useful information, but they don’t always give cities the detailed picture they need to take action. The challenge is to bring together all the different pieces of information we have – from air-quality monitoring stations and other limited sources of data – with highly detailed simulations of how air moves through a city.

“That’s what MODELAIR does, allowing us to make much more accurate predictions about how pollutants travel through urban areas,” said Alessandro Parente, an expert in air flows and AI for digital twins at Université Libre de Bruxelles in Belgium, and part of the MODELAIR team. “Cities are struggling to take decisions on air pollution,” he added.

Launched in 2023, the initiative combines computerised 3D city replicas with wind-tunnel experiments to test and refine its predictions.

Reacting in real time

Understanding how particles and gaseous pollution behave is complicated by the complex 3D environment of cities, where variables like pressure, wind and heat can change hourly and affect pollution levels.

Parente said the team wants a collaboration between scientists and AI agents to fill in the gaps and predict what is happening at a specific street corner or road junction.

“The AI agents bring together experimental data, run predictions and suggest possible responses,” Parente said. “But it’s important to be clear that AI can only make suggestions. It’s still up to scientists to assess those suggestions, and ultimately up to policymakers to decide whether and how to act on them.”

The real-time insights could help city planners weigh options such as changing traffic flows or deciding where to locate local industry.

“You could reroute traffic to avoid traffic jams or help control heat-island effects by how you build new areas of a city,” said Le Clainche.

Urban heat islands occur because asphalt, concrete and buildings retain heat, encouraging ozone formation and trapping pollutants in some streets.

City planning, traffic rerouting

The AI agents could suggest tree planting in specific locations to reduce temperatures, absorb some pollutants and introduce shade, for example. Ultimately, scientists and policymakers would use the detailed street-level insights provided by the digital twin to decide exactly where to intervene.

“A digital twin is a tool that will mimic a small area of a city, giving us information about how an air flow pattern is connected to high pollution levels,” said Le Clainche. “We’re creating tools that can be genuinely valuable for municipalities. Madrid is already very interested in using them.”

Having combined high-fidelity simulations with real-world data, the researchers are now preparing to test a real-time decision-making tool in Brussels’ Ixelles district. In Madrid, they will use the models to assess traffic routing options.

One project partner, Belgian engineering company BuildWind, develops digital city models to examine street-level wind flows, microclimates and air quality. Its existing BrusAir platform maps air pollution across Brussels, including near sensitive locations such as schools.

“This information is designed to help urban planners and the city administration understand exactly where pollutants concentrate,” said BuildWind’s CEO Alessandro Gambale.

BuildWind has worked with scientists such as Parente on real-world air pollution challenges and hopes the new research will strengthen BrusAir further. Findings from the MODELAIR research will be made more widely available towards the end of this year.

If the approach works as planned, it could give cities a more detailed view of the air people breathe on their own streets, making it easier to decide when and where action is needed before pollution builds up.

items.title: OpenAI Accuses a Former Employee of Taking More Than 100 Confidential Hardware Files Back to Apple
items.summary: OpenAI has accused a former employee of taking more than 100 confidential files about its unreleased hardware back to Apple , according to a court filing OpenAI submitted on Wednesday in the trade secrets case Apple brought against the company. OpenAI claims the employee, who joined from Apple and returned to Apple six months later, transferred sensitive documents to personal accounts before leaving. The filing does not name the employee. OpenAI has asked the court for time to investigate the matter and to consider counterclaims against Apple. OpenAI's Allegations Against Apple in the Trade Secrets Case According to the filing, the files included: detailed images of at least one unreleased OpenAI device engineering and manufacturing data supplier information and project files specifications for cosmetic finishes reports on coating and sealing hardware components OpenAI says some of the files were transferred just after midnight in Singapore on June 2, which the filing describes as the employee's final day at OpenAI. The filing goes further than the alleged file transfer. OpenAI claims the former employee presented OpenAI's product plans to Apple's senior leadership, including Apple's vice president of operations in Asia. According to OpenAI, that presentation took place months ago. OpenAI now points to Apple's latest AI hardware push, including its newly announced smart home products such as Apple's $299 HomeView smart display , as a reason for concern. OpenAI told the court it is worried that its confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where engineers could use it to shape upcoming Apple products. Apple rejects the claims. The company says it has found nothing to support OpenAI's allegations and that it has rules that stop employees from bringing former employers' secrets into Apple. How the Apple and OpenAI Trade Secrets Dispute Started The new filing reverses the direction of the original case. In July, Apple sued OpenAI and two former Apple employees, Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan, alleging that the pair took confidential engineering information, including details about unreleased products, to help OpenAI develop its own hardware. OpenAI denied those accusations at the time, saying it had no interest in other companies' trade secrets. With the new filing, OpenAI argues that confidential hardware information may have moved from OpenAI to Apple instead. OpenAI has not yet shown that Apple received or used any of the files it says were taken. For consumers, the dispute has no immediate effect on existing Apple or OpenAI products. It does show that both companies are developing AI hardware in parallel, with OpenAI working on at least one unreleased device and Apple expanding into AI-powered smart home products. Anyone following either company's hardware plans should watch the court docket for counterclaims, which would turn OpenAI's defense into a direct case against Apple. OpenAI has not filed any counterclaims yet, and the filing does not say when its investigation into the transferred files will be complete. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.
items.summary_html:
OpenAI has accused a former employee of taking more than 100 confidential files about its unreleased hardware back to Apple, according to a court filing OpenAI submitted on Wednesday in the trade secrets case Apple brought against the company.

OpenAI claims the employee, who joined from Apple and returned to Apple six months later, transferred sensitive documents to personal accounts before leaving.

The filing does not name the employee. OpenAI has asked the court for time to investigate the matter and to consider counterclaims against Apple.

OpenAI's Allegations Against Apple in the Trade Secrets Case

According to the filing, the files included:

  • detailed images of at least one unreleased OpenAI device
  • engineering and manufacturing data
  • supplier information and project files
  • specifications for cosmetic finishes
  • reports on coating and sealing hardware components

OpenAI says some of the files were transferred just after midnight in Singapore on June 2, which the filing describes as the employee's final day at OpenAI.

The filing goes further than the alleged file transfer. OpenAI claims the former employee presented OpenAI's product plans to Apple's senior leadership, including Apple's vice president of operations in Asia.

According to OpenAI, that presentation took place months ago. OpenAI now points to Apple's latest AI hardware push, including its newly announced smart home products such as Apple's $299 HomeView smart display, as a reason for concern.

OpenAI told the court it is worried that its confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where engineers could use it to shape upcoming Apple products.

Apple rejects the claims. The company says it has found nothing to support OpenAI's allegations and that it has rules that stop employees from bringing former employers' secrets into Apple.

How the Apple and OpenAI Trade Secrets Dispute Started

The new filing reverses the direction of the original case. In July, Apple sued OpenAI and two former Apple employees, Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan, alleging that the pair took confidential engineering information, including details about unreleased products, to help OpenAI develop its own hardware.

OpenAI denied those accusations at the time, saying it had no interest in other companies' trade secrets. With the new filing, OpenAI argues that confidential hardware information may have moved from OpenAI to Apple instead. OpenAI has not yet shown that Apple received or used any of the files it says were taken.

For consumers, the dispute has no immediate effect on existing Apple or OpenAI products. It does show that both companies are developing AI hardware in parallel, with OpenAI working on at least one unreleased device and Apple expanding into AI-powered smart home products.

Anyone following either company's hardware plans should watch the court docket for counterclaims, which would turn OpenAI's defense into a direct case against Apple.

OpenAI has not filed any counterclaims yet, and the filing does not say when its investigation into the transferred files will be complete.

Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post OpenAI Accuses a Former Employee of Taking More Than 100 Confidential Hardware Files Back to Apple appeared first on gHacks.

items.title: Google Removes Gemini Pro Models From the $4.99 AI Plus Plan Starting November 13
items.summary: Google will remove access to Gemini Pro models from its $4.99 per month Google AI Plus subscription on November 13, 2026, according to an email the Google One team is sending to AI Plus subscribers. From that date, selecting Pro models in the Gemini app and in AI Mode in Google Search will be limited to Google AI Pro subscribers and higher tiers. AI Plus is the cheapest paid Google AI plan. It has been sold with access to faster Gemini models and 400GB of Google storage, and Pro model access was one of its main selling points for subscribers who wanted more than the free tier. Google says AI Plus subscribers will keep access to its latest Flash-Lite model and to Flash, which the company describes as built for speed and intelligence. Existing conversations that used a Pro model are not deleted. Those chats can be continued after November 13, but with a different model. Why Google Is Moving Pro Models to Higher Tiers The change was signaled earlier. When Google rolled out Gemini 4 Argon, the company said the new model would only be available on AI Pro and AI Ultra plans, not AI Plus. Google also said at the time that AI Plus subscribers would later lose access to all Gemini Pro models. The November 13 email puts a date on that plan. After the change, Google's AI plans line up as follows: Free: Gemini Flash-Lite AI Plus ($4.99 per month): Gemini Flash-Lite and Gemini Flash AI Pro ($19.99 per month): everything in AI Plus, plus Gemini Pro models and Gemini 4 Argon AI Ultra 5x ($99.99 per month): AI Pro features with higher Pro model access and 5x higher usage limits AI Ultra 20x ($199.99 per month): AI Ultra 5x features with 20x higher usage limits and the highest Pro model access For AI Plus subscribers, the practical result is a gap of $15 per month between the plan they pay for and the cheapest plan that keeps Pro models. Google points subscribers to a Help Center article for details and says the subscription can be managed or canceled at any time. Subscribers who rely on Pro models have a little under a month to decide how to respond: Review the Google One plan comparison page to see which models, limits, and storage each tier includes. Test whether Gemini Flash handles typical prompts well enough, since Flash remains part of AI Plus. Finish or export important work from Pro model conversations before November 13, when those chats switch to another model. Upgrade to AI Pro, keep AI Plus, or cancel through Google One, depending on how much Pro model access matters. The trade-off is straightforward. Staying on AI Plus keeps the lower price and the storage, while Pro models and Gemini 4 Argon now require the $19.99 AI Pro plan. The email does not mention a price change for AI Plus or any change to the plan's 400GB of storage, and Google has not said whether existing subscribers will receive any compensation for losing Pro model access. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: Calling up Starlink customer service? You'll be talking to Grok.
items.summary: SpaceX says its AI is answering most of its customer calls. Anchiy/Getty Images - Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images SpaceX says Grok is taking 20,000 Starlink customer calls a day — and closing 70% without humans. The company revealed the stat while touting its voice-capable agent. It's part of a race to build AI agents that love to chat — possible (likely, even) with each other. Elon Musk's AI is a talker. This week, Musk's combined AI-and-space-exploration company, SpaceX, announced a new Grok Voice model — and revealed that Starlink call centers are already using the AI-as-a-conversationalist technology to answer 20,000 customer calls a day. The company said roughly 70% of those calls are resolved without humans. Grok Voice agents are verifying customers, troubleshooting Starlink hardware, issuing credits, and shipping replacement equipment, the company said. Its AI agents can take on those tasks in multiple languages, too. That makes Starlink a useful, real-world test case for AI voice technology — and particularly useful for its global expansion . The company says Starlink serves more than 6 million active customers around the world. Instead of building a massive human customer-service operation to power call centers, SpaceX is betting it can serve its multilingual customers with AI. SpaceX did not respond to Business Insider's questions about which languages Grok supports or what types of calls still require a person. AI companies have been quickly rolling out more powerful voice models that do their best Chatty Cathy impression. In July, OpenAI released GPT-Live-1 with call-capable support, while Google has launched similar enterprise systems. The same is true for AI companies that are focusing on consumers. Meta's Muse, for example, can also handle phone calls for those let into the beta feature. So, soon, your bot may dial one for English — while a company's bot answers the call. Grok Voice agents are verifying customers, troubleshooting Starlink hardware, issuing credits, and shipping replacement equipment, the company said. Its AI agents can take on those tasks in multiple languages, too.

That makes Starlink a useful, real-world test case for AI voice technology — and particularly useful for its global expansion. The company says Starlink serves more than 6 million active customers around the world.

Instead of building a massive human customer-service operation to power call centers, SpaceX is betting it can serve its multilingual customers with AI.

SpaceX did not respond to Business Insider's questions about which languages Grok supports or what types of calls still require a person.

AI companies have been quickly rolling out more powerful voice models that do their best Chatty Cathy impression. In July, OpenAI released GPT-Live-1 with call-capable support, while Google has launched similar enterprise systems.

The same is true for AI companies that are focusing on consumers. Meta's Muse, for example, can also handle phone calls for those let into the beta feature.

items.title: IBM Is a Gartner API Management Leader for the 11th Time. Now the Test Is AI Agent Governance
items.summary: Six vendors announced Leader placement in Gartner’s 2026 Magic Quadrant for API Management within ten days of its release, and each one tied the result to AI agents or AI governance. IBM says its placement is its 11th consecutive, a streak that, among the six, only Salesforce’s MuleSoft claims to match. A badge that crowded no longer tells a buyer much about which platform can govern an agent. What IBM Announced IBM published its announcement on October 1, three days after Gartner released the report on September 28. Analysts Shameen Pillai, Nicholas Carter and John Santoro assessed 17 vendors, the same number as in the 2025 edition. IBM’s post centers on IBM API Connect and its DataPower gateways, and frames the result around “the age of AI.” IBM describes API Connect as combining AI-assisted development, full lifecycle API management and runtime governance across hybrid environments. A feature called Flow Pilot lets developers use AI coding agents from their preferred coding assistants to design, build, test and publish APIs. DataPower Interact Gateway, in IBM’s words, turns existing APIs and integrations into “AI-ready tools that agents can securely discover and invoke,” while DataPower Nano Gateway enforces policy from a lightweight, Kubernetes-native component placed close to workloads. IBM also describes federated management that applies consistent governance across IBM and third-party gateways.
items.summary_html:
Six vendors announced Leader placement in Gartner’s 2026 Magic Quadrant for API Management within ten days of its release, and each one tied the result to AI agents or AI governance. IBM says its placement is its 11th consecutive, a streak that, among the six, only Salesforce’s MuleSoft claims to match. A badge that crowded no longer tells a buyer much about which platform can govern an agent.

What IBM Announced

IBM published its announcement on October 1, three days after Gartner released the report on September 28. Analysts Shameen Pillai, Nicholas Carter and John Santoro assessed 17 vendors, the same number as in the 2025 edition. IBM’s post centers on IBM API Connect and its DataPower gateways, and frames the result around “the age of AI.”

IBM describes API Connect as combining AI-assisted development, full lifecycle API management and runtime governance across hybrid environments. A feature called Flow Pilot lets developers use AI coding agents from their preferred coding assistants to design, build, test and publish APIs. DataPower Interact Gateway, in IBM’s words, turns existing APIs and integrations into “AI-ready tools that agents can securely discover and invoke,” while DataPower Nano Gateway enforces policy from a lightweight, Kubernetes-native component placed close to workloads. IBM also describes federated management that applies consistent governance across IBM and third-party gateways.

The post does not say which of these capabilities are generally available. Its only forward-looking line is that IBM “will continue to invest across the API lifecycle.” Gartner’s disclaimer, reproduced in the post, says it does not endorse any vendor depicted in its publications.

Six Leaders Announced the Same Result

Every placement below comes from the vendors’ own announcements. Gartner’s public abstract lists no vendors, and the full report is gated behind Gartner access or vendor registration forms.

VendorPlacement, as the vendor describes itIBMLeader for the 11th consecutive timeSalesforce (MuleSoft)Leader for the 11th time in a rowKongLeader for the seventh consecutive yearGraviteeLeader for the third consecutive yearBoomiLeader, described as its first timeWSO2Leader, no streak stated

The AI messaging is nearly uniform. Kong says its AI Gateway 2.0 release adds governed access for agents and MCP tools. Boomi CEO Steve Lucas said enterprises “are no longer treating the API layer and the agent layer as separate problems.” MuleSoft credits unified API and AI management through its Omni Gateway, and WSO2 describes its placement as validation of its approach to AI governance. Each is a vendor describing its own product.

Gartner’s Wording Gives the Pitch Some Cover

The vendors are not inventing the premise. The 2026 Magic Quadrant abstract opens with “APIs provide the foundation for AI initiatives, headless architectures, modernization and digital product monetization,” then adds that “their widespread use introduces significant challenges.” The companion Critical Capabilities abstract says API management platforms “now enable both conventional API use cases and advanced agentic and generative AI scenarios.” Its contents list on Gartner’s site includes entries such as AI Gateway Support, MCP Development and Management, and AI and Agent Management.

Gartner forecast in March 2024 that by 2026, more than 30% of the increase in demand for APIs would come from AI and tools using large language models. The figure is a forecast, not a measurement of current agent traffic.

IBM’s Use-Case Results Are More Mixed

Gartner’s Critical Capabilities report scores platforms against five use cases instead of placing them in a quadrant. IBM’s product pages say it ranked first in two of the five use cases in 2026 and among the top five vendors in all five. The same pages say it ranked first in five of six use cases in 2025. The number of use cases fell from six to five between editions, so the counts do not compare cleanly, and IBM’s public materials do not name the two use cases it won this year.

A rival has staked a claim in the use case closest to IBM’s pitch. Gravitee says it tied for the highest score in AI and Agent Management, though its page does not show the underlying scores. By IBM’s own count it sits in the top five for that use case too, so the question is the size of the gap, and the public material does not answer it.

What Buyers Should Ask Before Trusting the Badge

My take is that an 11-year streak reflects sustained scores on Gartner’s two axes, Ability to Execute and Completeness of Vision, and a single quadrant position cannot show how a given Leader performs when an agent, not a developer, is the one calling the API. Buyers should ask every Leader for its use-case scores and for the release status of its MCP and agent-governance features before treating the label as an answer.

For organizations that already run gateways from more than one vendor, IBM’s federated management claim is the part of its pitch to test first, because it targets the estate they have instead of asking them to replace it.

Gartner’s forecast date for AI-driven API demand is this year, and the six vendors above have all said they are ready for it. Buyers who press for release status and use-case scores now will not need to wait for the 2027 edition to learn which of those claims hold.

The post IBM Is a Gartner API Management Leader for the 11th Time. Now the Test Is AI Agent Governance appeared first on DataFLOQ.

items.title: Why Your LLM Agent's "Success" Might Be an Illusion
items.summary: Your LLM agent just told you it published the document. HTTP 200, all tokens logged, latency normal. The framework says success. But when you check the real system, nothing is there. This gap — between what an agent says it did and what actually happened in the real world — is where autonomous systems fail in ways that monitoring tools miss. The Two Contracts When an LLM agent runs, there are actually two success definitions happening at the same time , and they're almost never aligned: Framework success: The agent was instantiated, the model was called, tokens were consumed, the API returned HTTP 200, and the agent produced some output. From the orchestration layer's perspective, the execution succeeded. Business success: The consequence of that output — the document was actually published, the API request actually landed, the data was actually written to the target system. Most monitoring tools watch contract #1 and declare victory. But contract #2 is what your business actually cares about. Here's the trap: both can pass independently . An agent can fully satisfy the framework contract while completely failing the business contract. It generates valid-looking output, the LLM call succeeds, no errors are raised — and then your code tries to act on that output and finds the target system unchanged. Why This Happens Let me walk through a concrete scenario. An agent is tasked with publishing a support ticket to Slack. Here's what success looks like at each layer: Agent layer: "I called the Slack API." ✓ HTTP layer: "Slack returned 200 OK." ✓ Agent output layer: "My output says 'ticket posted to #support.'" ✓ Real world: The ticket never appeared in Slack. ✗ This isn't a hypothetical edge case. It happens when: The Slack token has the right format but insufficient permissions (Slack returns 200 but silently fails) The channel ID changed and your agent is using stale configuration A rate limit kicked in and Slack returned 200 but queued (then dropped) the message Network flakiness caused a partial send that the HTTP layer didn't catch From the agent's perspective, every checkpoint passed. From the real system's perspective, nothing happened. Why Monitoring Stays Blind Token counters can't see this. Cost baselines can't see this. Even output parsing can't reliably see this — a well-formed response that happens to be wrong looks identical to a well-formed response that's correct. And silent-failure detection for agents (checking whether an execution produced zero output tokens) can catch some of these — an agent that fails hard and returns nothing is detectable. But an agent that returns plausible output that describes an action that never actually landed? That's invisible to every layer except the one watching the real system. The Missing Layer: Action Confirmation This is where action confirmation comes in — a separate observability layer that asks a different question than the others. The idea is simple: after your agent claims it took an action, your own code independently verifies whether the action actually landed . Not by trusting the agent's word. Not by checking the HTTP status code. By reading the target system back. For publishing to Slack: Did the message actually appear in the channel? For writing to a database: Can I query back what I just wrote? For updating a CRM record: Does the field now contain what the agent said it would write? This requires your code to have independent visibility into the target system. But if you're building an agent that acts on real systems, you need that visibility anyway — for debugging, for audit, for confidence. How Action Confirmation Actually Works You structure it in two phases: The agent runs and produces output — normal LLM execution. It says "I published the ticket to #support." Your code verifies the consequence — you query Slack's API to check whether the message actually landed. You read the state of the target system independently , don't just trust the agent's output. Then you report that verdict alongside the agent execution . This creates a structured record: "Agent said: published. Verified: yes" or "Agent said: published. Verified: no." The verification can be strict or lenient: Strict: Alert unless the action is independently confirmed. Right for safety-critical operations. Lenient: Alert only if your code explicitly can't confirm. Right for operations that happen to not always take a real action, so absence of confirmation doesn't mean failure. Why This Matters Now LLM agents are starting to actually take actions — not just generating text for humans to review, but autonomously writing to databases, publishing to platforms, transferring funds, filing tickets. The moment your agent's output becomes a real-world action , the gap between framework success and business success becomes a liability. Monitoring frameworks are built for observing LLM execution — tokens, latency, cost, whether the model responded. But they're not built for verifying consequences. That's a different problem, and it requires a different monitoring layer. If you're building an agent that does real things, you need both: Framework monitoring to catch execution failures (token anomalies, model errors, cost spikes) Action confirmation to catch the agents that succeed at their own contract but fail at yours One monitors the agent. The other monitors the world the agent acts on. Further reading: The AI Agents Control Tower includes optional action confirmation (available in SDK 0.4.4+) — you call reportAction(note, confirmed) from your code after verifying the consequence, and it attaches to the execution record. But the principle is worth implementing even without tools: define what "success" means for each agent action, then instrument verification independently. The hardest part isn't the monitoring — it's thinking clearly about what success actually means before you ship.

Your LLM agent just told you it published the document. HTTP 200, all tokens logged, latency normal. The framework says success. But when you check the real system, nothing is there.

This gap — between what an agent says it did and what actually happened in the real world — is where autonomous systems fail in ways that monitoring tools miss.

The Two Contracts

When an LLM agent runs, there are actually two success definitions happening at the same time, and they're almost never aligned:

  1. Framework success: The agent was instantiated, the model was called, tokens were consumed, the API returned HTTP 200, and the agent produced some output. From the orchestration layer's perspective, the execution succeeded.

  2. Business success: The consequence of that output — the document was actually published, the API request actually landed, the data was actually written to the target system.

Most monitoring tools watch contract #1 and declare victory. But contract #2 is what your business actually cares about.

Here's the trap: both can pass independently. An agent can fully satisfy the framework contract while completely failing the business contract. It generates valid-looking output, the LLM call succeeds, no errors are raised — and then your code tries to act on that output and finds the target system unchanged.

Let me walk through a concrete scenario.

An agent is tasked with publishing a support ticket to Slack. Here's what success looks like at each layer:

  • Agent layer: "I called the Slack API." ✓
  • HTTP layer: "Slack returned 200 OK." ✓
  • Agent output layer: "My output says 'ticket posted to #support.'" ✓
  • Real world: The ticket never appeared in Slack. ✗

This isn't a hypothetical edge case. It happens when:

  • The Slack token has the right format but insufficient permissions (Slack returns 200 but silently fails)
  • The channel ID changed and your agent is using stale configuration
  • A rate limit kicked in and Slack returned 200 but queued (then dropped) the message
  • Network flakiness caused a partial send that the HTTP layer didn't catch

From the agent's perspective, every checkpoint passed. From the real system's perspective, nothing happened.

items.title: Default-Deny Egress Before Your Agent Meets a Free Model Endpoint
items.summary: Here is a script I keep watching play out. A team reads that a free tier exists, spins up an agent on someone else's host, points it at a hosted model, and ships a demo by Friday. Nobody asks where the data went until an auditor does. So let me ask the uncomfortable version early: if your agent runs on a host you don't fully control, what exactly is stopping it from sending your repository somewhere you never approved? I'm not going to re-report benchmark news I haven't verified myself. But the trend signal is easy to read. DEV's front page this week is full of AI fatigue, "AI got better while software didn't," and posts about thousands of open-source AI projects landing in a single weekend. Teams respond by trying free tiers. And a free tier is exactly when the trust-boundary question gets real, because you're adopting two new boundaries at once. This post is a security walkthrough. Threat model first, then two enforcement layers you can actually test, then a decision table for what may cross which boundary. Everything below is runnable fixture code, not a policy document. The threat model, in five lines Write this down before you write any agent code. If you can't fill all five lines, you don't have a threat model, you have a vibe. Asset: the plaintext your agent can read — source, .env files, logs, ticket bodies, fixture data with real customer rows. Actor: anything that can influence the payload. That includes prompt injection from a fetched file, a compromised dependency, and a helpful teammate who pastes a token "just for testing." Path: prompt assembly → HTTP client → TLS → someone else's inference host. Invariant: no secret-shaped string and no denied data class ever leaves the host, even when the agent is wrong. Evidence: a failing canary connection and a failing unit test, both executed in CI. Note line four. The invariant has to survive an agent that is confidently incorrect, because that is the normal state of agents. Two boundaries, and only one can see plaintext This is the part people get wrong, and it costs them a false sense of safety. Layer Where it lives What it can see What it can enforce Content gate Your process, before encryption Full plaintext payload Regex/classifier rules on strings Destination gate The kernel, on the host IP, port, protocol, volume Allowlist, default deny, counters The content gate can read everything and can be bypassed by any code path that skips it. The destination gate cannot read anything, and cannot be bypassed by application code — but it also can't tell a secret from a shopping list. You need both, and you need to know which one is load-bearing when they disagree. Step 1 — Write the egress contract before you write the agent The contract is a small file that both layers read. One source of truth, two enforcement points. { "version" : 1 , "reviewed_at" : "2026-10-16" , "allowed_destinations" : [ "203.0.113.10:443" ], "resolver" : "203.0.113.53:53" , "data_classes" : { "public_docs" : "send" , "internal_source" : "send_after_review" , "customer_pii" : "never" , "credentials" : "never" , "logs_with_tokens" : "never" } } Two rules for this file. Pin the destination by IP and port, not by hostname — DNS is a second trust boundary and I'd rather not argue about it in a review meeting. Second, date it. An undated contract is a rumor. Step 2 — Enforce destinations in the kernel On a host where you control the kernel, this is the whole game. Default deny, allow the one endpoint, count and log the rest. #!/usr/sbin/nft -f # /etc/nftables.d/agent-egress.nft table inet agent_egress { set allowed_dst { type ipv4_addr flags interval elements = { 203.0.113.10 } } chain output { type filter hook output priority 0; policy drop; oifname "lo" accept ct state established,related accept ip daddr @allowed_dst tcp dport 443 accept ip daddr 203.0.113.53 udp dport 53 accept meta nfproto ipv6 drop counter log prefix "agent-egress-drop " level warn } } Load it and confirm it took effect: sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.d/agent-egress.nft sudo nft list table inet agent_egress Now prove it with a canary. A rule you haven't tested is a comment with extra steps. CANARY = 203.0.113.99 if timeout 5 bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/ ${ CANARY } /443" 2>/dev/null ; then echo "FAIL: canary destination reachable" ; exit 1 else echo "PASS: egress blocked" fi sudo nft list table inet agent_egress | grep -c "agent-egress-drop" If the canary connects, stop. Fix the policy before you debug the agent. Step 3 — Enforce content where plaintext exists Kernel rules can't read a payload, so the string policy has to live in the process that builds the request. Keep it dumb and fast. # gate/preflight.py import json , re SECRET_PATTERNS = { " aws_access_key " : re . compile ( r " \bAKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}\b " ), " github_pat " : re . compile ( r " \bghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}\b " ), " private_key " : re . compile ( r " -----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY----- " ), " bearer " : re . compile ( r " \bBearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-]{20,} " ), } DENY_CLASSES = { " customer_pii " , " credentials " , " logs_with_tokens " } class EgressViolation ( Exception ): """ Raised before bytes leave the process. """ def assert_payload_allowed ( payload : str , contract : dict , declared : str ) -> str : if contract [ " data_classes " ]. get ( declared ) == " never " or declared in DENY_CLASSES : raise EgressViolation ( f " data class ' { declared } ' is not sendable " ) hits = sorted ( n for n , rx in SECRET_PATTERNS . items () if rx . search ( payload )) if hits : raise EgressViolation ( f " payload matched { hits } " ) return payload if __name__ == " __main__ " : contract = json . load ( open ( " egress.contract.json " )) print ( assert_payload_allowed ( " how do I pin nftables? " , contract , " public_docs " )) And the fixture pair, because one-sided tests are theatre: # tests/test_preflight.py import pytest from gate.preflight import EgressViolation , assert_payload_allowed CONTRACT = { " data_classes " : { " public_docs " : " send " , " customer_pii " : " never " }} def test_negative_secret_shaped_string_is_blocked (): with pytest . raises ( EgressViolation ): assert_payload_allowed ( " token: ghp_ " + " a " * 36 , CONTRACT , " public_docs " ) def test_negative_denied_class_is_blocked (): with pytest . raises ( EgressViolation ): assert_payload_allowed ( " email a@b.example " , CONTRACT , " customer_pii " ) def test_positive_public_question_passes (): assert assert_payload_allowed ( " regex help? " , CONTRACT , " public_docs " ) == " regex help? " Step 4 — Wire both layers into one gate Enforcement that isn't in CI is a suggestion. # .github/workflows/egress.yml name : egress-gate on : [ pull_request ] jobs : gate : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - run : pip install pytest - run : pytest -q tests/test_preflight.py - run : bash scripts/canary.sh The unit tests catch content regressions in seconds. The canary catches the day someone relaxes the firewall "temporarily." Different failure modes, different layers, same gate. Decision table: what may cross which boundary Data class Send to hosted model? Store on the host? Enforced by Public docs, OSS source Yes Yes Nothing — it's already public Internal source Only after review, pinned revision Yes Content gate + review Customer PII No Only if already required by policy Content gate, deny class Credentials, tokens No Canary/short-lived only Both layers, deny class Logs with tokens No Redact at write time Content gate, plus log sink policy Where a free tier genuinely helps, and where it doesn't Here's the honest version of the pitch. Two things matter for this workflow. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. First, the free model access matters because this whole approach depends on repeatedly running negative fixtures — canary probes, secret-shaped payloads, denied data classes. That is cheap, boring traffic, and paying per token to run it is silly. Second, the free server option matters because Layer 2 only exists if you control the kernel. On a pure client-side SaaS you can't write an output chain; you can only hope the application calls your gate. If the host you get is a locked-down container without NET_ADMIN , you cannot load that nftables table — plan for substituting a forced proxy plus a resolver you control, or accept that you only have Layer 1. Check before you design around it. The project advertises a free tier that at the time of writing includes 10M tokens and a free server. Treat that as operator-supplied and verify the current limits yourself on the project's own page before you build a budget on it; quotas move, and dated assumptions rot fast. If you want to try the negative-fixture suite against an endpoint you don't own, a free tier is a reasonable place to start — just bring your own contract. Limitations and failure modes Be clear-eyed about what this does not do. TLS is opaque to you. The destination gate sees IPs and ports. You cannot content-inspect the inference request without terminating TLS with a CA you control, which means running a broker you now have to secure too. DNS is a second door. Pin the resolver, or an attacker swaps the name behind an allowed IP. DoH/DoT bypass. A dependency that ships its own resolver walks around your port-53 rule. Package installs break. Default-deny means your mirror must be on the allowlist, or builds fail at 2 a.m. Counters lie by omission. If the log rule is the only evidence and nobody reads it, you have detection without detection. Who should not use this Don't build this for a throwaway weekend experiment on public sample data — the overhead isn't worth it, and default-deny rules will just slow you down. Don't use it if you need full payload inspection of encrypted traffic and you're not prepared to run a TLS-terminating broker with its own threat model. And don't adopt it as a substitute for data classification: the gate enforces what you declared. If your team can't say which column is PII, no firewall will guess for you. The boundary question The gate works when both layers are boring and both are tested. So the question I'd leave you with isn't whether to allowlist — it's where the decision belongs. Should the invariant "this data class never leaves" live in CI as a unit test, or in the kernel as a rule that ignores your application entirely? I have an opinion, but it depends on your blast radius. Which layer would you trust when the agent is confidently wrong?

Here is a script I keep watching play out. A team reads that a free tier exists, spins up an agent on someone else's host, points it at a hosted model, and ships a demo by Friday. Nobody asks where the data went until an auditor does.

So let me ask the uncomfortable version early: if your agent runs on a host you don't fully control, what exactly is stopping it from sending your repository somewhere you never approved?

I'm not going to re-report benchmark news I haven't verified myself. But the trend signal is easy to read. DEV's front page this week is full of AI fatigue, "AI got better while software didn't," and posts about thousands of open-source AI projects landing in a single weekend. Teams respond by trying free tiers. And a free tier is exactly when the trust-boundary question gets real, because you're adopting two new boundaries at once.

This post is a security walkthrough. Threat model first, then two enforcement layers you can actually test, then a decision table for what may cross which boundary. Everything below is runnable fixture code, not a policy document.

The threat model, in five lines

Write this down before you write any agent code. If you can't fill all five lines, you don't have a threat model, you have a vibe.

  1. Asset: the plaintext your agent can read — source, .env files, logs, ticket bodies, fixture data with real customer rows.
  2. Actor: anything that can influence the payload. That includes prompt injection from a fetched file, a compromised dependency, and a helpful teammate who pastes a token "just for testing."
  3. Path: prompt assembly → HTTP client → TLS → someone else's inference host.
  4. Invariant: no secret-shaped string and no denied data class ever leaves the host, even when the agent is wrong.
  5. Evidence: a failing canary connection and a failing unit test, both executed in CI.

Note line four. The invariant has to survive an agent that is confidently incorrect, because that is the normal state of agents.

Two boundaries, and only one can see plaintext

This is the part people get wrong, and it costs them a false sense of safety.

Layer Where it lives What it can see What it can enforce Content gate Your process, before encryption Full plaintext payload Regex/classifier rules on strings Destination gate The kernel, on the host IP, port, protocol, volume Allowlist, default deny, counters

The content gate can read everything and can be bypassed by any code path that skips it. The destination gate cannot read anything, and cannot be bypassed by application code — but it also can't tell a secret from a shopping list. You need both, and you need to know which one is load-bearing when they disagree.

Step 1 — Write the egress contract before you write the agent

The contract is a small file that both layers read. One source of truth, two enforcement points.

{
  "version": 1,
  "reviewed_at": "2026-10-16",
  "allowed_destinations": ["203.0.113.10:443"],
  "resolver": "203.0.113.53:53",
  "data_classes": {
    "public_docs": "send",
    "internal_source": "send_after_review",
    "customer_pii": "never",
    "credentials": "never",
    "logs_with_tokens": "never"
  }
}

Two rules for this file. Pin the destination by IP and port, not by hostname — DNS is a second trust boundary and I'd rather not argue about it in a review meeting. Second, date it. An undated contract is a rumor.

Step 2 — Enforce destinations in the kernel

On a host where you control the kernel, this is the whole game. Default deny, allow the one endpoint, count and log the rest.

#!/usr/sbin/nft -f
# /etc/nftables.d/agent-egress.nft
table inet agent_egress {
  set allowed_dst {
    type ipv4_addr
    flags interval
    elements = { 203.0.113.10 }
  }

  chain output {
    type filter hook output priority 0; policy drop;

    oifname "lo" accept
    ct state established,related accept
    ip daddr @allowed_dst tcp dport 443 accept
    ip daddr 203.0.113.53 udp dport 53 accept
    meta nfproto ipv6 drop
    counter log prefix "agent-egress-drop " level warn
  }
}

Load it and confirm it took effect:

sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.d/agent-egress.nft
sudo nft list table inet agent_egress

Now prove it with a canary. A rule you haven't tested is a comment with extra steps.

CANARY=203.0.113.99
if timeout 5 bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/${CANARY}/443" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "FAIL: canary destination reachable"; exit 1
else
  echo "PASS: egress blocked"
fi

sudo nft list table inet agent_egress | grep -c "agent-egress-drop"

If the canary connects, stop. Fix the policy before you debug the agent.

Step 3 — Enforce content where plaintext exists

Kernel rules can't read a payload, so the string policy has to live in the process that builds the request. Keep it dumb and fast.

# gate/preflight.py
import json, re

SECRET_PATTERNS = {
    "aws_access_key": re.compile(r"\bAKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}\b"),
    "github_pat": re.compile(r"\bghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}\b"),
    "private_key": re.compile(r"-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----"),
    "bearer": re.compile(r"\bBearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-]{20,}"),
}

DENY_CLASSES = {"customer_pii", "credentials", "logs_with_tokens"}


class EgressViolation(Exception):
    """Raised before bytes leave the process."""


def assert_payload_allowed(payload: str, contract: dict, declared: str) -> str:
    if contract["data_classes"].get(declared) == "never" or declared in DENY_CLASSES:
        raise EgressViolation(f"data class '{declared}' is not sendable")
    hits = sorted(n for n, rx in SECRET_PATTERNS.items() if rx.search(payload))
    if hits:
        raise EgressViolation(f"payload matched {hits}")
    return payload


if __name__ == "__main__":
    contract = json.load(open("egress.contract.json"))
    print(assert_payload_allowed("how do I pin nftables?", contract, "public_docs"))

And the fixture pair, because one-sided tests are theatre:

# tests/test_preflight.py
import pytest
from gate.preflight import EgressViolation, assert_payload_allowed

CONTRACT = {"data_classes": {"public_docs": "send", "customer_pii": "never"}}


def test_negative_secret_shaped_string_is_blocked():
    with pytest.raises(EgressViolation):
        assert_payload_allowed("token: ghp_" + "a" * 36, CONTRACT, "public_docs")


def test_negative_denied_class_is_blocked():
    with pytest.raises(EgressViolation):
        assert_payload_allowed("email a@b.example", CONTRACT, "customer_pii")


def test_positive_public_question_passes():
    assert assert_payload_allowed("regex help?", CONTRACT, "public_docs") == "regex help?"
Step 4 — Wire both layers into one gate

Enforcement that isn't in CI is a suggestion.

# .github/workflows/egress.yml
name: egress-gate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install pytest
      - run: pytest -q tests/test_preflight.py
      - run: bash scripts/canary.sh

The unit tests catch content regressions in seconds. The canary catches the day someone relaxes the firewall "temporarily." Different failure modes, different layers, same gate.

Decision table: what may cross which boundary
Data class Send to hosted model? Store on the host? Enforced by Public docs, OSS source Yes Yes Nothing — it's already public Internal source Only after review, pinned revision Yes Content gate + review Customer PII No Only if already required by policy Content gate, deny class Credentials, tokens No Canary/short-lived only Both layers, deny class Logs with tokens No Redact at write time Content gate, plus log sink policy
Where a free tier genuinely helps, and where it doesn't

Here's the honest version of the pitch. Two things matter for this workflow.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

First, the free model access matters because this whole approach depends on repeatedly running negative fixtures — canary probes, secret-shaped payloads, denied data classes. That is cheap, boring traffic, and paying per token to run it is silly. Second, the free server option matters because Layer 2 only exists if you control the kernel. On a pure client-side SaaS you can't write an output chain; you can only hope the application calls your gate.

If the host you get is a locked-down container without NET_ADMIN, you cannot load that nftables table — plan for substituting a forced proxy plus a resolver you control, or accept that you only have Layer 1. Check before you design around it.

The project advertises a free tier that at the time of writing includes 10M tokens and a free server. Treat that as operator-supplied and verify the current limits yourself on the project's own page before you build a budget on it; quotas move, and dated assumptions rot fast.

If you want to try the negative-fixture suite against an endpoint you don't own, a free tier is a reasonable place to start — just bring your own contract.

Limitations and failure modes

Be clear-eyed about what this does not do.

  1. TLS is opaque to you. The destination gate sees IPs and ports. You cannot content-inspect the inference request without terminating TLS with a CA you control, which means running a broker you now have to secure too.
  2. DNS is a second door. Pin the resolver, or an attacker swaps the name behind an allowed IP.
  3. DoH/DoT bypass. A dependency that ships its own resolver walks around your port-53 rule.
  4. Package installs break. Default-deny means your mirror must be on the allowlist, or builds fail at 2 a.m.
  5. Counters lie by omission. If the log rule is the only evidence and nobody reads it, you have detection without detection.
Who should not use this

Don't build this for a throwaway weekend experiment on public sample data — the overhead isn't worth it, and default-deny rules will just slow you down. Don't use it if you need full payload inspection of encrypted traffic and you're not prepared to run a TLS-terminating broker with its own threat model. And don't adopt it as a substitute for data classification: the gate enforces what you declared. If your team can't say which column is PII, no firewall will guess for you.

The boundary question

The gate works when both layers are boring and both are tested. So the question I'd leave you with isn't whether to allowlist — it's where the decision belongs. Should the invariant "this data class never leaves" live in CI as a unit test, or in the kernel as a rule that ignores your application entirely?

I have an opinion, but it depends on your blast radius. Which layer would you trust when the agent is confidently wrong?

items.title: WeightWatch: Detección Black-Box de Backdoors en LLMs Fine-Tuneados
items.summary: La cadena de suministro de modelos de IA representa un vector de ataque emergente y crítico. Los modelos open-weight fine-tuneados pueden contener puertas traseras (backdoors) latentes que solo se activan ante triggers específicos, siendo indetectables mediante inspección superficial. Presentamos WeightWatch (github.com/amurlaniakea/weightwatch), una herramienta de auditoría de seguridad diseñada para escanear modelos de lenguaje antes de su despliegue. Características técnicas principales: Análisis Black-Box: No requiere acceso a los datos de entrenamiento originales ni a un modelo base de referencia limpio. Detección Híbrida: Combina la técnica output-to-input loop (para forzar la convergencia de firmas anómalas) con inyección de muestras canary. Determinismo y Reproducibilidad: Ejecución con semilla fija, garantizando el mismo veredicto y hash sha256 para un modelo dado. La cadena de suministro de modelos de IA representa un vector de ataque emergente y crítico. Los modelos open-weight fine-tuneados pueden contener puertas traseras (backdoors) latentes que solo se activan ante triggers específicos, siendo indetectables mediante inspección superficial.

Presentamos WeightWatch (github.com/amurlaniakea/weightwatch), una herramienta de auditoría de seguridad diseñada para escanear modelos de lenguaje antes de su despliegue.

Características técnicas principales:

Análisis Black-Box: No requiere acceso a los datos de entrenamiento originales ni a un modelo base de referencia limpio.

Detección Híbrida: Combina la técnica output-to-input loop (para forzar la convergencia de firmas anómalas) con inyección de muestras canary.

Determinismo y Reproducibilidad: Ejecución con semilla fija, garantizando el mismo veredicto y hash sha256 para un modelo dado.

Integración CI/CD Nativa: Salida estructurada en JSON y códigos de salida (exit codes) para automatizar el bloqueo de modelos con veredicto SUSPICIOUS o BACKDOOR en pipelines de MLOps.

Estado actual: El MVP valida su lógica mediante fixtures sintéticos embebidos, sin dependencias de red. La validación a escala con modelos reales de Hugging Face está programada para la v0.2.

Invitamos a la comunidad de seguridad en IA, ingenieros de MLOps e investigadores a revisar el código, contribuir con heurísticas de detección y probar su integración en entornos de staging. La seguridad de la IA debe ser automatizable, transparente y de código abierto.

items.summary: The gate I skip is always the one that bites The DEV front page keeps arguing about AI output quality. Fair. But that debate skips the boring part. Features ship without release criteria. Criteria get written after the incident, not before. So here is a different approach. A readiness contract that fails closed, stored in the repo. It is not a vibe check. It is a file, a runner, and three tests. Three rules before any YAML Write these on the repo wall. They are short on purpose. Missing evidence is a failure, never a warning. Exit code 0 is not proof. Empty output fails. A waiver without an expiry and reason is invalid. Rule two is the one people fight me on. A command that exits 0 and prints nothing tells you nothing. Step 1: Put the gates in readiness.toml I use TOML because tomllib ships with Python 3.11. No dependencies. No lockfile churn. JSONDecodeError : verdict . issues . append ( " bad_json " ) else : value = data . get ( expect_json [ " field " ]) if value is None or value > expect_json [ " max " ]: verdict . issues . append ( " predicate_failed " ) return verdict def active_waiver ( waivers , gate_id , today = None ): today = today or time . strftime ( " %Y-%m-%d " ) for w in waivers : if w [ " gate " ] != gate_id : continue if not w . get ( " reason " , "" ). strip (): continue # no reason means no waiver if w [ " expires " ] < today : continue # expired means fail closed return w return None def run_gate ( gate , defaults , evdir ): evdir . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) path = evdir / gate [ " evidence " ] code = 0 if gate . get ( " run " ): proc = subprocess . run ( gate [ " run " ], shell = True , cwd = ROOT , capture_output = True , text = True ) code = proc . returncode path . write_text ( proc . stdout + proc . stderr ) return evaluate ( gate [ " id " ], code , path , gate . get ( " max_age_hours " , defaults [ " max_age_hours " ]), gate . get ( " expect_json " ), owner = gate . get ( " owner " , " unassigned " ), ) def main () -> int : cfg = tomllib . loads ( CFG . read_text ()) defaults = cfg . get ( " defaults " , {}) evdir = ROOT / defaults . get ( " evidence_dir " , " artifacts/readiness " ) verdicts = [ run_gate ( g , defaults , evdir ) for g in cfg . get ( " gate " , [])] blocked = [] for v in verdicts : if v . ok : continue w = active_waiver ( cfg . get ( " waiver " , []), v . gate ) if w : print ( f " WAIVED { v . gate } until { w [ ' expires ' ] } : { w [ ' reason ' ] } " ) continue blocked . append ( v ) print ( f " { len ( verdicts ) - len ( blocked ) } / { len ( verdicts ) } gates green " ) for v in blocked : print ( f " FAIL { v . gate } { ' , ' . join ( v . issues ) } owner= { v . owner } " ) return 1 if blocked else 0 if __name__ == " __main__ " : sys . exit ( main ()) Run it with python tools/readiness.py . Gate Evidence Fails closed when Max age Unit tests pytest.txt empty, nonzero, stale 24h Budget headroom budget.json spent_ratio_max > 0.6 12h Prompt hash prompt.sha256 hash differs from reviewed commit current commit Canary traffic canary.log zero lines, any 5xx 1h Rollback drill rollback.exit missing file 7d Waiver hygiene readiness.toml expired or empty reason n/a Nothing here needs a dashboard. Six files and one exit code are enough for a solo builder. Where free model access and a free server actually help Two gates in that table cost money if you run them naively. That is where a free allowance changes the experiment. Gate two measures budget headroom. I point it at a throwaway endpoint first, so a bad prompt loop burns nothing. MonkeyCode's free model access is the free tier I use for that pass, and its free server option gives me a disposable host for the canary gate instead of probing production. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Treat availability claims as claims. The free tier is advertised with a token allowance and a free server, but quotas, model lists, and terms change. Read the current terms on the project page before you wire a gate to them. Do not hardcode a number from a blog post into readiness.toml . Read it from the provider or from a config file you control. Limitations and who should not use this This is a release gate, not a security review. It proves evidence exists and is fresh. It proves nothing about correctness. Skip it if you have no rollback path yet. Every gate will fail closed, and you will learn nothing. Skip it in regulated environments where evidence needs formal sign-off chains. A TOML file is not an audit trail. Skip it past roughly five services. At that size you want a platform team and real policy tooling, not one Python file. Try it today in about 20 minutes touch readiness.toml and add the unit-test gate only. Write tools/readiness.py from the block above. Add the empty-evidence fixture and watch it fail on purpose. Run python tools/readiness.py and check the exit code. Add one waiver with a real expiry date, then let it expire in a test. Wire the runner into CI as a required step, not a report. That is the whole artifact. One file, one runner, three tests, six rows. Which field does your team keep forgetting in a gate like this: the evidence path, the owner, or the waiver expiry date? Tell me the missing one and I will fold it into the next version of the template.
items.summary_html:
The gate I skip is always the one that bites

The DEV front page keeps arguing about AI output quality. Fair. But that debate skips the boring part.

Features ship without release criteria. Criteria get written after the incident, not before.

So here is a different approach. A readiness contract that fails closed, stored in the repo.

It is not a vibe check. It is a file, a runner, and three tests.

Three rules before any YAML

Write these on the repo wall. They are short on purpose.

  1. Missing evidence is a failure, never a warning.
  2. Exit code 0 is not proof. Empty output fails.
  3. A waiver without an expiry and reason is invalid.

Rule two is the one people fight me on. A command that exits 0 and prints nothing tells you nothing.

Step 1: Put the gates in readiness.toml

I use TOML because tomllib ships with Python 3.11. No dependencies. No lockfile churn.

[defaults]
max_age_hours = 72
evidence_dir = "artifacts/readiness"

[[gate]]
id = "unit-tests"
run = "pytest -q"
evidence = "pytest.txt"
max_age_hours = 24
owner = "sam"

[[gate]]
id = "budget-headroom"
run = "python tools/token_budget.py --max-tokens 12000 --json"
evidence = "budget.json"
max_age_hours = 12
owner = "sam"
expect_json = { field = "spent_ratio_max", max = 0.6 }

[[gate]]
id = "rollback-drill"
run = ""
evidence = "rollback.exit"
max_age_hours = 168
manual = true
owner = "sam"

[[waiver]]
gate = "concurrent-load"
expires = "2026-11-01"
reason = "single-tenant canary, no concurrent load yet"

Two details matter. The manual = true gate runs nothing and only validates an evidence file a human produced. The expect_json predicate is a field comparison, not an expression, so nothing gets eval-ed.

Step 2: Write a pure core and a dumb shell

The bug in most checkers is mixed concerns. Shell edges stay dumb. The verdict logic stays pure.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail-closed readiness runner. Missing evidence is a failure, not a warning."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json, subprocess, sys, time, tomllib
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
CFG = ROOT / "readiness.toml"


@dataclass
class Verdict:
    gate: str
    issues: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    owner: str = "unassigned"

    @property
    def ok(self) -> bool:
        return not self.issues


def evaluate(gate_id, exit_code, evidence_path, max_age_hours,
             expect_json=None, now=None, owner="unassigned") -> Verdict:
    now = now or time.time()
    verdict = Verdict(gate=gate_id, owner=owner)
    path = Path(evidence_path)

    if not path.exists():
        verdict.issues.append("missing_evidence")
        return verdict

    if (now - path.stat().st_mtime) / 3600 > max_age_hours:
        verdict.issues.append("stale")
    if path.stat().st_size == 0:
        verdict.issues.append("empty_evidence")
    if exit_code != 0:
        verdict.issues.append("nonzero_exit")

    if expect_json and not verdict.issues:
        try:
            data = json.loads(path.read_text())
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            verdict.issues.append("bad_json")
        else:
            value = data.get(expect_json["field"])
            if value is None or value > expect_json["max"]:
                verdict.issues.append("predicate_failed")
    return verdict


def active_waiver(waivers, gate_id, today=None):
    today = today or time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    for w in waivers:
        if w["gate"] != gate_id:
            continue
        if not w.get("reason", "").strip():
            continue          # no reason means no waiver
        if w["expires"] < today:
            continue          # expired means fail closed
        return w
    return None


def run_gate(gate, defaults, evdir):
    evdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path = evdir / gate["evidence"]
    code = 0
    if gate.get("run"):
        proc = subprocess.run(gate["run"], shell=True, cwd=ROOT,
                              capture_output=True, text=True)
        code = proc.returncode
        path.write_text(proc.stdout + proc.stderr)
    return evaluate(
        gate["id"], code, path,
        gate.get("max_age_hours", defaults["max_age_hours"]),
        gate.get("expect_json"),
        owner=gate.get("owner", "unassigned"),
    )


def main() -> int:
    cfg = tomllib.loads(CFG.read_text())
    defaults = cfg.get("defaults", {})
    evdir = ROOT / defaults.get("evidence_dir", "artifacts/readiness")
    verdicts = [run_gate(g, defaults, evdir) for g in cfg.get("gate", [])]
    blocked = []
    for v in verdicts:
        if v.ok:
            continue
        w = active_waiver(cfg.get("waiver", []), v.gate)
        if w:
            print(f"WAIVED {v.gate} until {w['expires']}: {w['reason']}")
            continue
        blocked.append(v)
    print(f"{len(verdicts) - len(blocked)}/{len(verdicts)} gates green")
    for v in blocked:
        print(f"FAIL {v.gate} {','.join(v.issues)} owner={v.owner}")
    return 1 if blocked else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Run it with python tools/readiness.py. Exit code 1 blocks the release. Exit code 0 means every gate produced fresh, non-empty evidence.

Step 3: Add the failure fixture

A checker you never tested against failure is decoration. Two fixtures catch most of it.

# tests/test_readiness.py
from tools.readiness import active_waiver, evaluate


def test_silent_pass_is_a_failure(tmp_path):
    ev = tmp_path / "probe.txt"
    ev.write_text("")               # exited 0, printed nothing
    v = evaluate("health-probe", 0, ev, max_age_hours=24)
    assert "empty_evidence" in v.issues


def test_expired_waiver_does_not_apply():
    waivers = [{"gate": "load", "expires": "2020-01-01", "reason": "old"}]
    assert active_waiver(waivers, "load", today="2026-10-16") is None


def test_missing_evidence_is_a_failure(tmp_path):
    v = evaluate("canary", 0, tmp_path / "nope.log", max_age_hours=1)
    assert v.issues == ["missing_evidence"]

The first fixture is the important one. true exits 0 and produces nothing. Your checker must call that a failure.

The decision table

Copy this into the repo next to the TOML. Each row needs one owner name, not a team name.

Gate Evidence Fails closed when Max age Unit tests pytest.txt empty, nonzero, stale 24h Budget headroom budget.json spent_ratio_max > 0.6 12h Prompt hash prompt.sha256 hash differs from reviewed commit current commit Canary traffic canary.log zero lines, any 5xx 1h Rollback drill rollback.exit missing file 7d Waiver hygiene readiness.toml expired or empty reason n/a

Nothing here needs a dashboard. Six files and one exit code are enough for a solo builder.

Where free model access and a free server actually help

Two gates in that table cost money if you run them naively. That is where a free allowance changes the experiment.

Gate two measures budget headroom. I point it at a throwaway endpoint first, so a bad prompt loop burns nothing. MonkeyCode's free model access is the free tier I use for that pass, and its free server option gives me a disposable host for the canary gate instead of probing production.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Treat availability claims as claims. The free tier is advertised with a token allowance and a free server, but quotas, model lists, and terms change. Read the current terms on the project page before you wire a gate to them. Do not hardcode a number from a blog post into readiness.toml. Read it from the provider or from a config file you control.

Limitations and who should not use this

This is a release gate, not a security review. It proves evidence exists and is fresh. It proves nothing about correctness.

Skip it if you have no rollback path yet. Every gate will fail closed, and you will learn nothing.

Skip it in regulated environments where evidence needs formal sign-off chains. A TOML file is not an audit trail.

Skip it past roughly five services. At that size you want a platform team and real policy tooling, not one Python file.

Try it today in about 20 minutes
  1. touch readiness.toml and add the unit-test gate only.
  2. Write tools/readiness.py from the block above.
  3. Add the empty-evidence fixture and watch it fail on purpose.
  4. Run python tools/readiness.py and check the exit code.
  5. Add one waiver with a real expiry date, then let it expire in a test.
  6. Wire the runner into CI as a required step, not a report.

That is the whole artifact. One file, one runner, three tests, six rows.

Which field does your team keep forgetting in a gate like this: the evidence path, the owner, or the waiver expiry date? Tell me the missing one and I will fold it into the next version of the template.
