BYOD asset discovery usually starts the same way. Your asset sheet looks great. Every company laptop has a tag, an owner, and a color-coded status column someone spent a weekend on. Then a customer security review lands in your inbox with one simple question. Which personal devices can open your files?

The spreadsheet goes very quiet.

Here's the thing. Finding personal devices is the easy part, because your identity provider already knows about most of them. The hard part is turning that evidence into records you'd actually show an auditor, with a named owner, a known access path, and an honest level of confidence. Here's how one IT team did it in six steps, with two admins and two weeks.

The Question the Asset Sheet Couldn't Answer

Picture a 120-person company where a quarter of the staff are contractors. People work from the office, from home, and from cafés with questionable Wi-Fi. Two admins run IT on Microsoft 365, with Intune managing the company laptops.

Then a big customer's security questionnaire asks how many personal devices can access customer data. The deadline is two weeks away. The identity records list about two and a half times as many devices as the asset sheet.

BYOD asset discovery is the process of finding personal devices that access company systems or data, then recording who uses them, how they connect, and what they can reach. You track the access, not the ownership. For the basics of running a BYOD program, see our separate guide.

Why Personal Devices Never Reach the Asset Inventory

Most IT asset management(ITAM) records start with a purchase. IT buys a laptop, tags it, and adds it to the list. Personal devices skip that step completely. They show up through a sign-in instead, usually in one of three ways.

  • A personal phone with work email. An employee adds their work account in two minutes. The phone never appears anywhere IT checks.
  • A contractor's own laptop. They log in from it on day one. When the contract ends, the laptop leaves with them.
  • A shared family PC. Someone opens Slack "just for a minute." Now a computer used by two people has a company login on it.

The problem isn't the tools. It's the process. Onboarding never asks, "Which device will you use?" So the IT inventory only shows what the company bought, and BYOD asset discovery has to start with sign-ins, not purchases.

How to Turn BYOD Asset Discovery Into Accountable Records: 6 Steps

Most BYOD asset discovery can run on data you already have in your identity provider and MDM. Many personal devices never touch the office network, so identity data does the heavy lifting. A network scan covers the devices that do, and our guide to IT asset discovery explains how the methods fit together.

Step 1. Decide Which Company Data Puts a Device in Scope

Start with data, not devices. A device is in scope when it can reach something that would hurt if it leaked. Think customer files, finance systems, source code, and work email.

The team listed five sensitive apps. Any personal device that signs in to one of them counts. This took one afternoon.

Watch out. Don't try to inventory every phone on guest Wi-Fi. That's a lot of work for a list nobody will use.

What you get. A short scope list of apps and data that the whole team agrees on.

Step 2. Pull Device Evidence From Identity, MDM and Network Records

This step is about collecting evidence. Export from four sources.

  • Your identity provider. Pull the device list and sign-in logs from Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, or Google Workspace.
  • Your MDM. In Intune, filter by ownership type. In Jamf, check devices enrolled through account-driven User Enrollment.
  • Work mailboxes. List the mobile devices connected to them.
  • The office network. Our free Network Scanner finds every device on your LAN, including personal phones and laptops on office Wi-Fi. Export the results as a CSV and add them to your spreadsheet.

The team ended up with about 300 device entries. The asset sheet had 118 laptops.

Some entries won't have a device name. A laptop that signs in through a browser often shows only an OS and a browser in Entra sign-in logs. Keep those rows anyway. They're real access.

Watch out. Don't rely on MDM alone. The devices you most need to find are never enrolled, so MDM can't see them. Also, don't fully trust Intune's "Personal" label. Intune marks self-enrolled devices as Personal by default, so a few company laptops may be in that list.

What you get. One raw spreadsheet with a column showing where each record came from. You'll need it in Step 4.

Step 3. Clean the List Before You Count Anything

Raw device data is messy. Clean it with four rules before you report any number.

  • Merge duplicates. One phone can appear several times after a reset or an app reinstall. Match by user, model, and OS, not by name. Half your users' phones are just called "iPhone."
  • Match scan results by hostname. Phones use a random MAC address on office Wi-Fi, so the MAC can't tell you it's the same device.
  • Mark old devices as stale. No sign-in for 90 days means stale. Don't delete them, since you may need the history later.
  • Flag shared devices. Follow up instead of guessing the owner.

Here, cleanup merged 61 duplicates, marked 52 devices as stale, and flagged 6 shared ones. That left 187 active personal devices, after about two days of work.

Watch out. Don't send the raw number to management. The first BYOD asset discovery number always looks scary. Report the cleaned one.

What you get. A clean list of active personal devices.

Step 4. Sort Every Device: Seen, Attributed or Accountable

This is the step most teams skip, and it's the one that makes BYOD asset discovery worth trusting. Sort each device by how much IT actually knows about it.

Use these three levels to label every device on your clean list.

The goal isn't to make every device Accountable. The goal is that no device with access to sensitive data stays at Seen. Auditors trust honest uncertainty more than fake completeness.

Most devices on the team's list started at Seen, including every browser-only row from Step 2. A short message to each employee and contractor ("Is this your device?") moved most of them to Attributed within three days.

Watch out. "Registered in Entra ID" doesn't mean "managed." Registered only means the device signed in. It says nothing about whether IT controls it.

What you get. Every device has a confidence level.

Step 5. Choose Control Levels Based on Data, Not Device Type

Next, decide how much control each Attributed device needs. Let the data it can reach make the call.

  • Sensitive data. Use app protection (MAM, or mobile application management) or allow browser-only access.
  • Everything else. Require sign-in with conditional access rules, which check things like location and device health before letting someone in.

The team started with contractors. Their devices change the most, IT knows the least about them, and they leave when the project ends. We'd start there every time.

One manager refused to put MDM on their phone. Fair enough. A one-page note explaining what IT can and can't see fixed it. Track work access only. Never collect location, personal apps, or browsing history.

Watch out. Forcing full MDM on every personal device causes pushback, and people find workarounds. The workaround is usually worse.

What you get. Every Attributed device has a control level, which moves it to Accountable.

Step 6. Build Lifecycle Triggers So Records Stay Current

A BYOD record starts going out of date the day you create it. People buy new phones, and contractor projects end. Without triggers, BYOD asset discovery becomes a one-time project that's stale by next quarter. Tie updates to moments that already happen.

  • Onboarding. Add one question to the checklist, "Which device will you use?" Then create the record.
  • Device change. Update the record when someone gets a new phone or laptop.
  • Offboarding. Revoke access, wipe work data if the device is enrolled, and close the record with a date.


The team gives every contractor record an end date on day one, so access expires on time. That's what turns a one-time cleanup into real IT inventory tracking.

Watch out. Don't delete the record at offboarding. The closed record proves access ended. Auditors like proof. They're less fond of "we're pretty sure."

What you get. Records that update through normal work, plus a quick monthly check to move leftover Seen devices to Attributed.

What IT Can Answer Now That It Couldn't Before

The questionnaire is no longer scary. That's the practical payoff of BYOD asset discovery.

After two weeks, the team's 300 raw entries came down to 187 active personal devices. Of those, 142 were fully Accountable, 31 had a confirmed owner, and 14 were still unconfirmed and blocked from sensitive apps. The answer to the customer was short. In total, 173 personal devices can reach customer data, every one has a named owner, and 14 unconfirmed devices are blocked. It's not a perfect number. It's a defensible one.

The team can now also answer the usual follow-ups, like who owns each device, what IT actually controls, and which devices lose access when someone leaves.

This matters for security, too. Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report looked at devices infected with password-stealing malware. Of those that held company logins, 46% weren't managed by IT. Knowing your BYOD devices won't change that number. But it shows you which of those devices could be yours.

How AssetLoom Supports Accountable BYOD Records

Most inventory management software for IT assumes the company bought the device. BYOD breaks that assumption. Identity and MDM tools give you the evidence and the controls. AssetLoom is where the inventory record lives once BYOD asset discovery has done its job.

  • See what's on the office network. The free AssetLoom Network Scanner finds devices on your LAN without agents and exports the results as a CSV, ready to import into AssetLoom.
  • Bring device data into one place. Import your cleaned device list as a CSV, including scan results and identity-provider exports. 
  • Track every device through its lifecycle. Each record has a status, so you can see which devices are active and which have been closed.
  • Automate onboarding and offboarding. Workflows handle the repetitive steps, so offboarding doesn't depend on someone's memory.

Your MDM controls devices. AssetLoom keeps the inventory record of which devices exist and where they stand. It doesn't replace your MDM or wipe devices. It keeps the record that tells you which devices to act on.

Start With Evidence, End With Records You Can Defend

Personal devices were never missing from your company, only from your IT inventory. Scope by data, clean before you count, be honest about confidence, and let normal work keep records current.

Start with the free Network Scanner to see what's on your office network. Still on spreadsheets? AssetLoom offers free IT inventory management for teams under 250 assets. Accurate records are what make BYOD asset discovery worth the effort.

FAQs 1. What happens to a BYOD record when someone leaves?

Close it with a date and a note on how access was revoked. Don't delete it. The closed record proves that access ended.

2. Should personal devices be part of your ITAM inventory?

Yes, as a separate asset class. Track the owner, access scope, control level, and status. Skip cost and depreciation, since the company doesn't own the hardware.

3. Is it legal to record employees' personal devices?

Recording work access is common, but rules differ by country. Tell employees exactly what you collect and why. This isn't legal advice, so check with your legal team.

4. Why does one phone show up as several devices?

In identity records, resetting a phone or reinstalling a work app can register a new device object. On a network scan, phones often use a randomized MAC address on each Wi-Fi network. Match by user, model, and OS in identity data, and by hostname in scan results.

5. How is BYOD different from CYOD and COPE?

It comes down to ownership. With BYOD, the employee owns the device. With CYOD, employees choose from company-approved devices. With COPE, the company owns the device but allows some personal use.

items.title: AI Built My Friend’s MVP in 48 Hours. Then Real Users Showed Up.
items.summary: Why "vibe coding" feels like a superpower at first—and how to avoid the hidden architectural debt that hits when you scale. A month ago, a founder friend of mine showed me an entire web app he built over a single weekend. He didn't write a single line of raw code. Instead, he spent two days typing plain-English prompts into an AI coding assistant. The app was surprisingly smooth. The UI looked like a polished SaaS, features worked on test data, and he was convinced he had skipped six months of traditional dev work. Fast forward three weeks. He launched on Product Hunt, traffic spiked, real users onboarded—and the whole thing went up in flames. Payment webhooks randomly dropped state updates. Unindexed database queries caused the server to crawl under light load. When he tried to use the AI to "fix the bugs," the assistant refactored core files and silently broke three unrelated features. It was a classic reality check: generating code is easy, but making software work together when real life happens is still hard. The Illusion of the Zero-Effort App Tools like Cursor and Claude Code are genuinely incredible. They make boilerplates instant and writing syntax effortless. But syntax was never the hardest part of software engineering. When you write code line by line, you build a mental map of your system in your head. You naturally think through questions like: What happens if this API drops offline mid-request? How does this database query scale when we hit 50,000 rows? Is this state update thread-safe? When you delegate the typing to an AI, that mental map evaporates. You end up with hundreds of lines of code that look right on the surface, but nobody actually understands how the pieces fit together under stress. 3 Things AI Agents Get Wrong (That You End Up Fixing) If you use AI coding tools daily, these are the subtle failure modes to watch out for: 1. Over-Engineered Abstractions Ask an AI for a simple database route, and it will often give you five layers of interfaces, factories, and abstraction wrappers when a straightforward function would have done the job. When something breaks at 2 AM, tracing through those unnecessary layers is painful. 2. Context Blindness AI models are great at looking at a single file, but they struggle with global context. It’ll optimize a function in File A without realizing that File B relies on a specific side effect from it. It passes local unit tests while quietly breaking the broader system. 3. The "Happy Path" Bias AI code defaults to best-case scenarios. It writes clean code for when everything works, but rarely accounts for network timeouts, race conditions, or partial state updates unless you explicitly force it to. How I Use AI Daily Without Losing My Mind You don't need to stop using AI—you just need to change how you manage it. Treat the AI like a super-fast junior developer who needs strict guardrails. Set the rules before it types: Don't ask the AI to "build a feature." Define your types, interfaces, and data boundaries first, then ask it to write the implementation inside those constraints. Read every line in the pull request: If you don't understand what the AI wrote, don't merge it. If you can't explain it during a code review, you don't actually own your software. Test the ugly paths early: Before shipping, test what happens when external APIs rate-limit you, when connections time out, or when invalid data gets passed. The Real Future of Dev Work AI hasn't killed software development; it’s just changed what matters. Knowing raw syntax is no longer a moat. The developers who will stand out in the coming years aren't the ones who can prompt the fastest, but the ones who know system architecture, data modeling, and security well enough to guide AI output without getting trapped by it. Have you run into weird bugs or tech debt in AI-generated code recently, or has it been smooth sailing for your workflow? Let me know in the comments!

Have you run into weird bugs or tech debt in AI-generated code recently, or has it been smooth sailing for your workflow? Let me know in the comments!

items.summary_html:
A message like this lands in an engineering lead's inbox about once a quarter:

"MonkeyCode is open source. Free model access, and a free server option. Give it a try."

Two sentences. No workload, no data class, no expiry date. And still enough to start a standardization debate, because the alternative — self-hosting, or a paid seat — has an actual line item attached. Free is the only option in the room with a zero on the invoice.

So I ask a different question: what would have to be false for your team to walk away? If nobody can answer that, you don't have an evaluation. You have a mood.

The scenario below is a composite, and every number in it is illustrative. Vendor terms are dated and change. Re-verify them before you spend money or reputation on a decision.

Why "free tokens" is the wrong unit of analysis

Free capacity is real value. It's also a terrible unit for a standardization decision, for three structural reasons.

  1. Tokens are an input; work is an outcome. A lane that burns 2M tokens and closes 18 of 20 smoke tasks beats a lane that burns 800K tokens and closes 11. Token counts don't tell you which one you have.
  2. A grant is a stock; your workload is a flow. 10 million tokens sounds enormous until you know your team's monthly burn. A stock figure without a burn rate is a number with no denominator.
  3. The claim expires; the standard doesn't. Free tiers change. If four engineers have already written their rules files and prompt libraries around a lane, the price of reversal isn't the invoice — it's the rewrite.

That third point is where most teams quietly lose two weeks.

Why this specific lane makes a useful test case

MonkeyCode's operator describes it as an open-source project with free model access and a free server option, and states a free grant of 10 million tokens as of 2026-10-16. Those are operator-supplied claims, not verified benchmarks: no public burn rate, no hardware spec, no permanence guarantee. That isn't a defect of the product — it's the normal state of a zero-price offer. And it's exactly why the offer is a good exercise. When the price is zero, the only variables left to test are the ones that actually decide your outcome.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The artifact: a claim-to-test ledger

Stop writing evaluation docs. Write falsification docs. Every vendor sentence becomes one row with a test, an owner, and an expiry date.

Column What goes in it Claim (verbatim) Quote it. Never paraphrase a promise. Falsifying test The cheapest thing that could prove it false this sprint. Instrument Dashboard, CI job, task log, or a stopwatch. Minutes Real estimated cost of the test. Pass if A threshold you commit to before you see the result. Reverse signal What failure would change your decision, not just your mood. Owner One human, by name. Expiry The date the claim must be re-checked.
Define the variables first
  • T — number of claims under test
  • h — average minutes per falsification test
  • F = T × h / 60 — falsification hours
  • p — your honest probability of reversing the decision within one quarter
  • R — rework hours to undo the decision (rules files, prompt library, eval sets, CI wiring, docs)
  • W — loaded hourly cost

Run the ledger when p × R > F. The break-even threshold is p* = F / R.

W cancels out of both sides. That's the useful part: you never have to defend your loaded hourly rate to anyone.

Worked example (illustrative)

A platform team of six evaluates the lane with nine claims. F = 9 × 40 / 60 = 6 hours. They measure R = 60 hours of context rewrites with the shell snippet below rather than guessing. Then p* = 6 / 60 = 0.10.

Translation: if you believe there's more than a 1-in-10 chance you'd reverse this decision inside a quarter, the ledger pays for itself. That is a much easier argument to win than "let's do a proper evaluation."

The ledger, filled in
# Claim (abbreviated) Falsifying test Min Reverse signal C1 free grant, operator-stated run the 20-task smoke set twice; log tokens and tasks closed 45 grant covers < 5 working days at observed burn C2 free server option run the smoke set during a real PR window; record wall-clock queueing 45 queueing longer than your review window C3 open source clone it, build it, run the smoke set against your own copy 60 build path requires access you don't have C4 context export export rules files and prompt library; diff against your repo 30 export is lossy or manual C5 CI latency wire one nightly job; compare p95 wall clock to baseline 45 p95 blows the nightly budget C6 review latency count human review minutes on 20 lane-authored PRs 30 review minutes exceed authoring savings C7 data class ask policy whether your code class may be processed externally 15 policy answer is an absolute no C8 offboarding remove one engineer mid-week; confirm access and cost state 30 access or billing state becomes murky C9 version pinning pin a known-good configuration; re-run C1 after a restart 30 behavior drifts with no changelog

Note that C7 costs fifteen minutes and can end the entire evaluation. Cheap tests first. Always.

Sensitivity: when the ledger is not worth running
Scenario T h F p R p×R Verdict Beachhead: 2 engineers, 1 repo 4 30 2.0 0.15 12 1.8 Skip the ledger — just pilot Scale-up: 6 engineers, 3 repos 9 40 6.0 0.30 60 18.0 Run it this sprint Regulated: 40 engineers, 2 BUs 14 60 14.0 0.40 240 96.0 Run it, then gate on C7 alone

Look at row one. p × R = 1.8 beats F = 2.0 — barely. If your blast radius is one repo and two people, the correct decision is to skip the ceremony and use the lane for a week. Ledgers are for decisions that are expensive to reverse, not for curiosity.

Break-even moves fast: at R = 12 hours, p* = 17%. At R = 60, p* = 10%. At R = 240, p* = 6%. The more context you have to rewrite, the lower the bar for testing.

Measure R instead of estimating it

Rework hours are the one number teams routinely invent. Count your context assets first:

# context assets a reversal would force you to rewrite — count, don't guess
rg --files -g 'AGENTS.md' -g '*.mdc' -g 'prompts/**' -g 'evals/**' \
  | xargs -r wc -l | tail -1

Then keep the ledger in a file so it survives the meeting where everyone agrees verbally:

# ledger.yaml — one row per claim you are willing to falsify
# Scaffold only; the operator's stated terms are dated 2026-10-16 and must be re-checked.
decision: standardize-free-lane
owner: platform-lead              # a person, not a team
review_date: 2026-11-13           # claims expire; so does the decision
loaded_hourly_cost: 85
reverse_rework_hours: 60          # measured above, not estimated
claims:
  - id: C1
    claim: "free grant stated by operator (2026-10-16)"
    test: "run the 20-task smoke set twice; log tokens and completed tasks"
    pass_if: ">=18/20 tasks complete, twice"
    reverse_signal: "grant covers < 5 working days at observed burn"
    owner: platform-lead
    expiry: 2026-11-13
  - id: C7
    claim: "we may process this code class externally"
    test: "ask policy; get the answer in writing"
    pass_if: "written yes, with a scope"
    reverse_signal: "any conditional or verbal answer"
    owner: em
    expiry: 2026-11-13

# ledger.py — scaffold I wrote for this article; no tests, only PyYAML required
import sys, yaml, datetime as dt

doc = yaml.safe_load(open(sys.argv[1]))
claims = doc["claims"]
h = sum(c["minutes"] for c in claims) / len(claims)
F = len(claims) * h / 60
p_star = F / doc["reverse_rework_hours"]

print(f"T={len(claims)} h={h:.0f}min F={F:.1f}h break-even p*={p_star:.0%}")
print("run the ledger only if your reversal probability beats that number")

today = dt.date.today()
for c in claims:
    if dt.date.fromisoformat(str(c["expiry"])) < today:
        print(f"EXPIRED {c['id']} — owner {c['owner']}: re-check or drop the standard")

Run that on your own file before your next architecture sync, not after.

Free lane, self-host, or paid seat: fit criteria, not vibes
Criterion Free hosted lane Self-host Paid alternative Cash price zero (operator-stated) infra + ops hours per seat Whose machine processes the work vendor — test C7 yours vendor Reversal cost R context rewrites near zero if the repo is yours seat migration + retraining Ops hours you own lowest highest middle Failure mode terms change under you nobody maintains it renewal becomes the default

Fit rules I'd actually apply:

  • Take the free hosted lane when F < 8 hours, one team, two repos or fewer, and someone owns a recurring re-check. Free buys you falsification time; it doesn't buy you a standard.
  • Self-host when the code class can't leave, you already run the ops capacity, and the workload is steady enough to justify it. If self-hosting is a weekend project for one person, you've just created a bus factor.
  • Pay per seat when administration, procurement, and offboarding consistency matter more than unit price. That's a governance purchase, not an engineering one.
Hard gates, owner, expiry, exit
  • Gate 1 — owner. No named owner for the C1–C3 re-check, no standardization. The ledger decays the moment nobody owns it.
  • Gate 2 — spend. No paid commitment before C1, C2, and C7 have a recorded pass or fail.
  • Gate 3 — data class. If C7 comes back as an absolute no, this was never a ledger question. It's a stop.
  • Exit criteria. At expiry: standardize if 7 or more of 9 claims pass. Extend one cycle if 5–6 pass with a named owner. Stop if fewer than 5 pass, or if C7 fails.
Limitations, and who should skip this
  • Every number above is illustrative. A ledger is a conversation tool, not objective truth, and it will not settle a disagreement between people who want different answers.
  • Operator-stated terms — free model access, the free server option, the stated free grant, the open-source description — are dated 2026-10-16 and may change. The ledger's value is that it forces you to re-test rather than re-cite.
  • It does not price the human cost of a bad lane: review fatigue, morale, the senior engineer who quietly stops reviewing.
  • It assumes you can name R with some honesty. If your context assets live in one person's head, measure that problem first.

Skip this approach entirely if you're a solo developer with no shared context to rewrite (just use the thing for a week), if your data policy is already an absolute no, or if you want a benchmark verdict rather than a decision framework. Benchmarks tell you what a lane can do. Ledgers tell you what it would cost to leave.

If you want a lane that's cheap enough to falsify, MonkeyCode's repository is a reasonable place to run C1 and C2 against your own smoke set — the whole exercise costs about forty minutes, and that is the point of a zero-price offer.

One last question, and it's the only one that matters: which single claim in your ledger would flip your decision if it failed — and who is re-checking it on 2026-11-13?

items.title: [AINews] Agents disprove Polysemanticity; greatly improve Interpretability & Alignment
items.summary: A version of Muse Spark Open was released today, fulfilling their original promise but with a model weaker than their Spark 1.3. It’s also worth watching the Tesla Roadster demo - not strictly AI but nothing cooler than real life flying cars. Our title story today is a rare one on interpretability and alignment. We last caught up with Goodfire in Feb : and the bitter-lesson scaling of interpretability methods with Anthropic last year : And now Nick Cammarata at Goodfire has an important essay out stating his working theory that “ Neural Networks Are Already Clean ” — showing that many known cases of polysemanticity and superposition - causing tangled “knots” of weights that resist human interpretation - simply fall to further agentic analysis: Don’t take our word for it: and a global lowering of P(doom) seems worth celebrating: AI News for 10/14/2026-10/15/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Meta Releases Muse Spark Open, the Top-Scoring US Open-Weight Model Release : Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-total / 42B-active MoE with a 1M-token context window. It accepts text, image, video and audio input and is aimed at coding, long-horizon agents and multi-step reasoning ( announcement , Wang thread ). Lineage : Jack Rae says it was the first base model trained under the new MSL org, with additional training for the open release ( Rae ). Several posters describe it as roughly Muse Spark 1.2 level ( Yuchen Jin , TimDarcet ). License : The weights ship under the custom Muse Model License. It requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution and a separate agreement for Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue ( AA ). Nathan Lambert called the license “trash” ( natolambert ). Architecture : According to vLLM, the model has 62 decoder layers, all MoE, with 256 experts per layer and 8 active per token. A latent-MoE pooler projects the hidden state from 8,192 to 4,096 for expert computation and back again. Attention is hybrid: 46 layers use a 2,048-token sliding window and 16 attend to the full context. Image and video go through a Perception Encoder, and audio uses a separate 118M encoder ( vLLM arch ). Design comparison : Elie Bakouch notes that Muse is the only major US open model without shared experts. It also uses gated residuals, about 9 norms per layer and muP-like multipliers, including a router factor of 1/sqrt(number of experts) ( overview ). Independent measurement : Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index. That ranks it first among US open-weight models but behind GLM-5.3 (45) and Kimi K3 (44) ( AA , Rundown ). Strengths : It uses 40k output tokens per index task, the fewest among the nine highest-scoring open models. It also leads open models on AA-Omniscience (25). Weaknesses : It ranks last among those nine on the index’s four agentic evaluations. GLM-5.3’s entire 6-point lead comes from that agentic segment. Pricing and deployment : Launch pricing on Together, Fireworks and Baseten is $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.15 cached input). AA calculates this at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Together offers a free endpoint until Oct 18 ( Together ). Hardware footprint : BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts and comes to about 530GB, which runs on 4× Blackwell Ultra, 8× H200, or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX ( AA , Meta ). Ecosystem : llama.cpp had GGUF support on day 0 ( Delangue ), and Unsloth published quants, with UD-IQ1_S at 176GB ( Unsloth ). vLLM day-0 stack : vLLM support covers NVIDIA, AMD MI355X (FP8 and MXFP4) and TPU ( vLLM ). TPU throughput : Megakernels with DSpark speculation (acceptance length 6) exceed 650 tok/s on 4 TPU v7 chips and 960 tok/s on 8 ( hardware ). Speculator : Inferact trained a block-diffusion DSpark drafter that proposes up to 7 tokens per pass ( speculator ). LoRA RL : LoRA GRPO uses verl for training and vLLM for rollouts. Over 150 steps on 16 GB300s, AIME-2024 mean@8 rose from 0.56 to 0.85, with train-rollout KL around 2×10⁻⁴ ( RL ). Reception : Lambert says the release cuts the US–China open-model gap by about half ( natolambert ). Teortaxes calls it “grim at this param count” with “obsolete attention” and notes that Spark 1.3 is substantially stronger; these are attributed opinions ( teortaxes , Spark 1.3 comparison ). Other Model Launches: Nemotron 3.5, MAI-Base-2, Gemini 4 Argon, Image Models NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL : The model is a 120B / 12B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE VLM with a 1M-token context window and native MTP ( NVIDIA ). Training recipe : The tech summary describes a 1T-token distillation from a larger Nemotron 3 teacher, followed by agentic SWE mid-training on 65.4B tokens at 256K context. Post-training uses multi-teacher MOPD, and a final MTP-boosting step raises acceptance length by 21.8% to 4.61 ( Gordić ). Claimed results : NVIDIA reports 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro and 4,856 output tok/s per GPU on GB200. Independent evals : AA scores Super VL 26, the leading US open model before Muse, with NVFP4 within 0.1 points of BF16. The companion Nemotron 3.5 Bolt (74B-A9B, native 2-bit, 24GB) scores 21 ( AA ). Pricing : CoreWeave charges $0.25/$1.50 per 1M input/output tokens ( CoreWeave ). Microsoft MAI-Base-2 : Microsoft says it has a roughly 3T-parameter pre-trained base model, with post-training results to follow. It claims to match DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base on held-out code with 12× less training compute ( Suleyman , compute claim ). Technical blog details : The model has about 80B active parameters and a hybrid sliding-window design. It was trained with Muon and activation-gradient clipping on about 40T text tokens plus 10T multimodal tokens, using LR and weight-decay scaling laws ( Bakouch ). Training compute : The run used 16k GB200s over 38 days ( scaling01 ). Disputed comparison : Bakouch and teortaxes note that the bits-per-byte comparison uses MAI’s own validation data ( caveat ). Gemini 4 Argon evals and rollout : Epoch puts Argon at 165 on its Capabilities Index (ECI), level with Fable 5.1 and behind Opus 5.5 (167) and GPT-6 Astra (166). It ranks 8th on Math ECI and 6th on SWE ECI ( Epoch , domains ). ARC-AGI : Argon scores 97.5% on ARC-AGI-3 with a provider harness ($4.8K) and 49.8% with the standard harness ( ARC Prize ). Skepticism : Scaling01 argues that Argon underperforms on reliability and hallucination evals ( scaling01 ). Google claims : Argon optimized Gemma 4 E2B to a 2.85× vLLM speedup on A100, with 100% token parity ( Google ). Availability : Argon is now available in Antigravity for Pro subscribers, with a separate weekly quota ( Antigravity ). Anthropic and OpenAI product updates : Opus 5.5 fast mode : Fast mode is now GA with no waitlist, delivering up to 2.5× speed at $8/$40 per 1M tokens ( ClaudeDevs ). Claude Code Review : Code Review is GA for Team and Enterprise plans, with Quick, Standard and Deep levels ( ClaudeDevs ). GPT-Live-1.1 : OpenAI’s voice update adds multilingual voices and cuts filler, rolling out to ChatGPT, Codex and dots, with the API coming later ( OpenAI ). Image models : FLUX 3 Image Klein : Black Forest Labs released a 5.6B open-weight model with native 4K output, bounding-box control and multi-reference editing ( BFL ). Krea 3 : Krea claims 2K edits in under 8s at $0.06 per image ( Krea , pricing ). Interpretability, Safety and Eval Integrity Goodfire’s “already clean” essay : Nick Cammarata argues that most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters are legible. His 2023 OpenAI automated-interpretability effort found only about 2% legible, and he says many famous polysemantic examples were misread ( Cammarata , Goodfire ). Endorsements : tszzl and others called it a major moment ( tszzl ). Pushback : Neel Nanda says it does not change his cruxes. He still expects representational superposition and believes weak activations carry memorized facts ( Nanda ). A version of Muse Spark Open was released today, fulfilling their original promise but with a model weaker than their Spark 1.3. It’s also worth watching the Tesla Roadster demo - not strictly AI but nothing cooler than real life flying cars.

Our title story today is a rare one on interpretability and alignment. We last caught up with Goodfire in Feb:

and the bitter-lesson scaling of interpretability methods with Anthropic last year:

And now Nick Cammarata at Goodfire has an important essay out stating his working theory that “Neural Networks Are Already Clean” — showing that many known cases of polysemanticity and superposition - causing tangled “knots” of weights that resist human interpretation - simply fall to further agentic analysis:

Don’t take our word for it:

and a global lowering of P(doom) seems worth celebrating:

AI News for 10/14/2026-10/15/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

AI Twitter Recap

Meta Releases Muse Spark Open, the Top-Scoring US Open-Weight Model

  • Release: Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-total / 42B-active MoE with a 1M-token context window. It accepts text, image, video and audio input and is aimed at coding, long-horizon agents and multi-step reasoning (announcement, Wang thread).

    • Lineage: Jack Rae says it was the first base model trained under the new MSL org, with additional training for the open release (Rae). Several posters describe it as roughly Muse Spark 1.2 level (Yuchen Jin, TimDarcet).

    • License: The weights ship under the custom Muse Model License. It requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution and a separate agreement for Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue (AA). Nathan Lambert called the license “trash” (natolambert).

  • Architecture: According to vLLM, the model has 62 decoder layers, all MoE, with 256 experts per layer and 8 active per token. A latent-MoE pooler projects the hidden state from 8,192 to 4,096 for expert computation and back again. Attention is hybrid: 46 layers use a 2,048-token sliding window and 16 attend to the full context. Image and video go through a Perception Encoder, and audio uses a separate 118M encoder (vLLM arch).

    • Design comparison: Elie Bakouch notes that Muse is the only major US open model without shared experts. It also uses gated residuals, about 9 norms per layer and muP-like multipliers, including a router factor of 1/sqrt(number of experts) (overview).

  • Independent measurement: Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index. That ranks it first among US open-weight models but behind GLM-5.3 (45) and Kimi K3 (44) (AA, Rundown).

    • Strengths: It uses 40k output tokens per index task, the fewest among the nine highest-scoring open models. It also leads open models on AA-Omniscience (25).

    • Weaknesses: It ranks last among those nine on the index’s four agentic evaluations. GLM-5.3’s entire 6-point lead comes from that agentic segment.

    • Hardware footprint: BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts and comes to about 530GB, which runs on 4× Blackwell Ultra, 8× H200, or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX (AA, Meta).

    • Speculator: Inferact trained a block-diffusion DSpark drafter that proposes up to 7 tokens per pass (speculator).

    • LoRA RL: LoRA GRPO uses verl for training and vLLM for rollouts. Over 150 steps on 16 GB300s, AIME-2024 mean@8 rose from 0.56 to 0.85, with train-rollout KL around 2×10⁻⁴ (RL).

items.title: Tesla's flying Roadster is a weapon in the talent wars
items.summary: Tesla's second-generation Roadster is here. Did the automaker build it for shoppers or for its talent pipeline? Tesla Elon Musk stood onstage while the new Tesla Roadster (literally, and figuratively) flew by. Is it fully legal? Musk doesn't know. But is it a secret weapon in the ongoing talent wars? Very, very likely yes. Tesla's Roadster is back . Now, it kinda flies, and I'm not just being hyperbolic about its speed. (Although, I guess, that would be a fair read, too.) On Thursday, CEO Elon Musk unveiled the second-generation Roadster. It's capable of doing "crazy gymnastics," Musk said, like hopping off the ground and spinning in the air. The prototype also sprints from standing to 60 mph in 0.8 seconds, Tesla claims — and the automaker said the production model will be even quicker. Will the two-door electric sports car be street legal? Who knows. Instead, the car is accomplishing something more tangible — and more obviously Musk-like: make Tesla look like the kind of company that can build things other companies cannot. That's a useful message for Wall Street and for the engineers Tesla wants to hire. Tesla is already valued far more like a tech company than a traditional automaker. For years, investors have bet heavily on its ambitions in autonomy, artificial intelligence, robotics, and robotaxis. A flying (or, at least, hopping) Roadster does not prove those businesses will work, but it makes Tesla's technological ambitions more legible. Musk also has long treated product spectacles as recruiting events, too. At a 2019 Neuralink presentation, where he announced that the company had successfully implanted sensors in rats' brains, he said the "main reason for doing this presentation is recruiting." Ahead of Tesla's 2021 AI Day, Musk posted on X that "convincing the best AI talent to join Tesla is the sole goal." The Roadster reveal follows a very similar playbook. What better way to excite more techies than a flying car? Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, also agrees that Thursday's Roadster reveal was an exciting technical feat for up-and-coming tech talent: Two takeaways from tonight’s Roadster event. 1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can’t wait to bring $TSLA and $SPCX together. — Gene Munster (@munster_gene) October 16, 2026 Who knows if Tesla will even be able to bring this car to American roads. Musk said he doesn't even know. "I'm not sure it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said during the Thursday launch. When asked if the car was street legal, Musk responded: "Yeah, depends on your street." Either way, this car may not need to be a volume sales winner to be a hit for Tesla. It might just need to be the tech belle of the ball. Read the original article on Business Insider

  • Elon Musk stood onstage while the new Tesla Roadster (literally, and figuratively) flew by.
  • Is it fully legal? Musk doesn't know.
  • But is it a secret weapon in the ongoing talent wars? Very, very likely yes.

Tesla's Roadster is back. Now, it kinda flies, and I'm not just being hyperbolic about its speed.

(Although, I guess, that would be a fair read, too.)

On Thursday, CEO Elon Musk unveiled the second-generation Roadster. It's capable of doing "crazy gymnastics," Musk said, like hopping off the ground and spinning in the air. The prototype also sprints from standing to 60 mph in 0.8 seconds, Tesla claims — and the automaker said the production model will be even quicker.

Will the two-door electric sports car be street legal? Who knows.

Instead, the car is accomplishing something more tangible — and more obviously Musk-like: make Tesla look like the kind of company that can build things other companies cannot. That's a useful message for Wall Street and for the engineers Tesla wants to hire.

Tesla is already valued far more like a tech company than a traditional automaker.

For years, investors have bet heavily on its ambitions in autonomy, artificial intelligence, robotics, and robotaxis. A flying (or, at least, hopping) Roadster does not prove those businesses will work, but it makes Tesla's technological ambitions more legible.

Musk also has long treated product spectacles as recruiting events, too.

At a 2019 Neuralink presentation, where he announced that the company had successfully implanted sensors in rats' brains, he said the "main reason for doing this presentation is recruiting." Ahead of Tesla's 2021 AI Day, Musk posted on X that "convincing the best AI talent to join Tesla is the sole goal."

The Roadster reveal follows a very similar playbook. What better way to excite more techies than a flying car?

Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, also agrees that Thursday's Roadster reveal was an exciting technical feat for up-and-coming tech talent:

Two takeaways from tonight’s Roadster event. 1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can’t wait to bring $TSLA and $SPCX together.

— Gene Munster (@munster_gene) October 16, 2026

Who knows if Tesla will even be able to bring this car to American roads. Musk said he doesn't even know.

"I'm not sure it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said during the Thursday launch. When asked if the car was street legal, Musk responded: "Yeah, depends on your street."

Either way, this car may not need to be a volume sales winner to be a hit for Tesla. It might just need to be the tech belle of the ball.

items.title: Computers Made of Human Brain Tissue Identify Braille Letters In Breakthrough
items.summary: Scientists have made a breakthrough toward the mind-bending goal of creating computers made of brains by demonstrating that human neural tissue can classify letters of the Braille alphabet, according to a study published on Friday in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence . A team transmitted electrical signals corresponding to Braille letters to human brain organoids, which are living neural tissues derived from stem cells. The results revealed that a single organoid, consisting of about 10,000 neurons, could classify the letters with about 61 percent accuracy, while teams of three organoids reached 83 percent accuracy. “The human brain can perform incredibly complex information processing while consuming relatively little energy, and artificial neural networks were originally inspired by biological nervous systems,” said Tianyi Liu, a PhD candidate at Bristol University who led the new study, in an email to 404 Media. “If we've been trying to imitate biological neural networks all along, why not try using real biological neural networks directly?” she continued. “What kind of information processing capabilities might these tiny neural organoids have? Could they show some form of learning or adaptation? These are all questions we're very interested in.” The new study falls under the emerging field of organoid intelligence, which aims to use organoids as biological “wetware” for computing applications. Previous studies have established that organoids are capable of recognizing speech Japanese vowels or even playing the classic game Pong . Since Liu and her team specialize in how robots sense and respond to touch, they homed in on Braille as a way to convert tactile information into electrical stimuli that an organoid could receive, process, and classify. In their experimental setup, the researchers used a tactile sensor to scan data from the 26 letters of the Braille alphabet, which is built from arrangements of raised dots. This data was converted into electrical stimulation patterns that were fed to the organoids, which are smaller than a millimeter in scale and positioned on arrays that keep them alive. “Our original goal wasn't to prove that organoids could read Braille like humans, or that they were already ‘intelligent’ enough to understand Braille,” she added. “Rather, we wanted to use this task to explore whether real biological neural networks could participate in processing information from robotic tactile sensors.” The tactile sensor used to scan Braille letters. Image: Dr Benjamin Ward-Cherrier. In other words, the researchers aimed to discover if these stimulated inputs could be decoded by the organoids and returned back in discernable responses corresponding to the Braille letters. The results revealed that a single organoid could accurately classify the letters nearly two thirds of the time, while an "ensemble" of three organoids performed even better, with an accuracy of 83 percent. “We still don't know the exact mechanism behind this improvement,” Liu said. “Our hypothesis is that different organoids respond to the same stimulation in similar, but not identical, ways.” She added that “you can think of it as three people looking at the same object. Although they're all looking at the same thing, each person might notice different details. Some features might not be obvious to one person but could be quite easy for another to spot. By combining their observations, you might be able to make a more accurate and reliable judgement.” 🌘 Subscribe to 404 Media to get The Abstract , our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week. The results are undeniably trippy, conjuring up the classic scifi trope of a hyperintelligent brain-in-a-vat. But Liu emphasized that this was an open-loop experiment, meaning that the organoids only received initial inputs without getting new feedback about their performance on the tasks. For this reason, the study does not prove that the organoids actually learned Braille, or were altered in any permanent way, just that they could classify Braille letters after receiving the electrical inputs. “In the future, if we can build closed-loop systems where neural activity from the organoids actually participates in a robot's perception, decision making, and control, while the results of the robot's interactions with its environment are fed back to the organoids, we could begin to investigate whether these biological neural networks can adapt to new tasks through ongoing interaction,” she said. Liu also noted that while there are many potential advantages to organoid intelligence, there are plenty of limitations to biological computing systems. For example, organoids cannot be standardized, leading to natural variations that can complicate results, plus they have to be kept alive in cultures that are more difficult to maintain than electronic devices. “Compared with established computing chips, organoid systems still have a long way to go in terms of reliability, reproducibility, and scalability,” Liu said. Even so, organoid intelligence “gives us the opportunity to explore a way of computing that's very different from traditional computers,” she concluded.

items.title: DeepUnfolding_Agent: A Classical_Quantum Adaptive Control API
items.summary: Adaptive optimization workflows in machine learning, federated learning, quantum machine learning, and hybrid classical quantum systems often embed controller logic directly inside task specific training scripts. This coupling limits reuse, reproducibility, safety validation, and fair comparison across execution environments. This paper presents DeepUnfolding Agent, a schema-driven FastAPI platform that exposes deep unfolded adaptive control as an external software service. External executors register a strategy schema, submit round-level diagnostic variables, receive schema-bounded control actions, execute one optimization round, and return feedback for controller update. The framework separates controller intelligence from domain specific execution through a strategy registry, diagnostic to state adapter, controller factory, safety guard, executor abstraction, feedback update path, SQLite persistence layer, Docker deployment, and reproducible benchmark scripts. The implementation supports classical, quantum-aware, hybrid, Qiskit Aer, and optional IBM quantum processing execution pathways. We validate the software through unit, schema, API, safety, orchestration, Quantum execution, checkpointing, and Docker tests, and demonstrate external user fixed versus adaptive workflows across finance, healthcare, genomics, transport, noisy quantum simulation, and hardware backed IBM Quantum execution. The results show that DeepUnfolding-Agent provides a reusable and traceable adaptive control layer for heterogeneous optimization workflows. Our quantum experiments are interpreted as API level quantum control and hardware portability evidence.

items.title: PRISM: PRIvileged Sibling-guided Multi-Agent Topology Design
items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) based on large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful way to address complex problems, and their effectiveness depends critically on the collaboration topology that decides which agents participate and how they communicate. Recent work learns to generate this topology from the task query, fitting the generator to corpora of execution-verified graphs. The post-training method for such generators remains a limitation: a corpus lists the graphs that solved a query but never ranks them, leaving continued supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with no per-query preference to exploit. Without such a preference, the generator drifts toward the topologies the corpus contains most often rather than those that suit each query, so a gain on one task can come at a cost on another. We propose PRISM, which recovers per-query signal from the same corpus by learning with privileged information: a teacher reads, through a zero-initialized low-rank branch, a sibling graph that also solved the query and is unavailable at deployment, and the student matches its per-decision targets on trajectories the student samples itself. Across six diverse benchmarks PRISM improves over every topology-design baseline evaluated, and matched-teacher controls support the contribution of privileged query information. Code is available in this link.

items.title: A Large-Scale Dataset for Multi-Class Financial News Classification in Brazilian Portuguese
items.summary: The development of Financial Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems for Brazilian Portuguese is hindered by the scarcity of domain-specific datasets. To address this, we present a large-scale corpus of approximately 160,000 Brazilian Portuguese financial news articles collected from web sources. To establish initial benchmarks for a weakly supervised multi-class classification approach based on semantic similarity, we annotated subsets of this corpus both manually and using a Large Language Model (LLM). We evaluated three similarity-based methods -- cosine similarity, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and FAISS-based nearest-neighbor search -- using multilingual semantic embeddings. Our experiments reveal that the task is highly sensitive to label quality and class distribution. On the manually labeled subset, KNN achieved the best performance (47.3% accuracy, 31.9% F1-score), closely followed by FAISS. Conversely, on the LLM-annotated subset, while accuracy reached approximately 50%, F1-scores dropped to near 20%, highlighting the negative impact of label imbalance and noisy weak annotations. These findings establish foundational baselines for a challenging task, underscoring the critical need for high-quality manual annotations. Ultimately, this dataset and our preliminary results provide a reference point for future research in Brazilian Portuguese Financial NLP.

To establish initial benchmarks for a weakly supervised multi-class classification approach based on semantic similarity, we annotated subsets of this corpus both manually and using a Large Language Model (LLM). We evaluated three similarity-based methods -- cosine similarity, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and FAISS-based nearest-neighbor search -- using multilingual semantic embeddings. Our experiments reveal that the task is highly sensitive to label quality and class distribution. On the manually labeled subset, KNN achieved the best performance (47.3% accuracy, 31.9% F1-score), closely followed by FAISS. Conversely, on the LLM-annotated subset, while accuracy reached approximately 50%, F1-scores dropped to near 20%, highlighting the negative impact of label imbalance and noisy weak annotations. These findings establish foundational baselines for a challenging task, underscoring the critical need for high-quality manual annotations. Ultimately, this dataset and our preliminary results provide a reference point for future research in Brazilian Portuguese Financial NLP.

items.title: Real-time Chatbot Romance Scam Detection in Stage Classification
items.summary: Romance scam has become a serious problem via social media, and the improvement of artificial intelligence enable to fake identify easily. In the study, a chatbot has developed to detect romance scam in real-time through Line Messaging API. Using the seven stage theories in the social science field, the stages of romance scam can be detected through large language model. In addition, once a romance scam is detected, the chatbot provides explanations of the stage and prevention advices through large language model. The contribution of the work provides a practical application, and can be used in real scenario for reducing the risk of romance scam.

items.title: MeddeX: A Retrieval-Augmented LLaMA-3 System with Gemini Vision for Evidence-Backed Medical Report Analysis
items.summary: Modern healthcare generates increasingly complex medical reports that challenge clinical professionals in terms of time and interpretive burden. Manual review processes are slow, error-prone, and difficult to scale. This paper presents MeddeX, a Medical Report Analyzer that combines a QLoRA fine-tuned LLaMA-3 (8B) model with Retrieval-Augmented Gen eration (RAG) and a multimodal Gemini Vision layer to deliver accurate, concise, and evidence-backed summaries of medical documents. The system handles text-native PDFs, scanned image based PDFs, and direct radiological images through an intelligent hybrid extraction pipeline that includes a novel garbage-text detection mechanism for corrupted and UTF-16-encoded doc uments. Beyond single-report Q&A, MeddeX introduces report scoped retrieval for precise contextual grounding, an automated longitudinal report comparison engine, and a self-healing backfill pipeline that lazily processes legacy documents on demand. A FastAPI backend, Supabase vector store, and Next.js fron tend complete the end-to-end architecture. Evaluation against the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model demonstrates consistent improvements across ROUGE-1 (+9.2%), ROUGE-2 (+10.0%), ROUGE-L (+11.8%), BLEU (+71.4%), and BERTScore (+0.8%), validating the benefit of domain-specific fine-tuning. MeddeX represents a practical and robust step toward AI-assisted clinical decision support.

items.title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
items.summary: Long-horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end-task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400-step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re-injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate-recognition errors rise late in the episode -- from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 -- while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long-distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre-registered follow-ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re-aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length-matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.

items.title: Jev-as-a-Judge for RAG Claim Verification: Confidence-Gated Cascading Between a Non-Generative Verifier and a Frontier LLM
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation asks one question at volume: does this evidence support this claim? The answer is one bit, yet most pipelines obtain it from a text generator and pay generation prices for the prose wrapped around it. We compare a non-generative decision model, which returns a typed value from a declared enumeration together with a native probability and no text, against a frontier LLM configured as an engineer would deploy it for binary classification. Both answer the same 495 human-labelled claims from LLM-AggreFact, so every comparison is within-item. We report three things. First, the two systems are statistically indistinguishable on the metric this task is conventionally scored by, a paired difference of -0.56 points, Jev minus Astra, at a 187-fold cost difference. Second, that tie carries almost no information about deployment: the systems disagree on 15.2% of claims, and the cheaper one admits 23.2% of the claims annotators marked unsupported against the frontier model's 14.1%. A component whose job is to catch unsupported claims should be judged on that rate, and the conventional headline hides it. Third, because the errors differ they compose: routing the claims the cheap model is confident about and escalating the rest reaches 74.10 at USD 2.92 per thousand claims against 73.83 at USD 8.93, with the threshold chosen out of fold. But a matched random-escalation control at in-sample thresholds, spending the same budget by coin flip, does as well, so what buys the saving is the escalation share and not the probability that picks what to escalate. Measured against the cheap model it is built from, the cascade costs 61-fold more for 0.83 points, 95% CI [-3.36, 4.86], and it is the more permissive guard of the two. Equal accuracy conceals unequal errors. All predictions, prompts, pricing and code are released.

items.title: Exploring the Design Space of Permutation Diffusion LLMs
items.summary: Permutation generation with language models requires both text-conditioned ranking and a global one-to-one assignment between candidates and output positions. We study this problem through three diffusion-LLM parameterizations: hard-assignment prediction over shuffled candidate-index sequences, soft-assignment prediction over doubly stochastic matrices, and direct ordering-score prediction followed by sorting. The three families place permutation constraints at different stages of prediction and decoding and therefore support different training objectives and sampling procedures. We evaluate these designs on recommendation reranking across three Amazon domains with candidate sets of size 10 and 20. At one function evaluation, the hard- and soft-assignment variants achieve Recall@1 comparable to a constrained masked-diffusion baseline, whereas direct ordering-score prediction guarantees valid permutations without Hungarian assignment or Sinkhorn normalization. Additional function evaluations do not consistently improve ranking quality, and their effect depends strongly on the state representation and training objective. These results show that corruption, prediction parameterization, objective, and decoder should be designed jointly for permutation diffusion with language-model denoisers.

items.title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
items.summary: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.

items.title: CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary: Recent latent reasoning methods move beyond discrete Chain-of-Thought (CoT) by replacing sampled tokens with continuous soft embeddings or hidden states, enabling richer intermediate representations and preserving alternative reasoning paths. However, the need for latent reasoning varies across decoding steps: confident predictions favor discrete commitment, whereas ambiguous steps benefit from preserving multiple plausible alternatives. Existing approaches typically handle this variation through either global soft activation or hard switching based on uncertainty thresholds, treating latent intervention as an all-or-nothing decision rather than continuously adapting its strength. To address this limitation, we propose Competitive Token Selection (CoTS), a training-free framework that reframes latent intervention from binary mode selection into continuous allocation at the token level. CoTS uses the probability competition between the two most likely candidates to dynamically balance discrete commitment and soft exploration at each reasoning step. The second candidate represents the strongest alternative to the model's preferred continuation, so the separation between the two directly reflects the stability of the current discrete choice. When one candidate clearly dominates, CoTS keeps the representation close to the sampled discrete token to preserve a stable reasoning trajectory; as the competition strengthens, it increases the contribution of the soft representation to retain plausible alternatives. This competition-based allocation requires neither manually tuned switching thresholds nor mixing coefficients, and introduces no additional forward passes. Experiments across six reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that CoTS consistently outperforms standard CoT and state-of-the-art training-free latent reasoning methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/OkinoYu/CoTSReasoning.

items.title: Does Personalization Break Trust? Open-Set Rejection Calibration Under Few-Shot On-Device Intent Adaptation
items.summary: Always-on virtual assistants increasingly personalize on-device to new user-specific commands via few-shot fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA), but this adaptation is evaluated almost exclusively on whether it learns the new commands, not on whether the assistant can still recognize an input that matches none of its intents - the out-of-scope (OOS) rejection problem. We show that naive few-shot LoRA personalization degrades OOS-rejection AUROC (area under the ROC curve) on every one of five public intent-classification benchmarks (mean drop $0.055$--$0.258$, five seeds each), while in-scope accuracy is preserved. A scorer-invariant check shows part of this drop is an artifact of the standard confidence scorer's own miscalibration under adaptation, though a smaller, genuine effect remains under any scorer; we trace it to a measurable shrinkage of the embedding margin around known-intent regions (pooled Spearman rho=0.61$). A deployment-cheap fix is scoring rejection by Mahalanobis distance instead of softmax confidence without extra training/retraining recovers most of the lost quality on 3 of 5 datasets at no accuracy cost, beats two further OOD scoring baselines, and generalizes across shot count, LoRA rank, and a second base encoder. We report honestly where the fix falls short and release all code for reproducibility.

items.title: Reference-Guided Turn-Taking Style Transfer for Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models
items.summary: Full-duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take the floor, defining a conversational personality -- yet each set of weights encodes exactly one, which human speakers bracket rather than share. Existing controls mostly act from outside; none identifies the quantity that sets how much the model speaks. We identify it: a single late-layer residual-stream direction, the initiative vector, extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation. The same direction reads the decision, anticipating onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: scaled during generation, it moves speech ratio from 6-12% to 42-61% (no steering: 21-30%), consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora. A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker's turn-taking style to the model, and the transfer is reference-specific: swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93-98% of cases, whereas the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering. Turn-taking style is not frozen into the weights but a direction that can be read, shifted, and calibrated per person. Audio examples are available at https://elpsykongloo.github.io/initiative-vector/.

items.title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
items.summary: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.

items.title: APRiL: An Open-ended Benchmark for Chinese Social Awareness in Large Language Models
items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in social interactions, where appropriate responses require recognizing implicit cues, inferring mental states, identifying conflicts, and considering potential consequences. However, existing benchmarks often focus on specific social abilities, constrained task formats, or particular interaction settings, offering limited coverage of social awareness across diverse contexts. To address this gap, we introduce APRiL, an open-ended benchmark for Chinese social awareness with instance-specific rubrics. APRiL contains 2,196 Social Awareness Evaluation Instances across six categories and two complementary tasks: Social Scenario Analysis evaluates models' understanding of social cues, mental states, and conflict structures, while Socially Aware Response assesses whether they can translate this understanding into appropriate, natural responses. Experiments on 12 models from six families reveal a consistent understanding-to-response gap. Higher-quality scenario analyses improve responses, while weak analyses may reduce response quality. APRiL provides a systematic resource for advancing socially aware language models in Chinese contexts. Our data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/APRiL-05DE/.

items.title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
items.summary: Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower-resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross-lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five-language NF4-supervised directions successfully transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama-3.1-8B by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool-calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.

items.title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
items.summary: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

items.title: CoTranslator: Reverse to Forward Chain-of-Thought Translator for Reasoning Distillation
items.summary: Reasoning distillation requires chain-of-thought (CoT) data with correct answers, but obtaining such data efficiently remains challenging. Forward CoT generation (FCG) followed by rejection sampling (RS) produces verified, question-only responses, yet may require many teacher calls for difficult problems. Reverse CoT generation (RCG) is cheaper because it conditions on the known answer, but access to this answer can lead to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with the student's answer-free inference setting. We propose CoTranslator, which learns to translate reverse CoT responses toward the distribution of verified forward responses. Trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, it supports large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models evaluated on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to $5.82$ percentage points. For two 4B students, it retains $95.0\%$ of rejection sampling's average accuracy while using $35.9\%$ of its estimated compute. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by $4.88$ and $4.31$ percentage points for 4B and 8B students, respectively. These results show that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable approach to reasoning distillation.

items.title: PEDBench: Can Speech Models Detect Phonetic Errors?
items.summary: Phonetic error detection (PED) aims to identify phoneme-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions and is essential for educational and clinical speech assessment and intervention. Despite recent advances in speech models for phoneme recognition, their ability to reliably detect fine-grained phonetic errors remains unclear because of a lack of high-quality evaluation data. To address this gap, we introduce PEDBench, the first PED benchmark spanning a continuum from natural to controlled speech. It comprises real-world recordings of spoken errors made by children (N=334), scripted error productions by human actors (N=1,188), and synthetic error productions generated using phone-conditioned text-to-speech (N=1,083). All phonetic annotations were transcribed and verified by two phonetically trained annotators. Our evaluation of 13 state-of-the-art speech models shows that they fail to reliably detect phonetic errors, even under controlled conditions with acted and synthetic speech, where acoustic variability is reduced. The models also exhibit low precision, frequently misclassifying correctly pronounced phonemes as errors. Our speech-language models, fine-tuned on synthetic data, outperform commercial and open-source baselines on word-level PED, although a sim-to-real domain gap remains. We plan to publicly release our code and recipes, along with our acted and synthetic datasets, to support the development of more accurate PED systems.
